Let obs(G) denote the minimum number of simple polygonal obstacles in a plane obstacle representation of a graph G, where the vertices of G are represented by points in the plane, all represented points and obstacle vertices are in general position, and uv is an edge of G if and only if the straight-line segment joining the points for u and v avoids every obstacle. Define obs(n) := max{obs(G) : |V(G)| = n}. Improve the lower bound obs(n) = Ω(n/log^2 n).

For each integer h>1, determine the minimum number of vertices of a finite graph G with obstacle number obs(G)=h, where obs(G) denotes the minimum number of simple polygonal obstacles in a plane obstacle representation of G: the vertices of G are represented by points in the plane, two vertices are adjacent if and only if the segment joining their representative points avoids every obstacle, and all representative points and obstacle vertices are assumed to be in general position so that no such segment passes through another representative point or an obstacle vertex. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

For every finite simple planar graph G, is the obstacle number of G equal to 1; that is, does G admit an obstacle representation in the Euclidean plane with a single simple polygonal obstacle, where the vertices of G are represented by points and uv is an edge of G if and only if the straight-line segment joining the points for u and v avoids the obstacle, under the general-position assumption used in Section 2.5 that such segments pass through neither other vertex-points nor obstacle vertices?

Given a finite graph G in adjacency-matrix form, decide whether there exists a finite set S = {s_1, ..., s_m} of pairwise disjoint line segments in the Euclidean plane, with endpoint set P = {a_1, b_1, ..., a_m, b_m}, such that G is exactly the segment visibility graph of S: V(G) is in bijection with P; for endpoints p,q in P that belong to distinct segments, pq is an edge of G if and only if the straight segment joining p and q meets no segment of S except possibly at p and q (in particular, it does not pass through any other endpoint and does not graze along any segment of S); and for each i, the two endpoints a_i and b_i of s_i are adjacent in G.

Characterize precisely the finite undirected graphs G that occur as segment visibility graphs (segment endpoint visibility graphs) of finite sets S = {s_1, ..., s_n} of pairwise disjoint line segments in the plane: if s_i has endpoints p_i and q_i, then V(G) = {p_1, q_1, ..., p_n, q_n}, each pair p_iq_i is an edge of G, and for endpoints x and y lying on different segments, xy is an edge of G exactly when the straight segment joining x and y is otherwise disjoint from every segment of S, under the paper's convention that it may neither pass through another endpoint nor graze along a segment.

Let G be a graph that is known to be the segment visibility graph (equivalently, segment endpoint visibility graph) of some finite set S of pairwise disjoint line segments in the plane. Here the vertices of G correspond bijectively to the endpoints of the segments in S; two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when the straight segment joining the corresponding endpoints does not intersect any segment of S, with the additional convention that this line of sight may neither pass through another endpoint nor graze along a segment; and, for each segment of S, the two vertices corresponding to its endpoints are also adjacent. Construct such a set S of pairwise disjoint line segments in the plane whose segment visibility graph is exactly G.

Given only the adjacency matrix of a graph G, under the promise that G is the segment visibility graph of some finite set S of pairwise disjoint line segments in the plane—where V(G) is the set of all segment endpoints, and two vertices are adjacent iff they are the two endpoints of the same segment of S or the straight segment joining the corresponding endpoints meets no segment of S (in particular, it neither passes through another endpoint nor grazes along a segment)—can one identify, in time polynomial in |V(G)|, a Hamiltonian cycle of G, i.e. a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

Let S be a set of pairwise disjoint line segments in the plane, and let G be its segment visibility graph: the vertices of G are the endpoints of the segments of S; two vertices u and v are adjacent if the straight segment uv does not intersect any segment of S (with visibility not allowed to pass through another endpoint or graze a segment), and, in addition, the two endpoints of each segment of S are joined by an edge. Given only the adjacency matrix of G, determine which edges of G are exactly the distinguished edges joining the two endpoints of the original segments of S.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph G to be a unit bar visibility graph; that is, for G to admit a bar visibility representation by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane, one for each vertex of G, such that uv is an edge of G if and only if the bars for u and v have an unobstructed vertical line of sight between them, with the additional restriction that all bars have the same length.

Given a finite graph G, is it NP-complete to decide whether G is a unit bar visibility graph; that is, whether G admits a bar visibility representation by pairwise disjoint horizontal line segments in the plane, all of identical length, such that two vertices of G are adjacent if and only if their corresponding bars have an unobstructed vertical line of sight?

For a fixed integer k ≥ 0, characterize the graphs G for which there exists a set S of pairwise disjoint horizontal line segments in the plane, in one-to-one correspondence with V(G), such that for distinct vertices u,v ∈ V(G), uv ∈ E(G) if and only if there is a vertical segment with one endpoint on the bar for u and the other on the bar for v that intersects at most k other bars of S. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

Fix a nonnegative integer k. A graph is a bar k-visibility graph if its vertices can be represented by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane so that two vertices are adjacent exactly when some vertical segment joining the corresponding bars intersects at most k other bars. It is known that no triangle-free non-planar graph can occur as a subgraph of a bar k-visibility graph. Is there any other class of graphs that is likewise forbidden as a subgraph of bar k-visibility graphs?

For each integer k ≥ 5, does there exist a connected, non-complete simple graph G that is (2k + 2)-regular and admits a bar k-visibility representation in the plane; that is, can V(G) be represented by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars so that uv ∈ E(G) if and only if some vertical segment joining the bars for u and v intersects at most k other bars?

For some nonnegative integer k, do there exist an integer d with d ≥ 2k + 3 and a finite simple graph G such that G is d-regular and G is a bar k-visibility graph; that is, G admits a representation by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane in which two vertices are adjacent if and only if there exists a vertical segment joining the corresponding bars that intersects at most k other bars? citeturn7view0turn17search0

For each integer k≥0, improve the current general upper bound χ(G)≤6k+6 for bar k-visibility graphs: determine a smaller universal function f(k) such that every finite graph G that admits a representation by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane, with uv∈E(G) if and only if some vertical segment joining the bars for u and v intersects at most k other bars, satisfies χ(G)≤f(k). ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

For each integer k >= 1, find a universal function f(k) with f(k) < 2k(9k-1) such that every bar k-visibility graph G has thickness theta(G) <= f(k), where G is a bar k-visibility graph if it admits a strong visibility representation by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane in which two vertices are adjacent if and only if there exists a vertical sightline between their bars that intersects at most k other bars, and where theta(G) is the minimum number of planar graphs whose union is G.

For each fixed integer k >= 0 and n >= 1, determine the extremal function cr_k(n) = max{cr(G) : G is a finite simple n-vertex bar k-visibility graph}, where cr(G) denotes the minimum number of edge crossings in a drawing of G in the plane, and G is a bar k-visibility graph if its vertices can be represented by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane such that uv is an edge of G if and only if there exists a vertical segment joining the bars for u and v that intersects at most k other bars.

For a fixed nonnegative integer k, what is the largest possible graph-theoretic genus of a bar k-visibility graph, where a bar k-visibility graph is a graph that admits a representation by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane such that two vertices are adjacent exactly when some vertical segment joining the corresponding bars intersects at most k other bars? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

Characterize exactly the finite graphs G that admit a rectangle visibility representation, namely, a realization of the vertices of G by closed isothetic rectangles in the plane with pairwise disjoint interiors such that two distinct vertices u and v are adjacent in G if and only if their corresponding rectangles are vertically or horizontally visible from each other by a beam of unobstructed visibility of finite width. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

Given a finite simple graph G in adjacency-matrix form, decide whether there exists a simple polygon P in the plane and a bijection between V(G) and the vertices of P such that, for every two distinct vertices u,v in V(G), uv is an edge of G if and only if the line segment joining the corresponding vertices of P lies entirely within P; here visibility is understood in the paper's sense, so the segment may pass through a reflex vertex or graze along a polygonal edge.

Given a finite graph G in adjacency-matrix form, consider the decision problem of determining whether there exists a simple polygon P in the plane such that the vertices of G are in bijection with the vertices of P and two vertices of G are adjacent if and only if the line segment joining the corresponding vertices of P lies entirely within P (with visibility interpreted as in the paper, so the segment may graze a polygon edge or pass through a reflex vertex). Does this recognition problem for vertex visibility graphs of simple polygons belong to NP?

Given a simple undirected graph G = (V,E) in adjacency-matrix form and a Hamiltonian cycle C = (v1,v2,...,vn,v1) of G on the same labeled vertex set, decide whether there exists a simple polygon P whose vertices are v1,v2,...,vn in the cyclic boundary order prescribed by C and such that, for every distinct i,j, the edge vivj is in E if and only if the straight-line segment joining the corresponding vertices of P lies entirely within P; that is, whether G is the vertex visibility graph of a simple polygon whose boundary corresponds to the given Hamiltonian cycle C.

Give necessary and sufficient conditions for a finite simple graph G to be isomorphic to the vertex visibility graph of some simple polygon P in the plane; that is, characterize exactly those graphs for which the vertices of G can be put in bijection with the vertices of P so that two vertices are adjacent in G if and only if the straight-line segment joining the corresponding polygon vertices lies entirely within P, with visibility interpreted as in the paper (segments may pass through a reflex vertex or graze along a polygon edge).

Given only a graph G, promised to be the vertex visibility graph of some simple polygon P in the plane, construct a simple polygon P whose vertices are in bijection with V(G) and such that, for every pair of vertices u,v in V(G), uv is an edge of G if and only if the straight-line segment joining the corresponding vertices of P lies entirely within P, with visibility understood as in the paper (in particular, the segment may pass through a reflex vertex or graze a polygon edge), and without assuming any additional input such as the Hamiltonian cycle corresponding to the boundary of P. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

Let G be given, with the promise that G is the vertex visibility graph of some simple polygon P. Here the vertices of G correspond to the vertices of P, and two vertices are adjacent exactly when the line segment joining the corresponding polygon vertices lies entirely inside P (as defined in the paper, allowing the segment to pass through a reflex vertex or graze along a polygon edge). Since G may contain several Hamiltonian cycles, determine which Hamiltonian cycle of G is the one induced by the cyclic order of the vertices on the boundary of P.

Given a graph G = G(P) that is promised to be the vertex visibility graph of a simple polygon P in the plane—that is, V(G) is the vertex set of P and two vertices u,v are adjacent in G exactly when the segment uv lies entirely within P, with visibility allowed to pass through reflex vertices or graze along polygon edges—design a polynomial-time algorithm and an absolute constant c >= 1 that outputs a dominating set D of G such that every vertex of G is either in D or adjacent to a vertex of D, and |D| <= c * OPT(G), where OPT(G) is the minimum size of a dominating set of G.

Given as input a graph G that is the vertex visibility graph of a simple polygon P and a Hamiltonian cycle C of G corresponding to the boundary of P, compute a maximum hidden vertex set of G; that is, find a subset H ⊆ V(G) of maximum cardinality such that no two vertices of H are adjacent in G.

Given a graph G promised to be the vertex visibility graph of a simple polygon P—that is, V(G) is the vertex set of P and two vertices are adjacent exactly when the corresponding polygon vertices are mutually visible inside P—design a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for the maximum hidden set problem: compute a hidden set H ⊆ V(G), where a hidden set means an independent set of G, whose size is within a provable approximation factor of the maximum possible hidden-set size. Do not assume that the Hamiltonian cycle corresponding to the boundary of P is provided as part of the input.

Given only the adjacency matrix of a graph G that is known a priori to be the vertex visibility graph of some simple polygon P - meaning that V(G) corresponds to the vertices of P and two vertices of G are adjacent exactly when the straight-line segment joining the corresponding polygon vertices lies entirely inside P, with visibility allowed to pass through a reflex vertex or graze along a polygon edge - and with no Hamiltonian cycle corresponding to the boundary of P provided as part of the input, compute a maximum-cardinality clique of G.

For each integer n >= 3, let N(n) denote the number of pairwise non-isomorphic vertex visibility graphs G(P) arising from simple polygons P with n vertices, where G(P) has one vertex for each vertex of P and two vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining the corresponding polygon vertices lies entirely in P (with the paper’s convention that the segment may pass through a reflex vertex or graze along a polygon edge). Determine asymptotically sharper lower and upper bounds for N(n), improving on the bounds 2^(n-4) <= N(n) <= 2^{O(n log n)} quoted in Section 4.8. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

Let G be the vertex visibility graph of a simple polygon P with n vertices; that is, V(G) corresponds to the vertices of P, and two vertices of G are adjacent exactly when the segment joining the corresponding polygon vertices lies entirely within P. Must there exist some simple polygon P' realizing the same visibility graph G whose vertex coordinates all lie in Z^2 and whose x- and y-coordinates each have bit-length bounded by a polynomial in n? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

For n-vertex visibility graphs G of simple polygons, determine the tight worst-case asymptotic order, as a function of n, of the minimum number of bits used by an optimal covering set of G, where a covering set is a family of subgraphs of G, each of which is either a clique or a complete bipartite graph, and every edge of G lies in at least one member of the family. In the notation implicit in §4.9, close the gap between the recorded O(n log^4 n) upper bound and Omega(n log^2 n) lower bound.

Given the visibility graph G of a simple polygon with n vertices, construct in polynomial time a covering set F={H1,...,Ht} such that each Hi is either a clique or a complete bipartite subgraph of G, every edge of G belongs to at least one Hi, and the total number of bits needed to encode F matches, up to order notation, the tight asymptotic bound for optimal covering-set representations of n-vertex visibility graphs of simple polygons sought in Open Problem 42. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1012.5187))

Let P be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane. For distinct points v,w,x in P, say that x blocks v and w if x lies in the interior of the segment joining v and w; say that v and w are visible with respect to P if no point of P blocks them. Call P k-blocked if its points can be coloured with colours 1,...,k so that for every distinct v,w in P, the points v and w receive the same colour if and only if some other point of P blocks them (equivalently, v and w receive different colours if and only if they are visible). Is it true that for every integer k at least 1 there exists an integer n=n(k) such that every k-blocked point set P satisfies |P|<=n?

For every integer k >= 1, if P is a finite set of points in the plane and each point of P is assigned one of k colours so that for every distinct v,w in P, the points v and w receive the same colour if and only if some third point of P lies in the interior of the segment vw, must |P| <= k^2?

For every positive integer k, if P is a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane together with an assignment of one of k colours to each point such that, for any distinct points v,w in P, the points v and w receive the same colour if and only if there exists a third point x in P lying in the interior of the segment vw (equivalently, v and w are visible with respect to P exactly when they receive different colours), must every colour class of P contain at most k points?

Let G be the visibility graph of a finite set P of points in the plane, with no restriction on collinearities, where two vertices are adjacent if and only if the segment joining the corresponding points contains no other point of P. Must the vertex-connectivity κ(G) satisfy κ(G) ≥ (2δ(G)+1)/3, where δ(G) is the minimum degree of G?

Let k be an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic, let S={p_1,...,p_r} be a finite set of distinct points in P^N_k, and let f:X->P^N_k be the blow-up of p_1,...,p_r with exceptional divisors E_1,...,E_r. Write H=f^*(O_{P^N}(1)), and for each integer m>=1 define a(S,m)=min{d in Z : h^0(X,O_X(dH-m(E_1+...+E_r)))>0}. Let e(S)=lim_{m->infinity} a(S,m)/m. Develop computational or conceptual methods for evaluating, estimating, or bounding the asymptotic effectivity invariant e(S).

Let k be an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic, let N>=1, and let S={p1,...,pr} be a finite set of distinct points in P^N_k. For each integer m>=1, define a(S,m) to be the least integer d such that there exists a degree-d hypersurface in P^N_k vanishing to order at least m at every point of S, and set e(S)=lim_{m->infinity} a(S,m)/m. Must one always have (a(S,1)+N-1)/N <= e(S)?

Let k be an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic, let S = {p1, ..., pr} be a finite set of distinct points in P^N_k, and let f: X -> P^N be the blow-up of P^N at p1, ..., pr with exceptional divisors E1, ..., Er. Write H = f^*(O_{P^N}(1)) and, for integers d and m > 0, set L(d,m) = dH - m(E1 + ... + Er). Define a(S,m) = min{ d in Z : h^0(X, L(d,m)) > 0 } and e(S) = lim_{m->infinity} a(S,m)/m. Chudnovsky's conjectural bound in this setting is (a(S,1) + N - 1)/N <= e(S). If equality holds in the stronger finite-level form a(S,m)/m = (a(S,1) + N - 1)/N for some positive integer m, must S be either contained in a hyperplane or a star configuration? Likewise, if e(S) = (a(S,1) + N - 1)/N, must S be either contained in a hyperplane or a star configuration? Here 'star configuration' means that there exist s hyperplanes in P^N such that at most N of them meet at any single point and S is exactly the set of the binom(s,N) points where N of those hyperplanes meet.

Over an algebraically closed field k of arbitrary characteristic, let f: X -> P^N be the blow-up of distinct points p_1, ..., p_r with exceptional divisors E_1, ..., E_r, and let H = f^*(O_{P^N}(1)). For the integral divisor D = dH - sum_{i=1}^r m_i E_i on X, is there a way to determine whether O_X(D) is semi-effective; that is, whether there exists an integer n > 0 such that h^0(X, O_X(nD)) > 0?

Let k be a field, let I subset k[x,y] be a monomial ideal of finite colength n, and set Z = Spec(k[x,y]/I) (equivalently, I is (x,y)-primary and Z is supported at the origin). For every irreducible smooth projective surface S over k, let Hilb_I^S subset Hilb^n(S) denote the irreducible constructible locus whose closed points are the subschemes Y subset S that are isomorphic to Z. Describe Hilb_I^S: in particular, is Hilb_I^S locally closed in Hilb^n(S), and what closure/incidence (adjacency) relations occur among these monomial-type loci inside the Hilbert scheme?

Let k be a field, let I ⊂ k[x,y] be a monomial ideal of finite colength n = dim_k(k[x,y]/I), and set Z = Spec(k[x,y]/I). For an irreducible smooth projective surface S over k, let Hilb_I^S ⊂ Hilb^n(S) denote the irreducible constructible locus whose closed points are the subschemes Y ⊂ S isomorphic to Z. If Y is a general point of Hilb_I^S and D is a divisor on S, what can one say, or conjecture, about the cohomology of I_Y tensor O_S(D)? In particular, find conditions on S, I, and D ensuring that h^0(S, I_Y tensor O_S(D)) = max{0, h^0(S, O_S(D)) - n}, so that h^1 and h^2 are then determined by Riemann-Roch and duality.

Let k be an algebraically closed field, let S = P^2_k, and let I = (y, x^r)^m subset k[x,y], where r,m are natural numbers with r > 9. Set Z = Spec(k[x,y]/I), let n = dim_k k[x,y]/I, and let Hilb_I S subset Hilb^n(S) be the irreducible constructible locus whose closed points are the subschemes Y subset S isomorphic to Z. If Y is a general point of Hilb_I S, and if I_Y denotes the ideal sheaf of Y, is it true that for every integer d > 0 one has dim_k H^0(S, I_Y tensor O_{P^2_k}(d)) = max{0, binom(d+2,2) - r binom(m+1,2)}?

Let k be a field, let S = P^2_k, let I = (y, x^r)^m be the monomial ideal in k[x,y] with natural numbers r,m and r > 9, and let Z = Spec(k[x,y]/I). Write n = dim_k(k[x,y]/I), and let Hilb_I^S be the irreducible constructible subset of Hilb^n(S) whose closed points parameterize subschemes Y subset S isomorphic to Z. If Y is a general member of Hilb_I^S and H is the hyperplane class on S, is it true that for every integer d with d <= m sqrt(r) one has H^0(S, I_Y ⊗ O_S(dH)) = 0? ([math.colostate.edu](https://www.math.colostate.edu/~miranda/preprints/RecentDevelopments6_12.pdf))

Let pi: X -> P^2 be the blow-up of finitely many generic points p_1, ..., p_s in P^2, and let C subset X be any prime divisor (equivalently, any reduced irreducible curve on X). Must one have h^1(X, O_X(C)) = 0?

Let pi: X -> P^2 be the blow-up of points p_1,...,p_s, and let C be a prime divisor on X. In the form of the SHGH conjecture stated in the paper, if the points p_1,...,p_s are generic, then h^1(X, O_X(C)) = 0. How can one remove the genericity assumption on the points in this SHGH vanishing statement?

As posed in Conjecture 2.5.3: if X is a smooth projective surface, assumed either to be rational or to be defined over a field of characteristic 0, does there exist a constant c_X depending only on X such that for every prime divisor C ⊂ X one has h^1(X, O_X(C)) ≤ c_X h^0(X, O_X(C))?

Let X be a projective manifold (smooth projective variety) with large algebraic fundamental group, meaning that for every irreducible subvariety Z ⊂ X with normalization ν: Z^ν → X, the image of ν_*: hat pi_1(Z^ν) → hat pi_1(X) is infinite. Let L be an ample line bundle on X, and let N > 0. (1) Does there exist a finite étale cover p: X' → X such that the Seshadri number ε(p^*L; x) is greater than N for every point x ∈ X'? (2) Does there exist a finite étale cover p: X' → X such that, writing p-tilde := p × p: X' × X' → X × X, letting D' ⊂ X' × X' be the diagonal, and letting p_1, p_2: X × X → X be the two projections, the Seshadri number of p-tilde^*(p_1^*L ⊗ p_2^*L) along D' is greater than N? (3) If the answer to (1) or (2) is negative or unclear, what additional condition on the fundamental group of X guarantees an affirmative answer?

Let A = {H_1, ..., H_d} be a complex projective hyperplane arrangement in P^n, with H_i = V(alpha_i), and let R = C[y_1, ..., y_d]. For each linear dependence Lambda: sum_{j=1}^k c_{i_j} alpha_{i_j} = 0 among the defining linear forms, define f_Lambda = sum_{j=1}^k c_{i_j} y_{i_1} ... hat(y_{i_j}) ... y_{i_k}, let I(A) be the ideal of R generated by all such f_Lambda, and set C(A) = R / I(A). It is known that reg C(A) <= n for A subset P^n. Do the results for arrangements of lines in P^2 generalize to higher dimension? More specifically, can one give an explicit description of the graded Betti numbers beta_{i,j}(C(A)) = dim_C Tor_i^R(C(A), C)_{i+j} in terms of the geometry of the arrangement A?

Let X be a nonsingular variety of dimension n over the complex numbers, let Z ⊆ X be a reduced subscheme with radical ideal sheaf I = I_Z ⊆ O_X, and let e = bight(I), the maximum codimension of a component of V(I). Is it true that for every positive integer r and every integer m ≥ re − (e − 1), the symbolic power I^(m) is contained in the ordinary power I^r? ([impan.pl](https://www.impan.pl/~pragacz/bauer.pdf))

Let (R, \mathfrak m) be a regular local ring of Krull dimension n, let I \subseteq R be an arbitrary ideal of big height e := \operatorname{bight}(I) = \max\{\operatorname{ht} P : P is a minimal prime of I\}, and for each integer s \ge 1 let I^{(s)} := \bigcap_{P \in \operatorname{Ass}(R/I)} (I^s R_P \cap R) denote the s-th symbolic power of I. Is it true that for every integer r \ge 1, the following four uniform containments hold whenever the indicated lower bound on s is satisfied: (1) I^{(s)} \subseteq \mathfrak m^{rn-r} I^r for all s > rn; (2) I^{(s)} \subseteq \mathfrak m^{rn-r-(n-1)} I^r for all s > rn-(n-1); (3) I^{(s)} \subseteq \mathfrak m^{re-r} I^r for all s > re; and (4) I^{(s)} \subseteq \mathfrak m^{re-r-(e-1)} I^r for all s > re-(e-1)?

Let X be the blow-up of P^2 at r distinct points, where r is arbitrary and the points are in arbitrary position, and let L be an effective nef divisor on X. Is it true that at least one of the following holds: (a) there exists an integer m>1 such that H^1(X,O_X(mL))=0 (and, if the blown-up points are in general position, one expects that m=1 should suffice); or (b) there exists a possibly reducible curve C on X such that the complete linear system |L-C| is nonempty, the arithmetic genus p_a(C) is positive, and L.C=0?

Let X be a smooth projective surface over a field of characteristic zero. Does there exist a positive constant b(X), depending only on X, such that for every reduced, irreducible curve C contained in X, the self-intersection number of C satisfies C^2 > -b(X)?

Let X be a smooth projective surface in characteristic zero, and let g > 0 be a fixed integer. Does there exist a positive constant b(X,g) such that every reduced, irreducible curve C ⊂ X of geometric genus g (equivalently, such that the normalization of C has genus g) satisfies the self-intersection bound C^2 > -b(X,g)? ([math.colostate.edu](https://www.math.colostate.edu/~miranda/preprints/RecentDevelopments6_12.pdf))

Conjecture 3.3.5 (Very weak bounded negativity): Let X be a smooth projective surface over a field of characteristic zero, and let g ≥ 0 be an integer. Does there exist a positive constant b_s(X,g) such that C^2 ≥ -b_s(X,g) for every irreducible smooth curve C ⊂ X of geometric genus g, where C^2 denotes the self-intersection of C on X?

In the characteristic-zero bounded-negativity setting of Section 3.3, let f:Y->B be a morphism from a smooth projective threefold to a smooth curve such that the general fibre is a smooth surface. Fix an integer g>0. Does there exist a constant b(Y,g)>0 such that every vertical curve C subset Y with f(C) a point and geometric genus g (i.e. the genus of the normalization of C) satisfies C^2 > -b(Y,g), where C^2 is computed in the fibre of f containing C? ([math.colostate.edu](https://www.math.colostate.edu/~miranda/preprints/RecentDevelopments6_12.pdf))

Let X be a smooth projective surface. For an ample line bundle L on X and a point x in X, define epsilon(L,x) := inf{(L.C)/mult_x(C) : C subset X is an irreducible curve passing through x}, and define epsilon(L) := inf{epsilon(L,x) : x in X}. Is the global Seshadri constant epsilon(X) := inf{epsilon(L) : L in Pic(X) is ample} always strictly positive?

Weighted Bounded Negativity Conjecture. Let X be a smooth projective surface over a field of characteristic zero. Does there exist a positive constant b_w(X), depending only on X, such that for every irreducible curve C ⊂ X and every big and nef line bundle H on X with H·C > 0, one has the intersection-theoretic inequality C^2 > -b_w(X)(H·C)^2?

Let X be a smooth projective surface over a field of characteristic zero. Must there exist a positive constant b'(X), depending only on X, such that every reduced, possibly reducible curve C ⊂ X satisfies the self-intersection bound C^2 > -b'(X)?

Let π:X→P^2 be the blow-up of r general points, let D be an effective divisor on X, and let E⊂X be a (-1)-curve. Let ρ:H^0(X, OX(D))→H^0(E, OE(D|E)) be the restriction map, and let |D|E⊂|OE(D|E)| denote its image linear system on E. Is it true that: (1) every base point of |D|E arises from a fixed curve component (base curve) of the complete linear system |D| meeting E; and (2) if |D| has no fixed component, then ρ has maximal rank? ([math.colostate.edu](https://www.math.colostate.edu/~miranda/preprints/RecentDevelopments6_12.pdf))

In the projective plane P^2, let L(d | m1, ..., mn) denote the linear system of homogeneous polynomials of degree d passing through n generic points with multiplicities at least m1, ..., mn. Let L_col(d | m1, ..., mr; m_{r+1}, ..., mn) denote the analogous linear system in which the first r base points are collinear and the n points are otherwise general. For integers 1 <= r <= n, is it true that whenever d > m1 + ... + mr, the system L(d | m1, ..., mn) is nonempty if and only if L_col(d | m1, ..., mr; m_{r+1}, ..., mn) is nonempty? ([math.colostate.edu](https://www.math.colostate.edu/~miranda/preprints/RecentDevelopments6_12.pdf))

In the context of Tevatron injection measurements in 2005—where proton (N_p) and anti-proton (N_a) bunches underwent 71 long-range parasitic interactions and one head-on collision per turn with fixed horizontal and vertical tunes Q_p, Q_a, fixed beam separation d_{a−p}, fixed longitudinal emittance ε_L, fixed physical aperture distance D_{apert}, and over a fixed injection time t—what theoretical model can explain the empirical scaling law ΔN_p/N_p ∝ N_a · (ε_a)^2 · (Q′)^2, namely the linear dependence of the proton loss rate on the opposing anti-proton bunch intensity N_a and the quadratic dependence on the anti-proton transverse emittance ε_a and machine chromaticity Q′?

Why did the vertical beam–beam tune-shift parameter ξ_y in the 8 GeV electron (HER) ring at KEKB saturate at only ≃0.09 under single-crab-cavity operation—despite strong–strong beam–beam simulations predicting ξ_y≃0.15 for head-on (crab) collisions with a horizontal tune near half-integer (Section 2.8)—and what dynamic limitations, such as the physical aperture reduction around the crab cavities due to dynamic beta and dynamic emittance effects and residual chromatic x–y coupling at the interaction point (mitigated by skew-sextupole magnets), were identified or remain unaccounted for as the mechanisms limiting further luminosity increase?

In the CERN SPS proton–anti-proton collider, dedicated measurements in head-on collisions (two collisions per turn) showed that a proton bunch with rms normalized emittance ≈5.5 π mm·mrad was insensitive to the 13th and 16th order betatron resonances when colliding with an anti-proton bunch of ≈7.5 π mm·mrad (emittance ratio ≈4:1), but became highly sensitive to those same resonances after the anti-proton bunch was scraped to ≈5.5 π mm·mrad (emittance ratio ≈1:1), even though the per-interaction-point beam–beam tune shift parameter ξ was reduced by ≈40%. Existing scaling laws (e.g., equation (3) in the paper) fail to predict this behavior. What quantitative theoretical model can accurately reproduce and explain this enhanced proton loss sensitivity to the 13th and 16th order resonances under matched emittance conditions with reduced beam–beam parameter?

In the HERA proton–electron collider, Shiltsev and Val (2010) report that to maintain tolerable proton beam lifetime and background rates, the root‐mean‐square transverse sizes of the proton and electron beams at each interaction point had to be matched to within 20%, despite the proton head‐on beam–beam tune shift per IP being only ξ_p≈0.001—significantly smaller than ξ≈0.005 in the CERN SPS proton–antiproton collider and ξ≈0.008 in the Tevatron proton–antiproton collider. What underlying beam dynamics mechanisms explain this unusually stringent beam‐size matching requirement at HERA, in contrast to the less restrictive conditions at the SPS and Tevatron?

In the context of plans to operate the LHC at center-of-mass energies exceeding 14 TeV—where synchrotron radiation damping times become of order one hour—will the performance limit imposed by head-on beam–beam interactions be determined by (i) saturation of the beam–beam tune-shift parameter ξ through emittance growth, analogous to the first beam–beam limit in lepton colliders, or (ii) the development of nonlinear beam tails and consequent particle loss?

In Taneja’s specific block-wise constructions of normal bimagic squares of orders 256×256, 625×625, and 2401×2401, each parent square is partitioned into first-level contiguous blocks of orders 64×64, 125×125, and 343×343, respectively. Give a mathematical proof of the author’s page-5 observation that, within each of these three constructions, every such first-level block is itself a bimagic square and all of these first-level blocks have the same bimagic sum S2, where S2 denotes the common sum of the squared entries in each row, each column, and the two principal diagonals of the block.

Let f and g be distinct non-constant meromorphic functions on C, and let a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4 be four distinct values in \widehat{\mathbb{C}}. Suppose that for each 
u\in\{1,2,3,4\}, the set of a_
u-points of f equals the set of a_
u-points of g (and if a_
u=\infty, this means that f and g have the same pole set), and suppose moreover that for exactly one of these four shared values the multiplicities also agree, while for the other three no multiplicity agreement is assumed. Must it follow that f and g actually share all four values counting multiplicities, and hence, by Nevanlinna’s Four-Value Theorem, after a relabelling of the shared values one has (a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)=-1, two of the shared values are Picard values of both functions, and g is a Möbius transformation of f fixing the other two shared values and permuting the Picard pair? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03248))

Let f and g be non-constant meromorphic functions on C, and let a1,a2,a3,a4 be four distinct values in C∪{∞}. Assume that f and g share each of the values a1,a2,a3,a4 ignoring multiplicities, and that one of these four values, say a4, is shared counting multiplicities. Must it then follow that f and g in fact share all four values counting multiplicities?

Let f and g be distinct nonconstant meromorphic functions on C that share four distinct values a1,a2,a3,a4 in the Riemann sphere Ĉ, and assume that one of these four values is shared counting multiplicities, as in Conjecture 1.1. Can the general (1+3)-problem be reduced, via Zalcman/Yosida rescaling, to the special case of a nonconstant limit pair f̂,ĝ with bounded spherical derivatives on C in such a way that the information needed to recover the conclusion of Nevanlinna’s Four-Value-Theorem for the original pair is preserved? Equivalently, can one rule out the three obstructions identified in the paper: that an originally shared value becomes merely a Picard value of f̂ and ĝ, that a value not originally shared counting multiplicities becomes shared counting multiplicities in the limit, or that the limit pair collapses to f̂≡ĝ, so that proving Conjecture 1.1 in the bounded-spherical-derivative setting would imply Conjecture 1.1 in full generality?

For each positive integer n, with [n]={1,…,n}, let C(n) denote the number of Costas arrays of order n, equivalently the number of bijections f:[n]→[n] such that the vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) are all distinct for 1≤j<i≤n. Determine C(n) for every n. In particular, is C(n)>0 for all n>0? If not, determine the set X={n>0 : C(n)=0}. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

Given a positive integer n, let C(n) denote the number of Costas arrays of order n, where equivalently a Costas array of order n is a bijection f:[n] -> [n] such that all distance vectors {(i-j, f(i)-f(j)) : 1 <= j < i <= n} are distinct. What is the computational complexity, as a function of the order n, of deciding whether C(n) > 0? In particular, is the resulting existence problem E NP-complete?

For a positive integer n, let [n]={1,2,...,n}, and let C_n be the set of Costas permutations f:[n]->[n], i.e. bijections such that f(i+k)-f(i)=f(j+k)-f(j) implies i=j whenever i,j,i+k,j+k are all in [n]. Define d(n) to be the least integer k<=n for which there exist indices 1<=i1<...<ik<=n such that, for every choice of values f1,...,fk in [n], the set {f:[n]->[n] : f(ij)=fj for all j in [k]} contains at most one Costas permutation. Determine d(n) for Costas permutations of order n. If possible, improve this notion of degrees of freedom while staying within the same order-n Costas-permutation setting.

Let [n]={1,…,n}. For each n∈N*, let C(n) denote the number of Costas arrays of order n, equivalently the number of bijections f:[n]→[n] with the Costas property that the vectors {(i−j, f(i)−f(j)) : 1≤j<i≤n} are all distinct. Determine an upper bound for C(n) that improves on the published estimate C(n)=O((n−1)!) (equivalently, C(n)/n!=O(1/n)) and that reflects more closely the decay of the density C(n)/n! seen in the known data, which the paper reports as apparently monotone and exponential for n≤29. In particular, prove or disprove that the sequence {C(n)/n!}n≥1 is monotone decreasing and converges to 0. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

Let [n]={1,...,n}. A Costas array of order n is an n x n permutation array, equivalently a bijection f:[n]->[n], such that all displacement vectors between pairs of dots are distinct. Call an infinite family of Costas arrays generated if it is produced by an algorithm whose applicability is determined by a sufficient condition involving only n, and call an infinite family emergent if it is obtained from generated Costas arrays by transformation, either under a condition involving n and additional parameters or only by direct verification of the Costas property. A Costas array is sporadic if it belongs to neither a generated family nor an emergent family. Settle the status of sporadic Costas arrays: are there only finitely many sporadic Costas arrays, and are there new generally applicable construction techniques that produce them? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

Let [n] := {1, ..., n}, and call a bijection h:[m]->[m] a Costas permutation if the vectors (i-j, h(i)-h(j)) are pairwise distinct for 1 <= j < i <= m. Interpreting the evident size typo in Definition 7 in the natural way, let f:[n]->[n] be a Costas permutation and define g1,g2:[n+2]->[n+2] by g_j(i)=f(i-1)+1 for 2 <= i <= n+1, together with g1(1)=1, g1(n+2)=n+2, g2(1)=n+2, and g2(n+2)=1. If both g1 and g2 are Costas permutations, call {g1,g2} a twin Costas pair. Is the only known such pair—generated from a sporadic Costas array of order 21—the unique twin Costas pair, or do finitely many or infinitely many twin Costas pairs exist? If further pairs exist, can they be constructed systematically?

Does there exist a finite integer n > 1 and a bijection f:[n]→[n] such that f is a Costas permutation, i.e. all vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) with 1 ≤ j < i ≤ n are distinct, and such that the dot set {(i, f(i)) : i ∈ [n]} forms a configuration of n non-attacking queens on the n × n chessboard, meaning that no two dots lie on a common diagonal in either direction? Since the paper notes that any such finite example would necessarily be sporadic, determine whether any such finite Costas arrays exist; if they do, determine the total number of them and whether they admit a systematic construction.

Let [n]={1,\dots,n}, and let g:[l]->[l] be a Costas permutation (that is, a bijection whose distance vectors are all distinct). Does there exist a Costas permutation f:[n]->[n] for some n, together with integers a1,a2 and positive integers b1,b2, such that the arithmetic-progression sets S_j={a_j+b_j i : i in [l]} are subsets of [n] for j=1,2, satisfy f(S1)=S2, and obey g(i)=(f(a1+b1 i)-a2)/b2 for every i in [l]? Equivalently, is every Costas permutation a sub-permutation of some Costas permutation in the precise sense of Definition 8? In particular, does this hold for specific families of Costas permutations, such as sporadic Costas permutations?

Let [n] = {1, ..., n}, and let f:[n] -> [n] be a Costas permutation, meaning that f is a bijection such that the distance vectors {(i-j, f(i)-f(j)) : 1 <= j < i <= n} are all distinct. Write f^(0) = I for the identity permutation on [n], and define f^(k+1) = f o f^(k) for k >= 0. For i in [n], let the cycle of i under f be the finite set {f^(k)(i) : k in N}. For a given Costas permutation f, or for a specified family of Costas permutations, determine the disjoint cycle decomposition of f; decide which cycle lengths occur and which are absent; determine the maximum cycle length; and determine the least positive integer k such that f^(k) = I.

Let M range over the construction methods listed in Section 3.2 of the paper (in particular the theorem-level families W1, W2, G2, G3, G4, W3, G4*, G4**, and G5*, and, if one follows Problem 10 literally, the remaining Section 3.2 methods as well). For each integer n > 5, let C_M(n) denote the set of Costas arrays of order n produced by method M. Is it true that C_M(n) ∩ C_{M'}(n) = ∅ for every pair of distinct methods M ≠ M'?

For each of the five unpredictably emergent Costas-array construction heuristics in Section 3.2.2—obtained by prescribed transformations of algebraically generated Welch/Golomb Costas arrays and whose outputs must be checked for the Costas property by direct verification—determine the scope of the method. In particular, for each such heuristic, does there exist a method-dependent integer N such that the heuristic produces no Costas arrays of order n > N?

Let A1 and A2 be Costas arrays of orders n1 and n2, respectively, with n1≤n2. Here a distance vector means the vector between two dots of a Costas array; equivalently, if Ak corresponds to a Costas permutation fk:[nk]→[nk], its distance vectors are the pairs (i-j, fk(i)-fk(j)) with 1≤j<i≤nk. Is it true that any two sufficiently large Costas arrays must have at least one distance vector in common? More specifically, is it already enough to assume n1≥3 and n2≥5 to force A1 and A2 to share a common distance vector?

Develop a stochastic search method on the permutation space of [n] that, for target orders n in {30,31,32,33} and more generally for other sufficiently large orders of interest, successfully finds a Costas permutation f:[n] -> [n], meaning a permutation for which all displacement vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) with 1 <= j < i <= n are distinct.

Let f:[n] -> [n] be a Costas permutation (equivalently, let A_f be the associated order n Costas array), and suppose that for every t in {0, ..., n-1}, the array obtained from A_f by cyclically shifting its columns by t positions modulo n is again a Costas array. Must f belong to the Welch family W1; equivalently, must there exist a prime p = n + 1, a primitive root alpha of F_p, and c in {0, ..., p-2} such that either f(i) = alpha^(i-1+c) mod p for i = 1, ..., p-1, or f is the inverse (transpose) of such a permutation?

Let A be a Costas array of order n. Form an (n+1)×n dot array B by inserting one blank row above A. Assume that for every t∈{0,…,n}, the array obtained from B by cyclically shifting its rows by t positions still has the Costas property, in the sense that the displacement vectors between any two distinct dots are all distinct. Must A then be an exponential Welch array W_1^{exp}(p,α,c) for some prime p=n+1, some primitive root α of F(p), and some c∈{0,…,p−2}, i.e. the Costas array of the permutation f:[p−1]→[p−1] given by f(i)=α^{i-1+c} mod p? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

Let A be an n×n Costas array, meaning a permutation array whose pairwise dot-difference vectors are all distinct. Form an (n+1)×(n+1) binary array B by adjoining one all-zero row above A and one all-zero column to one side of A. Assume that for every r,c ∈ {0,1,…,n}, the array obtained from B by cyclically shifting its rows by r positions and its columns by c positions still has the Costas property in the distinct-differences sense, even though it need not be a permutation array. Must A belong to the Golomb G2 family; that is, must there exist a prime power q = n + 2 and primitive elements α,β ∈ F_q such that A is the order-(q-2) Costas array defined by α^i + β^{f(i)} = 1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ q-2?

For each finite field F(2^m) with q = 2^m > 2, and for each pair of primitive roots alpha, beta in F(q), let f:[q-2] -> [q-2] be the Golomb G2 Costas permutation defined by alpha^{f(i)} + beta^i = 1 for i in [q-2]. In the associated Costas array A_f, whose dots are at positions (f(i), i), determine the four parity populations ee, eo, oe, and oo, where ee, eo, oe, and oo denote respectively the numbers of dots with row-column parity even-even, even-odd, odd-even, and odd-odd. Equivalently, determine these populations exactly for all G2 arrays constructed over fields of characteristic 2, including any dependence on the choice of alpha and beta.

Let q be a prime power, and let r be an integer taken modulo q−1 (equivalently, choose 1≤r≤q−2) with gcd(r,q−1)=1. Determine the number of solutions x∈F(q) to the equation x^r + x = 1. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=1112b33e03d236e8189ac3f49b825656fd5198e5&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

Let p be a prime, let C be a nonzero element of the finite field F(p), and let alpha be a primitive root of F(p). Determine the number of solutions i in {1,2,...,p-1} to the congruence i ≡ C alpha^i (mod p).

Fix a positive integer n. A Costas array of order n is the n x n array associated with a bijection f:[n]->[n] having the Costas property, i.e. all distance vectors (i-j, f(i)-f(j)) with 1<=j<i<=n are distinct; equivalently, the array has exactly one dot in each row and column, with dots at the cells (f(i), i). Determine the set F_n = {(r,c) in [n] x [n] : there exists no Costas permutation f of order n with f(c)=r}, namely the forbidden positions for Costas arrays of order n, by a method that does not first enumerate all Costas arrays of that order. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

Let p be a prime and q a prime power, with primes counted among prime powers as in the paper. Let W1 be the Welch family from Theorem 1: exponential Welch permutations f:[p−1]→[p−1], f(i)=α^(i−1+c) mod p, where α is a primitive root of F(p) and c∈[p−1]−1, together with their logarithmic inverses; and let G2 be the Golomb family from Theorem 3: for q=p^m and primitive roots α,β∈F(q), the permutation f:[q−2]→[q−2] determined by α^(f(i))+β^i=1. For permutations f,g:[n]→[n], define Ψ_{f,g}(u,v)=|{(f(i)+v,i+u):i∈[n]}∩{(g(i),i):i∈[n]}| for (u,v)∈Z^2. Define Ψ_W1(p)=max_{(u,v)∈Z^2} max_{f1^pr≠f2} Ψ_{f1,f2}(u,v), where f1,f2 are W1 permutations of order p−1 and f1^pr≠f2 means that they are generated by different primitive roots, and define Ψ_G2(q)=max_{(u,v)∈Z^2} max_{f′1≠f′2} Ψ_{f′1,f′2}(u,v), where f′1,f′2 are distinct G2 permutations of order q−2. Prove the exact trichotomy stated in Problem 21: (1) with respect to Ψ_W1(p) and Ψ_G2(p), if p is a non-safe prime with p≠19, then Ψ_W1(p)=Ψ_G2(p)+1=(p−1)/t, where t is the smallest prime such that p≡1 mod (2t); if p=19, then Ψ_W1(19)=Ψ_G2(19)=6=(19−1)/3; and if (p−1)/2 is prime, then p is a local minimum of both Ψ_W1 and Ψ_G2; (2) with respect to Ψ_G2(q), if q≠16 and neither (q−1)/2 nor q−1 is prime, then Ψ_G2(q)=(q−1)/t−1, where t is the smallest prime such that q≡1 mod (2t) when q is odd, or q≡1 mod t when q is even; if q=16, then Ψ_G2(16)=5=(16−1)/3; and if either (q−1)/2 is prime or q−1 is prime, then q is a local minimum of Ψ_G2; derive formulas for the values of these local minima in both the prime and prime-power settings; and finally prove the paper’s origin-attainment statements, namely that for every non-safe prime p, Ψ_W1(p)=max_{f1^pr≠f2} Ψ_{f1,f2}(0,0), and that for every non-safe prime power q≠16,19 with q−1 not prime, Ψ_G2(q)=Ψ_{f′1,f′2}(0,0) for a pair of G2 permutations f′1,f′2 generated from (α,β) and (α^r,β), with r chosen as in the final sentence of Problem 21. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

For each q = 2^m and each G2 Costas permutation f:[q-2] -> [q-2] (where [n] = {1,2,...,n}) arising from primitive roots alpha,beta of the finite field F_q via alpha^{f(i)} + beta^i = 1 for all i in [q-2], determine a necessary property shared by all such G2 arrays/permutations, analogous in character to the anti-reflective symmetry of W1 arrays and to the odd-characteristic G2 identity f(mu+i) - f(mu-i) congruent to i(f(mu+1) - f(mu-1)) modulo q-1, where mu = (q-1)/2.

Fix positive integers m, n, and N > 2. Let [m] = {1, ..., m} and [n] = {1, ..., n}. For a set A subset of [m] x [n] with |A| = N, define its autocorrelation by Psi_A(u,v) = |(A + (u,v)) intersect A| for (u,v) in Z^2, where A + (u,v) = {(i + u, j + v) : (i,j) in A} and shifts are taken in ordinary integer arithmetic (no modular wraparound). Call A a Golomb rectangle if the range of Psi_A is exactly {N, 1, 0}. Let C(m,n,N) denote the number of m x n Golomb rectangles containing N dots. Determine C(m,n,N). In particular, for fixed m and n determine the maximal N for which C(m,n,N) > 0; conversely, for fixed N determine the smallest values of m and n for which C(m,n,N) > 0.

Determine all honeycomb arrays: for each r ∈ N, classify every dot/blank configuration on a finite hexagonal board of diameter 2r+1 having exactly one dot in each row in each of the three natural directions of the hexagonal grid, and satisfying the Costas-type condition that no two line segments joining pairs of dots have both the same length and the same slope. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

For integers m >= 1 and n >= 0, let a Golomb ruler of length n with m points mean a strictly increasing sequence of integers 0 = a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_m = n such that all positive differences a_i - a_j, with 1 <= j < i <= m, are distinct. Define G(m) to be the minimum n for which such a ruler exists, and M(n) to be the maximum m for which such a ruler exists. Determine exact formulas for G(m), the length of an optimally short Golomb ruler with m points, and for M(n), the number of points of an optimally dense Golomb ruler of length n.

Let A be an n x n Costas array, meaning a binary permutation array with exactly one dot in each row and each column and with all vectors between pairs of dots distinct; more generally, let A be a Golomb rectangle, meaning a rectangular binary array with N > 2 dots whose autocorrelation range is {N, 1, 0}. A Golomb ruler is a finite set G = {0 = g1 < ... < gm} subset of N whose pairwise differences are all distinct. Find efficient conversion procedures between Costas arrays (or, more generally, Golomb rectangles) and Golomb rulers in both directions. In particular, for a given n x n Costas array A, or for a specified family of Costas arrays, determine the least integer b >= 0 such that, after adjoining b blank rows below A and then concatenating the columns of the resulting array from left to right (each read top-to-bottom), the resulting one-dimensional binary vector is a Golomb ruler. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

Let (X, \mathcal{X}, \mu, T_1, ..., T_\ell) be a measure-preserving system in the paper's sense, meaning that T_1, ..., T_\ell are commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations of (X, \mathcal{X}, \mu), and let f_0, ..., f_\ell \in L^\infty(\mu). Define the multiple correlation sequence C: \mathbb{Z}^\ell \to \mathbb{C} by C(n_1, ..., n_\ell) := \int f_0 \cdot T_1^{n_1} f_1 \cdots T_\ell^{n_\ell} f_\ell \, d\mu. Let c>0 be a non-integer real number, let p_n denote the n-th prime, and define a(n)=⌊p_n^c⌋. Is the sequence (a(n))_{n∈ℕ} good for multiple recurrence and for multiple convergence of powers in the following precise sense: for every ℓ∈ℕ, every invertible probability-preserving system (X, 𝒳, μ, T), every nonzero integers k_1,…,k_ℓ, and every A∈𝒳 with μ(A)>0, does there exist n∈ℕ such that μ(A∩T^{-k_1a(n)}A∩⋯∩T^{-k_ℓa(n)}A)>0; and, for every ℓ∈ℕ, every integers k_1,…,k_ℓ, and every f_1,…,f_ℓ∈L^∞(μ), do the averages (1/N)∑_{n=1}^N ∏_{i=1}^ℓ T^{k_i a(n)}f_i converge in L^2(μ) as N→∞? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

Is it true that the integer-part sequence a(n) = floor(n sin n) is good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of powers; that is, for every ell in N and every integers k1,...,kell: (i) for every invertible measure-preserving system (X, X, mu, T) and every measurable set A with mu(A) > 0, there exists n in N with a(n) != 0 such that mu(A ∩ T^(-k1 a(n))A ∩ ... ∩ T^(-kell a(n))A) > 0; and (ii) for every invertible measure-preserving system (X, X, mu, T) and every f1,...,fell in L^infty(mu), the Cesaro averages (1/N) sum_{n=1}^N T^(k1 a(n))f1 ... T^(kell a(n))fell converge in L^2(mu) as N tends to infinity?

Let c>0 be a noninteger real number and set a(n)=⌊n^c⌋. Is it true that a(n) is good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence of commuting transformations, in the following precise sense: for every ℓ∈N, every probability space (X, 𝓧, μ), every commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T_1, ..., T_ℓ:X→X, and every A∈𝓧 with μ(A)>0, does there exist n∈N such that μ(A ∩ T_1^{-a(n)}A ∩ ··· ∩ T_ℓ^{-a(n)}A)>0; and, for every f_1, ..., f_ℓ∈L^∞(μ), do the averages (1/N)Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^{a(n)}f_1 ··· T_ℓ^{a(n)}f_ℓ converge in L^2(μ)? More strongly, is this L^2-limit always equal to the L^2-limit of the linear averages (1/N)Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^n f_1 ··· T_ℓ^n f_ℓ? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))

Fix ℓ∈N and positive real numbers c,c1,...,cℓ, and write [x]=⌊x⌋. Do there exist infinitely many pairs of positive integers (m,n) such that every element of {m, m+[n^c], m+2[n^c], ..., m+ℓ[n^c]} is prime, and likewise infinitely many pairs of positive integers (m,n) such that every element of {m, m+[n^{c1}], ..., m+[n^{cℓ}]} is prime?

Let (Ω, F, P) be a probability space, let (X_n)_{n∈N} be independent {0,1}-valued random variables with P(X_n=1)=σ_n and P(X_n=0)=1-σ_n, where (σ_n) is a decreasing sequence of positive reals with Σ_{n=1}^∞ σ_n = ∞ and nσ_n → ∞, and for each ω let a_1(ω)<a_2(ω)<··· be the increasing enumeration of {n∈N : X_n(ω)=1}. Is it true that there exists Ω_0 ∈ F with P(Ω_0)=1 such that for every ω∈Ω_0 the following hold simultaneously: (i) for every ℓ∈N, every probability-preserving system (X, 𝓧, μ, T_1, ..., T_ℓ) of commuting invertible transformations, and every A∈𝓧 with μ(A)>0, there exists n∈N such that μ(A ∩ T_1^{a_n(ω)}A ∩ ··· ∩ T_ℓ^{a_n(ω)}A)>0; and (ii) for every ℓ∈N, every such system, and every f_1, ..., f_ℓ ∈ L∞(μ), the averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^{a_n(ω)}f_1 ··· T_ℓ^{a_n(ω)}f_ℓ converge in L^2(μ), and their limit coincides with the L^2-limit of the classical linear averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N T_1^n f_1 ··· T_ℓ^n f_ℓ?

Let (Ω, F, P) be a probability space, let (X_n)_{n≥1} be independent {0,1}-valued random variables with P(X_n=1)=σ_n and P(X_n=0)=1−σ_n, where (σ_n) is decreasing, positive, and satisfies Σ_{n=1}^∞ σ_n=∞, and let a_n(ω) be the increasing sequence of integers k for which X_k(ω)=1 (equivalently, a_n(ω) is the least k with X_1(ω)+⋯+X_k(ω)=n). Assume that nσ_n → ∞. Is it true that there exists a full-probability set Ω_0 such that for every ω∈Ω_0, every probability space (X, 𝓧, μ), every pair of commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T,S:X→X, and every f,g∈L∞(μ), one has

lim_{N→∞} (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N T^n f · S^{a_n(ω)} g = E(f | I_T) · E(g | I_S)

with convergence in L2(μ), where I_T and I_S denote the T-invariant and S-invariant σ-algebras? Moreover, if σ_n = n^{-a} for some a∈(0,1), must the same averages also converge pointwise μ-almost everywhere?

Let (\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P) support mutually independent Bernoulli random variables X_1,Y_1,X_2,Y_2,\dots with \mathbb P(X_n=1)=n^{-a} and \mathbb P(Y_n=1)=n^{-b}, where a,b\in(0,1) and a\neq b. For each \omega\in\Omega, let a_n(\omega) and b_n(\omega) be the increasing enumerations of \{m\in\mathbb N:X_m(\omega)=1\} and \{m\in\mathbb N:Y_m(\omega)=1\}. Is it true that there exists a set \Omega_0\in\mathcal F with \mathbb P(\Omega_0)=1 such that, for every \omega\in\Omega_0, every probability space (X,\mathcal X,\mu), every pair of commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T,S:X\to X, and every f,g\in L^\infty(\mu), the averages (1/N)\sum_{n=1}^N T^{a_n(\omega)}f\cdot S^{b_n(\omega)}g converge in L^2(\mu) — or, in the stronger version, pointwise — to E(f\mid I_T)\,E(g\mid I_S), where I_T and I_S are the T-invariant and S-invariant \sigma-algebras? ([math.uoc.gr](https://www.math.uoc.gr/~nikosf/OpenProblems/OpenProblems.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Let (X, 𝓧, μ, (T_n)_{n∈N}) be a measure preserving system with multiplicative structure, meaning that (X, 𝓧, μ) is a probability space, each T_n is an invertible measure-preserving transformation, T_1 = id, and T_m ∘ T_n = T_{mn} for all m, n ∈ N. If A ∈ 𝓧 satisfies μ(A) > 0, must there exist integers m, n ∈ N with m > n such that μ(T_{2mn}A ∩ T_{(m-n)(m+n)}A) > 0? Equivalently, does every measure preserving system with multiplicative structure exhibit this recurrence pattern associated with Pythagorean pairs?

Let (X, X, mu, (T_n)_{n in N}) be a measure preserving system with multiplicative structure; that is, (X, X, mu) is a probability space, each T_n is an invertible measure-preserving transformation, T_1 = id, and T_{mn} = T_m o T_n for all m,n in N. If A is a measurable set with mu(A) > 0, must there exist m,n in N such that mu(T_{m(m+n)}^{-1}A ∩ T_{(m+2n)(m+3n)}^{-1}A ∩ T_{(m+4n)(m+5n)}^{-1}A) > 0?

Among the nonabelian groups used as cryptographic platforms in the protocols surveyed in this paper - typically groups given by finite presentations - which group or class of groups is the most appropriate platform group for non-commutative cryptography, in the sense that it admits efficiently computable unique normal forms whose product normal forms do not reveal secret factors, has an efficiently solvable word problem and exponential growth, makes the relevant conjugacy/conjugator search problems computationally hard (ideally exponential-time), and, for Ko-Lee- and Shamir-type constructions, contains sufficiently large commuting subgroups (large enough to support random choices and not merely cyclic), while avoiding generic subgroup vulnerabilities such as those seen in braid groups?

For a candidate nonabelian platform group G for the non-commutative cryptographic protocols surveyed in this paper, should G be chosen to be finite or infinite, where G is understood to be a platform group with efficiently computable normal forms (hence an efficiently solvable word problem), ideally exponential growth and a hard conjugacy/conjugator-search problem, and, for Ko-Lee-type schemes, sufficiently large commuting subgroups?

In the setting of the non-commutative group-based cryptosystems surveyed in this paper, how can one formulate rigorous criteria and proof methods showing that a candidate nonabelian platform group G is provably secure for the specific schemes considered here—public-key exchange, digital signatures, and authentication/password-verification—where G is used via a finite presentation with efficiently computable normal forms and solvable word problem, the relevant scheme-specific hard problems (such as conjugator/conjugacy search or the authentication-related word-problem/equation-solving attacks) are infeasible, any required large commuting subgroups exist, and the security proof is evaluated in the appropriate sense (practical, worst-case, average-case, or generic-case)? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

In the framework of noncommutative group-based cryptography considered in the paper—namely, public-key constructions implemented over finitely presented nonabelian platform groups with efficiently computable normal forms—can one design additional public-key constructions, such as public-key cryptosystems or public-key exchange protocols, whose underlying one-way functions are based on search or decision problems from combinatorial group theory other than the problems already used in the surveyed schemes (including conjugacy, conjugator search, word, decomposition, simultaneous search conjugacy, twisted conjugacy, search conjugacy, search power conjugacy, and related cited decision problems)? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/abs/1103.4093))

For the non-commutative group-based cryptographic schemes surveyed in this paper—public-key exchange protocols such as Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld and Ko–Lee, the noncommutative ElGamal analog, Shamir-type key transport, and the digital-signature and authentication/password-verification constructions built on finitely presented nonabelian platform groups with efficiently computable normal forms and, where required, large commuting subgroups—can one give a rigorous security analysis by relating attacks to the underlying hard group-theoretic problems (such as conjugacy, conjugator search, simultaneous search conjugacy, the word problem, or recovery of commuting subgroups) and by determining the appropriate notion of security for these protocols: practicality, complexity, average-case complexity, or generic complexity?

For the non-commutative group-based cryptographic schemes surveyed in this paper—particularly public key exchange, digital-signature, and authentication protocols based on group-theoretic search or decision problems—what should be taken as the primary measure of security: practical resistance to attacks, worst-case computational complexity of the underlying problem, average-case complexity with respect to the protocol's input generation, or generic-case complexity on asymptotically most inputs?

As of the 2011 survey on noncommutative algebraic cryptography, only three non-commutative digital signatures were known. Can one construct further non-commutative public-key digital signature schemes on non-commutative algebraic platforms, in the Section 6 sense of probabilistic polynomial-time key-generation, signing, and verification algorithms, beyond those three? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.4093))

Can one design new non-commutative group-based authentication schemes—distinct from the paper's separately listed problem of constructing more non-commutative digital signatures—and, in particular, secure challenge-response/password-verification protocols that support two-way authentication between prover and verifier, using finitely presented groups with solvable word problem and the group-randomizer/challenge-group framework described in Section 6? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Let G be a finitely presented polycyclic group used as a platform group, with an efficiently computable normal form. For the earlier described protocols that require secret large subgroups A, B <= G that commute elementwise—specifically the Ko-Lee key-exchange protocol and the Shamir three-pass/key-transport construction—what is the appropriate choice of commuting subgroups A and B, large enough for random private selections, that makes these schemes secure?

For an arbitrary polycyclic group G, given by a consistent polycyclic presentation so that elements are represented in normal form, what is the worst-case time complexity of the search conjugacy problem: on input two conjugate elements u,v∈G, compute a conjugator x∈G such that x^{-1}ux=v? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

For a polycyclic group G given by a finite presentation (in the computational setting of Section 8, typically a consistent polycyclic presentation with its normal forms) and two words u,v in the generators of G, what is the worst-case computational complexity of the decision conjugacy problem of determining whether there exists x in G such that x^{-1}ux = v? In particular, what is the complexity of the Eick-Ostheimer algorithm [EO] for this decision problem?

Given a polycyclic group G specified by a consistent polycyclic presentation, and a word w in the generators of that presentation, what is the computational complexity of the collection algorithm that repeatedly applies the presentation's power and conjugacy relations to rewrite w to the unique polycyclic normal form of the element represented by w? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

What is the worst-case computational complexity of the following search problem over polycyclic groups, in the natural input model of Section 8? Given a polycyclic group G by a consistent polycyclic presentation, a specified twisting endomorphism φ of G (encoded by its action on the generators), and elements u,v ∈ G (given as words or in normal form) such that v = x^{-1}uφ(x) for some x ∈ G, find such an element x.

Determine the worst-case computational complexity of the Reidemeister-Schreier rewriting procedure for finitely generated subgroups of finitely generated free groups: if F = F(X) is a free group on a fixed finite basis X, H ≤ F is specified by a fixed Schreier transversal T for H in F and the associated Schreier generating set Y obtained from the Reidemeister-Schreier process, and w ∈ H is given as a reduced word over X^{±1}, what is the time complexity, as a function of |w| and of the description size of T (equivalently of Y or H, if these are not treated as fixed), of rewriting w as the corresponding reduced word over Y^{±1}?

For an arbitrary polycyclic group G given by a consistent polycyclic presentation, with elements represented by words or their normal forms, what is the generic-case time complexity of the search conjugacy problem: on input a conjugate pair g,h ∈ G, find an element x ∈ G such that x^{-1} g x = h, where genericity is understood in the asymptotic-density sense described in Section 9?

Beyond Watrous's polynomial-time quantum algorithm for computing the order of a finite solvable (hence polycyclic) black-box group, can one construct quantum algorithms for other group-theoretic decision problems in polycyclic groups, for both finite and infinite polycyclic groups, especially for cryptographically used decision problems such as the word problem and the decision conjugacy problem? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Let G be a polycyclic group represented by a consistent polycyclic presentation, so that elements admit unique normal forms. Given conjugate elements a,b in G, is there a quantum algorithm for the search conjugacy problem—i.e., for finding x in G such that b = x^{-1}ax—that reduces the computational complexity of solving this problem compared with the corresponding classical algorithms for polycyclic groups used in cryptography? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

For the noncommutative/nonabelian group-based cryptosystems surveyed in this paper, how can one give concrete practical implementations by choosing explicit finitely presented platform groups and effective representations of group elements so that normal forms and the word problem are efficiently computable, protocol-specific operations such as multiplication/inversion and rewriting procedures (for example, Reidemeister-Schreier rewriting in the free-group setting and collection in the polycyclic setting) are practical, and any required large commuting subgroups can be generated, while the underlying hard group-theoretic search problems on which security is based remain computationally infeasible?

Can the computer algebra system GAP be used as an implementation platform for the noncommutative group-based cryptosystems discussed in this paper—namely the nonabelian key-exchange, key-transport, signature, and authentication schemes based on the paper's platform groups—in a way that is both computationally practical and cryptographically secure?

For cosmological gamma-ray bursts observed by instruments with different energy bandpasses and sensitivities (e.g. BATSE: 30–2000 keV; Swift/BAT: 15–150 keV), how can one construct a detector-independent, physically motivated classification scheme—beyond the traditional observer-frame T90 duration (>2 s vs <2 s) and spectral hardness ratio—that reliably assigns each GRB to its progenitor class of massive star collapse (Type II) versus compact object merger (Type I)? Specifically, which combination of multi-wavelength observational signatures (such as supernova association, host galaxy morphology, spectral lag, rest-frame peak energy E_p,z, isotropic energy E_iso) and redshift-dependent parameter ε≡E_iso,52/E_p,z,2^{5/3} should be adopted to map observed bursts to their physical origins?

At the prompt-emission radius R_em (above the photosphere) of gamma-ray bursts, what is the magnetization parameter σ(R_em) ≡ (Poynting flux)/(matter flux), and what are the characteristic number ratios of leptons to protons f_e ≡ n_e/n_p and neutrons to protons ξ ≡ n_n/n_p? Specifically, do prompt GRB outflows satisfy σ(R_em) << 1 (matter-dominated fireballs), σ(R_em) ≃ 1 (quasi-magnetized flows), or σ(R_em) >> 1 (Poynting-flux-dominated jets), and what ranges of f_e and ξ best describe the ejecta composition at the emission site?

Which radiation mechanism is responsible for the prompt emission of gamma-ray bursts—whose spectra are characterized by the empirical Band function, a smoothly-connected broken power law defined by low-energy photon index α, high-energy photon index β, and spectral peak energy Epeak—among the competing processes of (1) synchrotron or jitter radiation from shock-accelerated electrons, (2) synchrotron self-Compton emission, (3) Compton upscattering of thermal seed photons from the jet photosphere or other thermal sources, or (4) hadronic processes (proton synchrotron or proton-photon interactions), given that the correct mechanism must reproduce typical observed values of α≈−1, β≈−2.2, and Epeak≈10^2–10^3 keV, satisfy cooling-time and flux-amplitude constraints, and explain the observed photon spectral slopes in the prompt phase.

Which of the mechanisms proposed in Zhang (2011)—namely fragmentation of the collapsing star, fragmentation of the accretion disk (in both massive‐star and compact‐star GRBs), intermittent magnetically-barrier-regulated accretion, magnetic bubble ejection in a post-merger proto-neutron star, helium-synthesis–driven episodic accretion, quakes in solid quark stars, fallback accretion onto the black hole, spin-down of a millisecond magnetar, hyperaccretion onto a neutron star, or phase transition into a quark star—can best account for the observed late‐time central engine activity in GRBs, characterized by (1) erratic X-ray flares with sharp rise and decay and (2) smooth internal plateaus followed by steep decay (α>3), lasting up to ≳10^5 s after the prompt emission trigger, while satisfying the requirement for magnetic collimation of low-luminosity late jets?

In Swift-era gamma-ray burst afterglows, the observed X-ray lightcurve typically consists of five segments: (I) an early steep decay and (V) late-time X-ray flares, both attributed to internal central-engine dissipation, sandwiched around segments (II) shallow decay (plateau), (III) normal decay, and (IV) a late steep decay often associated with a jet break. Once the internal steep-decay and flare components are removed, which of the remaining X-ray and contemporaneous optical/infrared features — including the plateau, normal-decay, late-steep-decay segments, and any reverse-shock optical signatures — can be unambiguously identified as arising from the external forward shock and the reverse shock within the standard external-shock model (characterized by the isotropic-equivalent kinetic energy E_iso, circumburst medium density, electron spectral index p, and energy-partition fractions ε_e and ε_B)? Furthermore, how should (a) the presence or absence of an achromatic late-time jet-break signature, (b) the occurrence of chromatic breaks between X-ray and optical bands, and (c) the diversity of reverse-shock optical emission profiles — including their sensitivity to ejecta magnetization parameter σ and ejecta stratification — be interpreted in the external-shock framework after subtraction of all internal engine contributions?

Based on Fermi LAT and GBM observations of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), what is the physical origin of emission above 100 MeV? Specifically, how can one explain (i) the delayed onset of >100 MeV photons detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) relative to prompt emission in the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) band, (ii) the long-lived LAT-band emission that decays as a power law (slope ∼−1.4) after the GBM-band prompt phase ceases, and (iii) the diverse spectral behavior—ranging from a single Band function spanning keV to GeV energies to the presence of thermal-like and extra power-law components—between the MeV and GeV regimes? Determine whether the >100 MeV emission is produced by internal dissipation within the relativistic jet, by external-forward-shock afterglow processes, or by a superposition of multiple emission components.

Assuming that the comoving event rate density of massive star (Type II) GRBs R_GRB(z) is proportional to the cosmic star formation rate density ρ_SFR(z) modulated by potential redshift-dependent factors, to what extent does R_GRB(z) trace ρ_SFR(z) across 0<z≲10? In particular, what deviations from a direct proportionality—arising from metallicity bias or luminosity-function evolution—are required to account for the observed excess of GRB 080916 at z≃6.7 and GRB 090423 at z≃8.2 compared to simple SFR extrapolations?

In the context of Zhang (2011, Section 2.10), to what extent do long-duration (Type II) gamma-ray bursts preferentially occur in host galaxies with sub-solar metallicities, and is a metallicity-dependent GRB formation efficiency required to reproduce the observed excess of GRB detections at redshifts z ≳ 4 (e.g. GRB 080916C at z = 4.35 and GRB 090423 at z = 8.2) relative to predictions based on the extrapolated cosmic star formation history?

Within the observed redshift interval z≈0.0085 to z≈8.2 for long-duration (massive star) gamma-ray bursts, does the rest-frame isotropic-equivalent peak luminosity function φ(L_iso,z) exhibit redshift evolution such that its characteristic luminosity increases systematically with z, after accounting for the standard cosmic star formation history and potential metallicity bias?

Let P(h) = -h^2Δ/2 + V(x) on R^d with V ∈ C_c^∞(R^d), and fix E > 0 such that the trapped set K_E = {ρ ∈ p^(-1)(E) : Φ^t(ρ) remains bounded for all t ∈ R} of the Hamiltonian p(x, ξ) = |ξ|^2/2 + V(x) is a hyperbolic repeller of pure Minkowski dimension 1 + 2ν. Is the fractal Weyl law true near energy E, in the sense that: (i) for C, γ > 0 large enough, there exist C_γ > 0 and h_{C,γ} > 0 such that for all 0 < h < h_{C,γ}, the number of resonances of P(h), counted with multiplicity, in the strip [E - Ch, E + Ch] - i[0, γ h] is at least C C_γ h^(-ν); and, more sharply, (ii) does there exist an increasing, nonidentically vanishing function F : R_+ → R_+ such that for every fixed C, γ > 0 one has #{Res P(h) ∩ ([E - Ch, E + Ch] - i[0, γ h])} = C F(γ) h^(-ν) + o(h^(-ν)) as h → 0?

Let Ω ⊂ ℝ^d be the exterior of finitely many strictly convex obstacles satisfying the no-eclipse condition, and let Reson(Δ_Ω) be the resonance set of the exterior Dirichlet Laplacian. Assume the billiard flow on the trapped set K ⊂ S*Ω is hyperbolic, let ϕ+ be the logarithm of its unstable Jacobian, and let γ_cl := -P(-ϕ+, Φ^t|_K) > 0 be the classical decay rate. Define the asymptotic obstacle-scattering resonance gap Γ_obs to be the supremum of all Γ ≥ 0 such that, for every ε > 0, there exists k_ε > 0 with Reson(Δ_Ω) ∩ ([k_ε, ∞) - i[0, Γ - ε]) = ∅. Theorem 1 gives Γ_obs ≥ max(0, -P(-ϕ+/2, Φ^t|_K)). Is the true high-frequency gap for such obstacle problems equal to γ_cl/2, i.e. the random-phase candidate suggested by equation (62), or must one have Γ_obs < γ_cl/2? ([imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr](https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~stephane.nonnenmacher/publis/Nonnen2011%28Nonlinearity%29.pdf))

Let κ: V ⊂ Σ → κ(V) be a smooth open symplectic map with compact hyperbolic trapped set K, and let M(α, ħ) be the associated ħ-Fourier integral operator/open quantum map with symbol α ∈ C_c^∞(V) nonzero near K (with α ≡ 1 near K in the usual open-map case, and, for monodromy operators, α = α_z(ρ) = e^{-i(z-E)τ(ρ)/ħ} + O(ħ) near K). In the Markov decomposition of M(α, ħ)^n into admissible components M_β for logarithmic times n ≍ c log(1/ħ), can one rigorously prove enough cancellation in the off-diagonal terms ⟨M_β u_0, M_β' u_0⟩, coming from the accumulated actions θ_β, to justify the pseudo-random-phase heuristic of §8.2 and thereby upgrade Theorem 9's pressure bound to the sharper estimate: for every ε > 0, there exists ħ_ε > 0 such that for all 0 < ħ ≤ ħ_ε, rsp(M(α, ħ)) ≤ exp{(1/2) P(-φ^+ + 2 log|α|, κ|_K) + ε}?

Let Omega = R^d \ setminus union_{i=1}^J O_i be the exterior of finitely many strictly convex smooth obstacles satisfying the no-eclipse condition, let Delta_Omega be the Dirichlet Laplacian on Omega, and let phi^t be the billiard flow on S^*Omega with outgoing tail K^+ = {rho in S^*Omega : phi^t(rho) stays uniformly bounded as t -> -infinity}. For a semiclassical/high-frequency sequence of long-living resonances k_j of -Delta_Omega with Re k_j -> infinity, choose associated purely outgoing resonant states u_j solving (Delta_Omega + k_j^2)u_j = 0 and normalized in the interaction region B(0,R_0).
