Under otherwise identical choices of Ω, g, R, boundary conditions, initial data, and parameters, what key differences, if any, arise in the resulting time-dependent solutions and spatially non-constant steady states—equivalently, in the qualitative space-use dynamics—solely from treating ki as a relative magnitude versus a probability-density-type quantity?

For the movement-only dynamic-memory models from Sect. 2.2.2 of Wang and Salmaniw—namely nonlocal advection-diffusion population models in which the density u_i(x,t) is biased by a dynamic cognitive map, possibly through auxiliary map variables such as p_i(x,t) or k_i(x,t), with perception operator a_{g,R}(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy—how does augmenting the population equation(s) by birth/death processes change the qualitative dynamics? In particular, do the resulting time-dependent and steady-state problems admit solutions, and how are the existence and profiles of spatially non-constant steady states altered relative to the corresponding movement-only models?

Let Ω be a bounded periodic domain (equivalently, a torus in higher dimensions), and consider the consumer-resource system u_t = D1Δu - γ∇·(u∇v_{g,R}) + cβuv/(α+v) - du, v_t = D2Δv + rv(1 - v/K) - βuv/(α+v), where u(x,t) and v(x,t) denote the consumer and resource densities, respectively, γ > 0 and D1, D2, r, K, β, α, c, d are positive constants, and v_{g,R} denotes the periodic spatial convolution from (2.5) with the top-hat detection kernel g from (2.3) of perceptual radius R. For admissible periodic initial data, in what sense (for example, weak, mild, or classical; local or global in time) do solutions to this time-dependent problem exist? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Let Ω be a bounded spatial domain with periodic boundary conditions (equivalently, a torus in higher dimensions), let g_R be the periodic top-hat detection function of perceptual radius R > 0, and define the perception operator by f^{g,R} = g_R *_{per} f. For n interacting populations u_i(x,t) with conflict-zone cognitive maps k_i(x,t), consider the memory-smearing extension of the conflict-zone model given, for i = 1, ..., n, by ∂_t u_i = d_i Δu_i - γ_i ∇·(u_i ∇k_i^{g,R}) and ∂_t k_i = ε_i Δk_i + u_i Σ_{j=1}^n ρ_{ij}u_j - (μ + βu_i)k_i, with periodic initial data and 0 < ε_i << d_i. In what sense (for example, weak, strong, or classical; local or global in time) do time-dependent solutions to this bounded periodic top-hat problem exist?

For the n-population, magnitude-valued conflict-zone memory system with perception, where k_i^{g,R}(x,t) := ∫_Ω k_i(y,t) g(x - y) dy and the unregularized model is ∂_t u_i = d_i Δu_i + γ_i ∇·(u_i ∇k_i^{g,R}), ∂_t k_i = u_i ∑_{j=1}^n ρ_ij u_j - (μ + βu_i) k_i, consider its memory-smearing regularization obtained by replacing the k_i-equation with ∂_t k_i = ε_i Δk_i + u_i ∑_{j=1}^n ρ_ij u_j - (μ + βu_i) k_i, with 0 < ε_i < d_i. When the two systems are posed on the same domain with the same compatible data, in what solution class and topology do solutions of the memory-smearing system converge, as each ε_i → 0+, to solutions of the conflict-zone memory system? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Let Omega be a bounded domain equipped with periodic boundary conditions (equivalently, a flat torus in higher dimensions), let g_R be the top-hat detection kernel of perceptual radius R, and let a^{g,R}(x,t) denote the corresponding periodic perception operator. For n interacting populations u_i(x,t) with conflict-memory variables k_i(x,t), consider the nonlocal-conflict-zone extension of the conflict-memory model given by
∂_t u_i = d_i Δu_i + gamma_i ∇·(u_i ∇k_i^{g,R}),
∂_t k_i = u_i^{g,R} sum_{j=1}^n rho_ij u_j - (mu + beta u_i) k_i,
for i = 1, ..., n, where d_i > 0, gamma_i >= 0, rho_ij >= 0, mu >= 0, beta >= 0, and the same top-hat kernel g_R and perceptual radius R are used for each population. In what sense do time-dependent solutions to this system exist on Omega under periodic boundary conditions?

Let Ω be a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions (equivalently, a torus in higher dimensions), let g be the top-hat detection kernel with perceptual radius R > 0, and define the perception operator by a^{g,R}(x,t) = ∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x−y)dy. For n interacting populations u_i and conflict-memory maps k_i, consider the nonlocal conflict-generation model obtained by keeping the movement equation from (2.13) and using the cognitive-map equation (2.16): ∂_t u_i = d_i Δu_i + γ_i ∇·(u_i ∇k_i^{g,R}) and ∂_t k_i = u_i^{g,R} Σ_{j=1}^n ρ_{ij}u_j − (μ + βu_i)k_i, for i = 1, ..., n, with the same perceptual kernel and perceptual radius for each population. In what sense do spatially non-constant steady-state solutions of this periodic bounded-domain problem exist, and what qualitative properties do these steady states exhibit? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Let Ω be a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions, let g be the top-hat detection kernel with perceptual radius R, and for any scalar field f define f^{g,R}(x,t)=∫_Ω f(y,t)g(x-y)dy. For n interacting populations u_i(x,t) with conflict-memory maps k_i(x,t), compare the spatially non-constant steady states of the local conflict-zone memory model ∂_t u_i=d_iΔu_i+γ_i∇·(u_i∇k_i^{g,R}), ∂_t k_i=u_i∑_{j=1}^nρ_iju_j−(μ+βu_i)k_i, and the nonlocal conflict-generation model ∂_t u_i=d_iΔu_i+γ_i∇·(u_i∇k_i^{g,R}), ∂_t k_i=u_i^{g,R}∑_{j=1}^nρ_iju_j−(μ+βu_i)k_i, where d_i>0, γ_i≥0, ρ_ij≥0, μ≥0, β≥0, and the same kernel/radius are used for each population. Assuming such spatially non-constant steady states exist in this periodic top-hat setting, how do their qualitative features differ between the two models, and hence how does nonlocal conflict generation alter the predicted space-use outcomes relative to model (2.13)? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Let Ω ⊂ ℝ^d be a bounded domain, and for i = 1, …, n let u_i(x,t) denote the density of population i and k_i(x,t) its cognitive map of conflict zones. Consider the time-dependent nonlocal conflict-zone model from Section 2.2.2 obtained from (2.13) by keeping the movement equation ∂_t u_i = d_i Δu_i + γ_i ∇·(u_i ∇k_{i,g,R}) and replacing the memory equation by ∂_t k_i = u_{i,g,R} Σ_{j=1}^n ρ_ij u_j − (μ + βu_i)k_i, where d_i > 0, γ_i ≥ 0, μ, β ≥ 0, the populations share the same perceptual radius R and the same top-hat detection function g_R, and f_{g,R}(x,t) denotes the perceived version of f via the top-hat kernel (with a bounded-domain definition near ∂Ω chosen so the nonlocal terms are meaningful). For suitable nonnegative initial data, under which notions of solution—weak, strong, or classical, and local or global in time—can one prove existence for this time-dependent problem when Ω is endowed, respectively, with zero-flux, homogeneous Neumann, or homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions?

For each of the two consumer-resource systems on a bounded domain Omega with periodic boundary conditions, where u(x,t) and v(x,t) denote the consumer and resource densities and q(x,t) is a dynamic cognitive map of previously found resources, namely
u_t = D1 Delta u - gamma div(u grad q_{g,R}) + c beta u v/(alpha+v) - d u,
v_t = D2 Delta v + r v(1-v/K) - beta u v/(alpha+v),
with either q_t = b v - mu q (model (2.18)) or q_t = b u v - (mu + xi u) q (model (2.19)), where q_{g,R}(x,t) = integral over Omega of q(y,t) g(x-y) dy and g is the top-hat detection kernel g(z)=1/(2R) for |z|<=R and 0 otherwise (or the corresponding radial top-hat kernel in higher dimensions), and with parameters D1, D2, gamma, c, beta, alpha, d, r, K, b > 0, mu >= 0, xi >= 0, in what solution sense do the time-dependent problems admit solutions for suitable initial data, do there exist spatially non-constant steady states, and what qualitative properties do such non-constant steady states possess?

Let Ω⊂R^n be a smooth bounded domain, let τ>0, d1>0, γ∈R, and let f∈C1(R+) satisfy f(0)=f(1)=0 and f(u)<0 for u>1. For nonnegative solutions u of the delayed scalar diffusion-advection equation u_t = d1Δu − γ∇·(u∇u(x,t−τ)) + f(u), posed with suitable compatible initial/history data, determine how the Shi et al. (2019) analysis carried out under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions changes when one instead imposes either periodic boundary conditions (equivalently, studies the problem on a torus) or homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on ∂Ω. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Consider the scalar delayed diffusion-advection model from equation (2.20), u_t = d_1 u_xx - gamma d/dx(u d/dx u_tau) + f(u), where u_tau(x,t)=u(x,t-tau), d_1>0, gamma in R, tau>0, and f in C^1(R_+) is of logistic type with f(0)=f(1)=0 and f(u)<0 for u>1. On a bounded one-dimensional periodic domain Omega=(0,L), replace the local delayed cue u_tau by its top-hat perceptual average u_tau^{g,R}(x,t)=integral_Omega g_R(x-y)u(y,t-tau)dy, with g_R(z)=(2R)^(-1) for |z|<=R and 0 otherwise, interpreted periodically. How does this single-discrete-delay plus top-hat-nonlocal-perception modification change the Shi et al. (2019) stability/bifurcation analysis and the resulting dynamical outcomes, especially the stability of the spatially constant state and the onset and qualitative type of nonconstant spatiotemporal patterns, in the periodic setting where no boundary truncation of the kernel is required?

For the one-dimensional discrete-delay scalar model from Section 2.3.1, namely
u_t = D1 u_xx + D2 d/dx(u d/dx u(x,t-tau)) + f(u(x,t), ubar(t)) for x in Omega=(0,L), t>0,
where tau>0, D1>0, D2 is real, and ubar(t) = |Omega|^{-1} integral_Omega u(y,t) dy is the spatial average of the population over the whole domain, under what assumptions on the coefficients, the growth law f, and the prescribed initial/history data on Omega x [-tau,0] does the problem with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions u_x(0,t)=u_x(L,t)=0 admit a unique solution for t>0? In the same model, can analogous existence-and-uniqueness results be established on bounded domains in higher spatial dimensions or under other boundary conditions?

Let Omega be a bounded domain in R^n, let tau,sigma > 0, let d be a real parameter and lambda > 0, and consider the delayed diffusion-advection equation
u_t = Delta u + d div(u grad u_tau) + lambda u F(u,u_sigma) in Omega for t > 0,
where u_tau(x,t) = u(x,t-tau) and u_sigma(x,t) = integral over Omega of K(x,y)u(y,t-sigma)dy for a sufficiently regular spatial kernel K(x,y). Under what assumptions on the domain Omega, the kernel K, the nonlinearity F, and the prescribed initial history of u does the homogeneous Dirichlet problem u = 0 on partial Omega for t > 0 admit a unique time-dependent solution in a precisely stated solution class?

For the delayed consumer-resource system (2.24) in the paper, where u(x,t) denotes the consumer density and v(x,t) denotes the resource density, tau > 0, d11 > 0, d22 > 0, d21 >= 0, and in one spatial dimension on a bounded interval I one has u_t = d22 u_xx - d21 d/dx(u d/dx v(x,t-tau)) + f(u,v) and v_t = d11 v_xx + g(u,v), determine assumptions on the reaction terms f and g and on suitably regular compatible initial/history data under which the time-dependent problem with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions u_x = v_x = 0 on partial I admits a unique solution. Moreover, does an analogous existence-uniqueness theory hold for the natural higher-dimensional version on a bounded smooth domain Omega subset of R^n, obtained by replacing u_xx and v_xx with Delta u and Delta v and replacing d/dx(u d/dx v(x,t-tau)) with div(u grad v(x,t-tau))?

Let a_tau denote the delayed advective potential in the discrete-delay models (2.20) and (2.24), so that a_tau = u(x,t-tau) in the scalar equation (2.20) and a_tau = v(x,t-tau) in the one-dimensional consumer-resource system (2.24). For the corresponding top-hat-perception extensions obtained by replacing a_tau with its perception convolution a_tau^{g,R}(x,t) = integral over Omega of a_tau(y,t) g(x-y) dy, where g is the top-hat detection function with perceptual radius R, determine on a bounded spatial domain with periodic boundary conditions in what precise sense the resulting time-dependent problems admit solutions. In particular, under what assumptions on the delayed initial histories and on the reaction terms can one establish an existence theory for the top-hat-perception version of (2.20) with d1>0, gamma in R, and logistic-type f in C^1(R+), and for the top-hat-perception version of the one-dimensional system (2.24) with d11,d22>0, d21>=0, and reaction terms f(u,v), g(u,v)?

For the explicit discrete-delay movement models of Section 2.3.1 obtained from the scalar equation u_t = d1 Delta u - gamma div(u nabla u_tau) + f(u) and the one-dimensional consumer-resource system u_t = d22 u_xx - d21 (u (v_tau)_x)_x + f(u,v), v_t = d11 v_xx + g(u,v), where u_tau(x,t) = u(x,t - tau), v_tau(x,t) = v(x,t - tau), tau > 0, d1 > 0, gamma is real, d11,d22 > 0, and d21 >= 0, replace the delayed local potential by its top-hat perceptual average a_tau^{R}(x,t) = integral over Omega of a(y,t - tau) g_R(x-y) dy (with a = u in the scalar model and a = v in the consumer-resource model), where g_R(z) = 1/(2R) for |z| <= R and 0 otherwise. On a bounded one-dimensional domain, preferably first with periodic boundary conditions as suggested in the paper, in what sense do solutions of these nonlocal-perception, discrete-delay problems converge as R -> 0+ to the corresponding local delayed problems obtained by replacing a_tau^{R} with a(x,t - tau), and what qualitative differences persist between the local and nonlocal delayed solutions?

Let Ω ⊂ R^n be a smooth bounded domain, and consider the distributed-delay movement model
∂u/∂t = d1Δu + d2∇·(u∇v1) + f(u,v2) in Ω × (0,∞),
with homogeneous Neumann boundary condition ∂_n u = 0 on ∂Ω × (0,∞), where d1 > 0, d2 ∈ R, and for i = 1,2,
vi(x,t) = ∫_{-∞}^t ∫_Ω G_N(d1;x,y,t-s) Gi(t-s;τi) u(y,s) dy ds,
with τ1 > 0 the memory/learning delay, τ2 > 0 the maturation delay, and each Gi chosen from the weak/strong Gamma kernels Gw(t;τ)=τ^{-1}e^{-t/τ} and Gs(t;τ)=tτ^{-2}e^{-t/τ} (hence covering all four weak/strong combinations). Under what assumptions on the reaction term f, the past history u(·,s) for s≤0, and—more generally—on a space-time kernel K(x,y,t,s) that specializes to the Neumann heat-kernel product above, does problem (2.30) admit a unique solution? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Can one formulate and analyze, on a bounded spatial domain Omega, a knowledge-based movement model in which a dynamic cognitive map a(x,t) of the type introduced in Section 2.2 (together with its own auxiliary evolution law from the chosen dynamic-map model) is coupled to nonlocal perception and an explicit temporal delay—either discrete, for example K(t) = delta(t-tau), or distributed via one of the weak/strong Gamma kernels in (2.27)—through the spatiotemporal convolution v_a(x,t) = ∫_{-∞}^t ∫_Omega G(d_3,x,y,t-s) K(t-s) a(y,s) dy ds, so that the population equation has the form u_t = d_1 Delta u + d_2 div(u grad v_a) + f(u); and, for such a bounded-domain model, how does the addition of the discrete or distributed delay change the resulting space-use outcomes relative to the corresponding no-delay dynamic-cognitive-map model, and can a standard boot-strapping argument of the kind used for simpler delay models establish existence and uniqueness of time-dependent solutions when nonlocal perception and delay are both present?

For the Section 2.4 bi-component memory diffusion-advection model on a spatial domain Omega, given by partial_t m_s = alpha_s a_s(x,t) - beta_s m_s, partial_t m_l = alpha_l a_l(x,t) - beta_l m_l with alpha_l < alpha_s and beta_l < beta_s, a(x,t)=c_1 m_s(x,t)+c_2 m_l(x,t) (with application-dependent signs of c_1,c_2), and partial_t u = d Delta u - div(u grad a_{g,R}), where a_{g,R}(x,t)=int_Omega a(y,t) g(x-y) dy for a detection kernel g and perceptual radius R, determine the distinct mathematical roles of the short-term layer m_s and the long-term layer m_l in the well-posedness of the model and in the existence and qualitative form of steady-state space-use profiles, and decide whether the simultaneous inclusion of both memory layers is necessary and/or sufficient for any space-use phenomena that cannot occur in otherwise comparable models with only one memory compartment.

For the newly proposed continuous-time deterministic diffusion-advection model in Section 2.4, where short- and long-term memory layers m_s and m_l satisfy ∂_t m_s = α_s a_s(x,t) - β_s m_s and ∂_t m_l = α_l a_l(x,t) - β_l m_l with α_l < α_s and β_l < β_s, the cognitive map is a(x,t) = c_1 m_s(x,t) + c_2 m_l(x,t), and movement is governed by ∂_t u = dΔu - ∇·(u∇a_{g,R}) with a_{g,R}(x,t) = ∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy for a detection kernel g and perceptual radius R, can one give a mathematically and biologically meaningful correspondence between this two-compartment short/long-memory mechanism and a time-since-last-visit (TSLV) rule, and, under a precisely stated predictive-performance or model-comparison criterion for comparable models, does the full two-compartment model outperform the one-compartment reductions that retain only short-term memory or only long-term memory, thereby linking the paper’s continuous-time deterministic PDE framework to the discrete-time probabilistic TSLV models of Schlagel et al. (2017)?

Within the Section 2.4 multi-layer cognitive-map PDE framework, for example the short/long-term memory model in which m_s and m_l satisfy ∂_t m_s = α_s a_s(x,t) - β_s m_s and ∂_t m_l = α_l a_l(x,t) - β_l m_l with α_l < α_s and β_l < β_s, the cognitive map is a(x,t) = c_1 m_s(x,t) + c_2 m_l(x,t), and the population density u moves according to ∂_t u = dΔu - ∇·(u∇a_{g,R}) with perceived potential a_{g,R}(x,t) = ∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy for a detection kernel g and perceptual radius R, how does the prioritization of information—implemented through the relative ordering/strength of the advection effects associated with distinct information layers or covariates—affect the resulting space-use patterns and, in settings where persistence/extinction is meaningful, the persistence/extinction outcomes? In particular, can such a model mechanistically explain why avoiding predation may take priority over seeking food, and what does it predict when that priority is reversed?

Let Ω⊂ℝ be a one-dimensional spatial domain, let x0∈Ω be a fixed den site, let m=m(x,t) be a prescribed local resource density, and let u=u(x,t) denote the density of foragers. Define the satisfaction variable s(x,t)=m(x,t)/u(x,t) and the starvation-dependent switch ω̃(s)=γ+ for 0≤s<1 and ω̃(s)=0 for 1≤s<∞, where d>0 and 0<γ<γ+. For the learning model ∂_t u = ∂_x(d ∂_x u - u ∂_x[ω̃(s)m + γ|x-x0|]), which turns resource attraction on when the forager is hungry and otherwise leaves den attraction dominant, in what precise sense can one prove existence of solutions to problem (2.38) for appropriate initial and boundary data, given that the equation may remain linear in u but has irregular coefficients at higher order?

For the one-dimensional starvation-driven learning model introduced in Section 2.5, namely
\partial_t u=\partial_x\!\left(d\,\partial_x u-u\,\partial_x\big[\tilde{\omega}(s)m+\gamma\|x-x_0\|\big]\right),
with satisfaction measure s(x,t)=m(x,t)/u(x,t), switch \tilde{\omega}(s)=\gamma^+ for 0\le s<1 and 0 for 1\le s<\infty, and 0<\gamma<\gamma^+, how should one formulate a nonlocal-perception extension consistent with the paper’s perception operator a_{g,R}(x,t)=\int_{\Omega} a(y,t)g(x-y)\,dy and with the requirement that any variable advection rate appear inside the gradient, i.e. in the form -\nabla\cdot\big(u\nabla(\gamma(x,t,u)a_{g,R})\big)? In particular, can one construct such a combined model, for example using the local-versus-expected resource ratio s(x,t)=m(x,t)/\bar m(t) suggested immediately after Open Problem 36, and then characterize how its qualitative solution behaviour differs from that of the learning-only model and from that of a perception-only model without the satisfaction-based learning mechanism? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

For the newly proposed local one-dimensional model
∂u/∂t = ∂/∂x(d ∂u/∂x - u ∂/∂x(omega_tilde(s(x,t)) m(x,t) + gamma|x-x0|)),
where u(x,t) is the forager density on a one-dimensional domain Ω, m(x,t) is the local resource density, x0∈Ω is a central den site, 0 < gamma < gamma_plus, s(x,t)=m(x,t)/u(x,t), and omega_tilde(s)=gamma_plus for 0 ≤ s < 1 and omega_tilde(s)=0 for 1 ≤ s < ∞ so that hungry foragers prioritize resource attraction while otherwise defaulting to home attraction, determine whether this starvation-driven switching mechanism can generate nontrivial spatiotemporal dynamics or pattern formation, whether such switching is biologically beneficial or detrimental to the species, and whether other satisfaction measures—especially the alternative s(x,t)=m(x,t)/m(t), with m(t) the average resource density at time t—can serve as comparable behaviour-modification mechanisms in the same modelling framework. ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

For any previously introduced PDE model in this paper whose existence theory remains open, determine—within the natural solution class for that model and under its prescribed domain, boundary conditions, kernel/delay structure, and, for evolutionary problems, fixed initial data—whether there are necessary and/or sufficient conditions ensuring that the model admits a unique non-trivial solution once existence has been established.

For the dynamic-memory advection–diffusion and advection–diffusion–reaction problems introduced in §2.2.2, in which nonlocality enters through a perceived potential of the form a_g,R(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy, work on a bounded domain and replace the periodic 'spill-over' interpretation of the top-hat perceptual kernel by the boundary-truncated, renormalized operator used in (4.3) (in one dimension, T_R[a](x,t)=|((x-R,x+R)∩(0,L))|^{-1}∫_{(x-R,x+R)∩(0,L)} a(y,t)dy). Under what hypotheses do solutions exist when homogeneous Neumann or homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed, and how do the resulting existence results compare with those in the corresponding periodic-boundary setting? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

For bounded-domain nonlocal animal-movement models with perception operator a_{g,R}(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy, where g is a perceptual kernel with perceptual radius R and, away from boundary effects, is typically taken to be symmetric, normalized to unit mass, nonincreasing from the origin, and convergent to a Dirac delta as R→0+, what alternative boundary-aware definitions or constructions of g can replace the usual periodic spillover interpretation or the cutoff-type kernel near x∈∂Ω so that the kernel remains biologically reasonable while the resulting nonlocal movement equations still lend themselves to rigorous mathematical analysis?

For a knowledge-based animal movement PDE with explicit population dynamics, let u(x,t) denote population density on a spatial domain Ω over a prescribed time interval (t', t_max), and define relative fitness by Net Growth(u) = ∫_{t'}^{t_max}∫_Ω f(x,t,u) dx dt, where f(x,t,u) is the explicit growth/death reaction term obtained after spatial integration removes the movement terms. What biological consequences and predictions does this fitness measure produce for such models? In particular, do cognition-dependent parameters—especially perceptual radius and advection rate toward or away from environmental covariates—admit optimal ranges that increase relative fitness in this sense, and how does that fitness comparison differ from the corresponding null-hypothesis model with no cognitive-based movement mechanism? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

For the paper’s PDE movement models that combine cognitive memory and nonlocal perception with population dynamics—i.e. models whose advective bias is driven by a nonlocal perception operator a_{g,R}(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy, with particular attention to the top-hat detection function—can one formulate a useful principal-eigenvalue problem, or analogous threshold problem such as a basic reproduction number when that is the natural object, for the linearization about the trivial steady state, and determine how that threshold quantity depends on the perceptual radius R, the advection strength, the diffusion coefficients, and the memory uptake and decay parameters?

For the nonlocal-perception movement model (2.4) discussed in the paper, with forager density u(x,t) satisfying partial_t u = d partial_xx u - gamma partial_x(u partial_x h), perceived resource field h(x,t) = int_Omega m(y,t) g(x-y) dy, and conserved total population int_Omega u(x,t) dx = 1, compare the optimal-strategy predictions obtained from the two correlation-based criteria FS = int_{t_*}^{t_max} int_Omega u(x,t)m(x,t) dx dt, where t_* is chosen after transients have settled, and FE = (1/t_max) int_0^{t_max} int_Omega sqrt(u(x,t)m(x,t)) dx dt (with the paper's normalization convention when needed). Do these two measures select the same optimal movement strategies—such as the same diffusion rate d, attraction/advection strength gamma, perceptual kernel g, and perceptual radius R—or can they rank strategies differently? More generally, within knowledge-based movement models with explicit resources and no birth/death dynamics for which both measures are well defined, what strategy predictions does each measure produce?

For knowledge-based movement models with explicit resource density m(x,t) but no explicit birth/death dynamics—such as the conserved-population nonlocal perception model (2.4) for population density u(x,t)—can one formulate one or more biologically meaningful measures of foraging success that improve on the overlap-based quantities int_{t'}^{t_max} int_Omega u(x,t)m(x,t) dx dt and the normalized Bhattacharyya-type overlap measure (4.7) by incorporating the costs of foraging, including metabolic or other expenditures, so that the resulting measure reflects a species’ fitness as a consequence of successful foraging rather than merely predicting success from correlation with resource density?

For the two-pack Lewis–Moorcroft fitness framework discussed in Sect. 4.2.3, and in particular for the dynamic scent-marking / cognitive-map model (2.11), can one carry out a comparable analysis of optimal movement strategies using the pack-fitness functional r_u = -μ_0 + ln(σψ) - α∫_Ω u(x)v(x) dx + ln(∫_Ω u(x) H(u(x),v(x)) dx), where u and v are the packs’ space-use distributions, μ_0 > 0 is the natural mortality rate, α is the inter-pack aggression coefficient, σ is the prey-to-offspring conversion rate, ψ is the encounter rate, and H(u,v) is the average prey density induced by the space-use patterns u and v; and, within this framework, how does the resulting pack fitness of u change as the cognitive movement mechanism is varied, especially through the choice of perceptual kernel g or perceptual radius R? If one instead studies another cognitive movement model with no growth dynamics or explicit resources, what biologically justified modification of the functional (4.8) is needed before the same optimal-strategy comparison is meaningful? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

Within a single deterministic PDE model of knowledge-based animal movement that simultaneously includes (i) a cognitive movement mechanism, (ii) an explicit resource density or resource variable, and (iii) explicit birth/death (reaction) processes, compare the success criteria introduced in the paper—population-growth/persistence criteria such as net growth over a time window and principal-eigenvalue/basic-reproduction-number based fitness, resource-overlap criteria such as foraging success and normalized foraging efficiency, and, when appropriate, a Lewis-Moorcroft-style reproductive-fitness functional. For the same family of admissible cognitive strategies or parameter choices (for example, perceptual kernel or radius, advection or diffusion rates, or memory parameters), do these measures rank strategies consistently, or can they fundamentally disagree about which strategy is optimal?

For the two static cognitive-map movement models with prescribed resource density m(x,t) on a spatial domain Ω,
(1) ∂_t u = dΔu − γ∇·(u∇∫_Ω [m(y,t)/m̄(t)] g(x−y)dy), where m̄(t)=|Ω|^{-1}∫_Ω m(y,t)dy,
and
(2) ∂_t u = dΔu − γ∇·(u∇∫_Ω [m(y,t)/u(y,t)] g(x−y)dy),
with g a perceptual kernel (for example local, top-hat, Gaussian, or exponential, with perceptual radius R), determine which knowledge-based movement strategies maximize the foraging success functional FS = ∫_{t_*}^{t_max}∫_Ω u(x,t)m(x,t) dx dt, where t_* is chosen after transient dynamics have settled, and determine under what environmental conditions or for which model ((2.7) versus (2.8)) a given strategy is advantageous; then compare these optimality predictions with those for the benchmark nonlocal perception model ∂_t u = dΔu − γ∇·(u∇h), h(x,t)=∫_Ω m(y,t)g(x−y)dy, as discussed in Fagan et al. (2017).

For the knowledge-based animal-movement models surveyed in this review, namely the nonlocal reaction-diffusion-advection PDEs in which cognition enters through the advective potential via perception, memory, cognitive maps, temporal delays, and learning-related mechanisms, determine how each added modelling component changes the local stability of spatially constant steady states and, especially in otherwise environmentally homogeneous settings, classify the spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal patterns that can arise; identify the bifurcation or other dynamical mechanisms responsible for those patterns; relate the analytical predictions to the patterns already observed numerically, including temporally periodic uniform states, stripe states, and checkerboard states; decide whether further pattern classes are possible; and explain how such patterns should be interpreted mathematically, biologically, and, where data are available, in relation to patterns observed in nature.

For the scalar nonlocal aggregation/segregation equation (2.9) on the natural unbounded one-dimensional travelling-wave domain Omega = R, namely u_t = d u_xx - gamma d/dx(u d/dx u_{g,R}) with u_{g,R}(x,t) = integral over R of u(y,t) g(x-y) dy and g chosen as one of the perceptual kernels in (2.3) (top-hat, Gaussian, or exponential, with perceptual radius R >= 0), do there exist travelling-wave solutions u(x,t) = w(x-ct)? If so, can the wave speed c be computed or estimated as a function of the detection kernel g, the perceptual radius R, and the advection and diffusion rates gamma and d? ([math.ualberta.ca](https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~hwang/WangSalmaniwReview.pdf))

For the scalar discrete-delay explicit-memory model on the unbounded line, given by
u_t(x,t) = d1 u_xx(x,t) − γ ∂_x(u(x,t) ∂_x u(x,t−τ)) + f(u(x,t)),
with fixed delay τ > 0, diffusion coefficient d1 > 0, advection coefficient γ ∈ ℝ, and either (i) f ≡ 0 or (ii) a birth/death term f(u) (as in the discussion of (2.20), e.g. logistic-type), do there exist travelling-wave solutions of the form u(x,t) = w(x−ct)? If such waves exist, can one calculate or estimate the wave speed c, and determine how c depends on the delay τ and on the advection and diffusion parameters?

For the scalar distributed-delay animal-movement equation on an unbounded one-dimensional domain x∈R, u_t = d1 u_xx - γ ∂_x(u ∂_x v_u) + f(u), where v_u(x,t)=∫_{-∞}^t ∫_R G(d3,x,y,t-s) K(t-s;τ)u(y,s) dy ds with G(d3,x,y,t-s) the heat-equation Green function of diffusion rate d3 and K equal to either the weak kernel G_w(t;τ)=τ^{-1}e^{-t/τ} or the strong kernel G_s(t;τ)=tτ^{-2}e^{-t/τ}, do travelling-wave solutions u(x,t)=w(x-ct) exist; and, if so, can the wave speed c be computed or estimated as a function of the delay parameter τ and of the advection/diffusion parameters governing the model?

Consider the n-species nonlocal system on an unbounded one-dimensional spatial domain, given by ∂_t u_i = d_i Δu_i − ∇·(u_i ∇(∑_{j=1}^n γ_{ij}(u_j)_{g,R})) for i = 1, …, n, where (u_j)_{g,R}(x,t) = ∫_ℝ u_j(y,t) g(x−y) dy and g is chosen from the detection kernels in (2.3): the top-hat kernel g(z) = 1/(2R) for |z| ≤ R and 0 otherwise, the Gaussian kernel g(z) = (1/(√(2π)R))e^(−z^2/(2R^2)), or the exponential kernel g(z) = (1/(2R))e^(−|z|/R). Do there exist travelling-wave solutions of the form u_i(x,t) = W_i(x−ct) for this system? If so, can the common wave speed c be computed or estimated as a function of the detection-kernel choice, the perceptual radius R, and the advection/diffusion parameters γ_{ij} and d_i?

For the explicit dynamic-map nonlocal system (2.11), consider first its single-species reduction on an unbounded one-dimensional domain, u_t = d u_xx - gamma (u (p_{g,R})_x)_x and p_t = alpha u - mu p, where p_{g,R}(x,t) = integral over R of p(y,t) g(x-y) dy and g is one of the three detection functions in (2.3) (top-hat, Gaussian, or exponential) with perceptual radius R > 0. Do there exist nontrivial travelling-wave solutions of the form (u,p)(x,t) = (U,P)(x-ct)? If so, can the wave speed c be computed explicitly or estimated in terms of the detection function g, the perceptual radius R, and the remaining model parameters d, gamma, alpha, mu? Finally, can analogous travelling-wave existence and wave-speed results be extended from this single-species case to the full n-species system (2.11)?

For the single-species dynamic-memory model (2.9), u_t = d u_xx - gamma d/dx( u d/dx u_{g,R} ) on x in (0,L), t>0, with d>0, gamma real, 0<R<L, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0, and boundary-truncated top-hat perception operator u_{g,R}(x) = (1/(R+x)) int_0^{x+R} u(y)dy for 0<x<R, u_{g,R}(x) = (1/(2R)) int_{x-R}^{x+R} u(y)dy for R<x<L-R, and u_{g,R}(x) = (1/(R+L-x)) int_{x-R}^L u(y)dy for L-R<x<L, does there exist a critical domain length L* = L*(R,gamma,d) such that the associated steady-state problem has only the trivial solution u identically 0 when 0<L<L* and admits at least one positive steady state u(x)>0 on (0,L) when L>L*; if so, how does L* depend on the perceptual radius R and the advection and diffusion parameters gamma and d, and can an analogous critical-threshold statement be extended to the n-species model (2.10)?

Is there a general numerical technique that can efficiently solve, on bounded spatial domains, the nonlocal dynamic-memory movement models introduced in Section 2.2.2—namely the PDE systems (2.9)–(2.19), whose movement terms involve perceptual/cognitive-map convolutions a_{g,R}(x,t)=∫_Ω a(y,t)g(x-y)dy or an appropriate boundary-modified version of this nonlocal term—when the boundary condition is not periodic (for example zero-flux, homogeneous Neumann, or homogeneous Dirichlet)?

Within the two-population implicit-memory conflict-zone setting most closely related to model (2.13), where
∂_t u_i = d_i Δu_i + γ_i ∇·(u_i ∇(g_i*k_i)),
∂_t k_i = u_i Σ_{j=1}^2 ρ_{ij}u_j − (μ + βu_i)k_i,
for i=1,2, with (g_i*k_i)(x,t)=∫_Ω k_i(y,t)g_i(x−y)dy and g_i a perceptual kernel of perceptual radius R_i, assume the chosen domain and boundary conditions admit a positive spatially constant steady state. How do unequal diffusion coefficients d_i, advection coefficients γ_i, perceptual radii R_i, and/or perceptual kernels g_i change the linear-stability/pattern-formation conclusions known from the symmetric or simplified implicit-memory case? In particular, do the trends summarized in §5.2.1 persist—namely, that decreasing R enlarges the unstable wavenumber set and leads to ill-posedness as R→0+, sufficiently large memory decay μ or sufficiently small update rate β suppresses pattern formation, larger advection enlarges the unstable wavenumber set, and diffusion/conflict rate ρ affects growth rates rather than the unstable wavenumber set—or, if not, under exactly which parameter regimes and boundary-condition assumptions do these conclusions change, without using a quasi-steady-state approximation?

Consider the implicit-memory multi-population conflict-zone model most closely related to equation (2.13): for i = 1, ..., n, let u_i(x,t) denote the density of population i and k_i(x,t) its memory of conflict zones, with perception defined by a_{g,R}(x,t) = integral_Omega a(y,t) g(x-y) dy. In the bounded one-dimensional periodic setting emphasized in the paper, with top-hat detection kernel g of perceptual radius R > 0 and movement-only dynamics, study the system partial_t u_i = d_i Delta u_i + gamma_i div(u_i grad((k_i)_{g,R})) and partial_t k_i = u_i sum_{j=1}^n rho_ij u_j - (mu + beta u_i) k_i, where d_i > 0, gamma_i >= 0, rho_ij >= 0, mu >= 0, and beta >= 0. Extending the two-population linear-stability and pattern-formation analysis discussed in Section 5.2.1, can one determine for n >= 3 how increasing the number of interacting populations changes the stability of positive constant steady states and the resulting spatiotemporal patterns, and in particular rigorously characterize the oscillatory behaviour observed for three populations and whether genuinely more complicated, possibly chaotic, dynamics can occur for three or more populations in this setting?

Determine a general characterization/classification of geodetic graphs: classify, up to isomorphism, all graphs G such that for every pair of distinct vertices u,v in V(G), there exists exactly one geodesic in G joining u and v, where a geodesic is a shortest u-v path.

Let G be a graph homeomorphic to the Petersen graph, meaning that G is obtained from the Petersen graph by subdividing edges. Call a vertex of degree at least 3 a node, and call a segment a path whose only nodes are its endpoints. A geodesic is a shortest path, and G is geodetic if every pair of distinct vertices is joined by a unique geodesic. Is it true that G is geodetic if and only if (i) every path consisting of two successive segments is a geodesic in G, (ii) every cycle containing exactly five segments has odd length, and (iii) all cycles containing exactly six segments have the same length, where path and cycle length are measured by number of edges?

Let M be a Moore graph of degree k and diameter d, so |V(M)| = 1 + k Σ_{j=1}^d (k - 1)^{j-1}, with k >= 3 and M not isomorphic to K_n for any n >= 5. Let G be a graph homeomorphic to M, where 'homeomorphic' means obtained by subdividing edges, and call a path in G a segment if its only vertices of degree at least 3 are its endpoints. The paper states that G is geodetic (that is, every pair of distinct vertices is joined by a unique shortest path) if (i) every path of G formed by d successive segments is a geodesic, (ii) every cycle of G containing 2d + 1 segments has odd length, and (iii) all cycles of G containing 2d + 2 segments have the same length. Is the converse true? Equivalently, if G is geodetic, must conditions (i)-(iii) necessarily hold?

Assuming the characterization conjecture stated immediately before Section B—namely, that for graphs homeomorphic to the Petersen graph the three conditions listed in Section A are necessary as well as sufficient for geodeticity—can it be rigorously proved that, for every integer d ≥ 2, the paper’s general enumeration count of geodetic graphs of diameter d homeomorphic to the Petersen graph is the binomial coefficient (d + 3 choose 5), where a graph is geodetic if every pair of distinct vertices is joined by a unique geodesic and two graphs are homeomorphic if both are obtained by inserting vertices on edges?

Assuming the paper’s preceding characterization conjecture for graphs homeomorphic to Moore graphs—namely, that a graph G homeomorphic to a Moore graph of diameter d is geodetic exactly when (i) every path of d successive segments is a geodesic, (ii) every cycle with 2d+1 segments has odd length, and (iii) all cycles with 2d+2 segments have the same length—can one devise an explicit computer program (the paper informally says “to be run in a modern computer in real time”) which, for the Hoffman-Singleton graph H (the Moore graph of degree 7 and diameter 2), constructs and solves the associated geodetic system of linear Diophantine equations, enumerates all of its natural-number solutions, and thereby, for each integer D ≥ 2, generates every geodetic graph of diameter D homeomorphic to H and determines the paper’s “general number” of such graphs, i.e. the total count rather than only the count up to isomorphism? ([dizzw.com](https://dizzw.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Deutsche-internationale-Zeitschrift-f%C3%BCr-zeitgen%C3%B6ssische-Wissenschaft-%E2%84%9636-2022.pdf))

Assuming the characterization conjectures stated in Section A, does there exist a common hidden structure in the distribution of the variables of the geodetic systems of Diophantine equations associated with K4, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman-Singleton graph that would allow one to construct the geodetic system of Diophantine equations generating every geodetic graph homeomorphic, by edge subdivision, to the still-undiscovered diameter-2 Moore graph of degree 57, including that Moore graph itself? ([dizzw.com](https://dizzw.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Deutsche-internationale-Zeitschrift-f%C3%BCr-zeitgen%C3%B6ssische-Wissenschaft-%E2%84%9636-2022.pdf))

Do there exist infinitely many graphs G that are both geodetic and strongly regular, where geodetic means that every pair of distinct vertices of G is joined by a unique geodesic and strongly regular means that G is k-regular with integers λ and μ such that adjacent vertices have exactly λ common neighbors and nonadjacent vertices have exactly μ common neighbors; or does there exist at least one such graph G that is not a Moore graph, meaning a regular graph of degree k and diameter d with |V(G)| = 1 + k Σ_{j=1}^d (k - 1)^{j - 1}? ([dizzw.com](https://dizzw.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Deutsche-internationale-Zeitschrift-f%C3%BCr-zeitgen%C3%B6ssische-Wissenschaft-%E2%84%9636-2022.pdf))

For a computer network modeled by a geodetic graph G (that is, a graph in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by a unique geodesic), and specifically among homeomorphic geodetic graphs of a fixed diameter d that represent the same network topology, how does changing the topology of connections affect the network's operational-quality indices named in the paper—systemic hierarchy, diameter, vertex connectivity, reliability, cost, and flexibility of topological change? ([dizzw.com](https://dizzw.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Deutsche-internationale-Zeitschrift-f%C3%BCr-zeitgen%C3%B6ssische-Wissenschaft-%E2%84%9636-2022.pdf))

In the topological design of complex computer networks, and in the geodetic-graph setting emphasized in the paper, can one determine a single unified model that simultaneously takes into account multiple characteristics of the quality of network operation—such as systemic hierarchy, diameter, vertex connectivity, reliability, cost, and flexibility of topological change—and also determine an adequate technique for optimizing those characteristics within that one model? ([dizzw.com](https://dizzw.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Deutsche-internationale-Zeitschrift-f%C3%BCr-zeitgen%C3%B6ssische-Wissenschaft-%E2%84%9636-2022.pdf))

Let G be a locally finite simple geodetic graph, and let t be a natural number. Suppose C is an embedded cycle in G (that is, a cycle with no repeated vertices except its initial/final vertex) such that the diameter of V(C), measured in the graph metric of G, is greater than t, and such that C has minimum length among all embedded cycles in G whose diameter is greater than t. Must C contain a contiguous subpath with t + 1 edges that is a geodesic in G?

For a fixed ν in [0,1], let μ be a non-negative finite Borel measure on R^3 with μ(R^3)=ν, let Vμ(x)=∫R^3 |x−y|^(-1) dμ(y), and let Hμ be the distinguished self-adjoint realization on L^2(R^3,C^4) of Hμ = D0−Vμ, where D0 = −i α·∇ + β in units m=c=ħ=1. Is the first gap eigenvalue (equivalently, the first min-max level in the paper’s setup) always bounded below by the one-centre hydrogenic value, namely λ1(Hμ) ≥ λ1(D0−ν/|x|)=√(1−ν^2), so that among all non-negative charge distributions of total charge ν the most attractive one is the point charge νδ0 (up to translation)?

Let mu be a nonnegative finite measure on R^3 with total charge nu := mu(R^3) <= 1, and define the electrostatic potential V_mu(x) := -(mu * |.|^{-1})(x). Let D_0 = -i alpha·nabla + beta on L^2(R^3, C^4), and let lambda_1(D_0 + V_mu) denote the first min-max level in the spectral gap (-1,1) of the distinguished self-adjoint extension of D_0 + V_mu. Is it true that for every such mu one has lambda_1(D_0 + V_mu) >= lambda_1(D_0 - nu/|x|) = sqrt(1 - nu^2)? In other words, among all nonnegative charge distributions with fixed total charge nu <= 1, is the lowest gap level minimized when the whole charge is concentrated at a single point?

Let D0 = -iα·∇ + β on L^2(R^3, C^4), in units m = c = ħ = 1, and let λ1(D0 - μ * |x|^{-1}) denote the first eigenvalue in the spectral gap (-1,1) of the distinguished self-adjoint Dirac operator with Coulomb potential generated by a non-negative finite Borel measure μ on R^3. If ν := μ(R^3) belongs to [0,1], is it always true that λ1(D0 - μ * |x|^{-1}) ≥ λ1(D0 - ν|x|^{-1}) = √(1 - ν^2), i.e. that among all charge distributions with fixed total charge ν, the smallest gap eigenvalue is attained when the whole charge is concentrated at a single point (up to translation)?

For the space-homogeneous Cauchy problem ∂_t f(t,v)=Q(f,f)(t,v) on [0,∞)×R^d, where Q is the standard non-cutoff Boltzmann collision operator (2.2) with collision kernel B satisfying the inverse-power-law bounds (2.3) for some 0<s<1 and very soft parameters γ+2s<0, does every sufficiently smooth initial datum f_0(v) with sufficient decay as |v|→∞ and finite mass, energy, and entropy generate a global-in-time classical solution for arbitrary data, rather than only in a perturbative near-Maxwellian regime? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2204.06401))

For the inhomogeneous non-cutoff Boltzmann Cauchy problem ∂t f + v·∇x f = Q(f,f), with the standard inverse-power-law non-cutoff collision kernel B(|v-v*|,cosθ) of the form (2.3) and in the hard-potential regime gamma > 0, can one prove a short-time classical existence theorem for generic sufficiently smooth initial data whose velocity decay is only polynomial, for example f0(x,v) ≲ ⟨v⟩^{-q} for some sufficiently large q, instead of the Gaussian velocity decay required by the currently documented hard-potential Cauchy theory? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/2204.06401))

For the Cauchy problem for the inhomogeneous Boltzmann equation on [0,infinity) x T^d_x x R^d_v, partial_t f + v . grad_x f = Q(f,f), f(0,x,v) = f_in(x,v) >= 0, with Q the standard non-cutoff Boltzmann collision operator for inverse-power-law interactions (so the collision kernel has the form B(|v-v_*|, cos theta) = |v-v_*|^gamma b(cos theta), with a nonintegrable angular singularity of the usual physical type), can one prove that every smooth initial datum f_in in a class admitting short-time classical solvability gives rise to a global-in-time smooth solution, without any smallness assumption near a Maxwellian or near vacuum? More concretely, can one establish constants m_0, M_0, E_0, H_0 such that for all t >= 0 and x in T^d one has 0 < m_0 <= integral_{R^d} f(t,x,v) dv <= M_0, integral_{R^d} |v|^2 f(t,x,v) dv <= E_0, and integral_{R^d} f(t,x,v) log f(t,x,v) dv <= H_0, which Theorem 3.1 would then turn into global smoothness?

Let f=f(t,v)≥0 be a classical space-homogeneous solution of ∂_t f = Q(f,f) on [0,T)×ℝ^d, where Q is either the non-cutoff Boltzmann collision operator with parameters (γ,s) or the Landau operator (the case s=1), and assume the potential is very soft, i.e. γ+2s<0 (so, for Landau, γ<−2). If the initial data have finite mass, finite energy, finite entropy, and enough decay as |v|→∞ to justify the homogeneous conservation laws for classical solutions, can one obtain an unconditional a priori L^∞_v bound for f on every finite time interval [0,T] from prescribed data alone?

Let f:[0,T]xR^3->[0,infinity) be a classical solution of the space-homogeneous Landau equation in dimension 3 with Coulomb kernel, namely partial_t f = Q_L(f,f), where Q_L is the Landau-Coulomb operator Q_L(f,f)(v) = div_v int_{R^3} |v-v_*|^(-1) (I - ((v-v_*) tensor (v-v_*))/|v-v_*|^2) (f(v_*) grad_v f(v) - f(v) grad_{v_*} f(v_*)) dv_*, and let f_0(v)=f(0,v). Is it true that every such classical solution satisfies the universal estimate ||f(t,.)||_{L^infty(R^3)} <= sqrt(250/(9 pi)) ||f_0||_{L^infty(R^3)} for every t in [0,T]? In particular, would this dimension-three, mass-momentum-energy-independent L-infinity bound rule out finite-time blow-up for the space-homogeneous Landau-Coulomb equation?

Let f:(-\infty,0]\times \mathbb{R}^3 \to [0,\infty) be a smooth classical ancient solution of the space-homogeneous Landau equation with Coulomb potential, \partial_t f = Q(f,f), where Q is the standard Landau-Coulomb collision operator in velocity space, for instance
Q(f,f)(v)=\nabla_v\cdot \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |v-v_*|^{-1}\Big(I-\frac{(v-v_*)\otimes (v-v_*)}{|v-v_*|^2}\Big)\big(f(v_*)\nabla_v f(v)-f(v)\nabla_{v_*}f(v_*)\big)\,dv_*.
Assume that 0 <= f(t,v) <= 1 for every (t,v) in (-\infty,0]\times \mathbb{R}^3, and that for every t <= 0 there exists a constant C_t < \infty such that
\int_{\mathbb{R}^3} f(t,v)\langle v\rangle^{-1}\,dv \le C_t, \qquad \langle v\rangle=(1+|v|^2)^{1/2}.
Must f be a stationary Maxwellian, i.e. a time-independent Maxwellian equilibrium of the Landau-Coulomb equation?

In the inhomogeneous, boundary-free Boltzmann/Landau settings considered in Section 3.1 of the paper (namely, the same regimes as Theorems 3.1 and 3.2, so excluding the very soft-potential case), let f(t,x,v) solve partial_t f + v·nabla_x f = Q(f,f) or partial_t f + v·nabla_x f = Q_L(f,f). Can one prove from the equation and admissible smooth initial data alone, rather than assume a priori, uniform hydrodynamic bounds of the form 0 < m_0 <= int_{R^d} f(t,x,v) dv <= M_0, int_{R^d} |v|^2 f(t,x,v) dv <= E_0, and int_{R^d} f(t,x,v) log f(t,x,v) dv <= H_0 for all (t,x) on the interval of existence? Equivalently in the paper's sense, can the hypotheses (3.1), (3.2), and (3.3) in Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 be proved rather than assumed, thereby turning the conditional regularity theory into unconditional global smoothness for the corresponding inhomogeneous Landau and non-cutoff Boltzmann equations?

For the inhomogeneous kinetic equation f_t + v . grad_x f = Q(f,f), with Q equal to the non-cutoff Boltzmann collision operator (and analogously for the Landau operator in the parallel setting of Theorem 3.2), can a classical solution develop a macroscopic implosion singularity in which the flow concentrates toward a single spacetime point and the local mass and energy densities blow up there in a way resembling the implosion profile of the compressible Euler equation? In particular, can such an implosion occur so that the hydrodynamic bounds (3.1)-(3.3) fail, despite the fact that Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 show the solution remains smooth for as long as those bounds hold?

Let d >= 1, and let f be a bounded classical solution of
\partial_t f + v\cdot\nabla_x f = \sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}(t,x,v)\,\partial_{v_i v_j}f
in the unit kinetic cylinder Q_1 := (-1,0] x B_1 x B_1 \subset R_t x R_x^d x R_v^d. Assume that the coefficient matrix A=(a_{ij}) is merely measurable and uniformly elliptic in the velocity variables, in the sense that for every (t,x,v) in Q_1 and every xi in R^d,
\lambda |xi|^2 <= \sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}(t,x,v) xi_i xi_j <= \Lambda |xi|^2.
Does there exist an exponent alpha > 0 and a constant C = C(d,lambda,Lambda) such that the interior Hölder estimate
\|f\|_{C^alpha(Q_{1/2})} <= C \|f\|_{L^\infty(Q_1)}
holds, where Q_{1/2} := (-1/2,0] x B_{1/2} x B_{1/2}?

Fix d ≥ 1 and s ∈ (0,1), and let Q_r denote the kinetic cylinder associated with the scaling (t,x,v) ↦ (r^{2s}t, r^{1+2s}x, rv). Suppose f is a classical solution in Q_1 ⊂ R^{1+2d} of the nonlocal kinetic equation ∂_t f + v·∇_x f = ∫_{R^d}(f(t,x,v') − f(t,x,v)) K(t,x,v,v') dv' + h(t,x,v), where h ∈ L^∞(Q_1), the kernel is symmetric in the velocity variables, K(t,x,v,v') = K(t,x,v',v), and there exist constants 0 < λ ≤ Λ < ∞ such that λ|v'−v|^{−d−2s} ≤ K(t,x,v,v') ≤ Λ|v'−v|^{−d−2s} for all (t,x,v,v'). Must there exist constants δ > 0 and C < ∞, depending only on d, s, λ, and Λ, such that f satisfies the interior estimate ‖f‖_{C^δ_ℓ(Q_{1/2})} ≤ C(‖f‖_{L^∞(Q_1)} + ‖h‖_{L^∞(Q_1)}), where C^δ_ℓ is the kinetic Hölder space associated with the left-invariant kinetic geometry used in Definitions 5.3–5.4?

Find a least-action, preferably geodesic, formulation for the motion of an ideal fluid in a fixed domain M containing sources and sinks. More precisely, for incompressible Euler flow ∂_t v + v·∇v = −∇p and div v = 0 with initial velocity v(0), determine the correct variational principle for this open system, where energy may be supplied or drained through the boundary; in the 2D case, specify how the prescribed normal boundary flux v·n on the penetrable boundary and the prescribed inflow vorticity ω := curl v on the source part of the boundary are incorporated, and decide whether exterior forces and/or fluid-memory effects must enter the action.

Can one develop, for problems of elasticity theory, an analogue of the Lie-groupoid Euler-Arnold framework already available for incompressible multiphase fluids, generalized flows, and vortex sheets by identifying the appropriate Lie groupoid of elastic configurations and its Lie algebroid, together with a geodesic and Hamiltonian formulation analogous to the known L^2-type right-invariant (source-wise) metric picture on Lie groupoids of multiphase volume-preserving diffeomorphisms? ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

Let M be a Riemannian manifold, and consider the Lie groupoid of multiphase or generalized volume-preserving diffeomorphisms that serves as the configuration space for incompressible multiphase fluids/generalized flows on M. In the multiphase case, the fluid is described by phase densities ρ_1, ..., ρ_n ∈ C^∞(M), phase velocities v_1, ..., v_n ∈ Vect(M), and a common pressure p ∈ C^∞(M), satisfying ∂_t v_j + v_j·∇v_j = -∇p, ∂_t ρ_j + div(ρ_j v_j) = 0, and Σ_{j=1}^n ρ_j = 1; for generalized flows, the discrete phase index is replaced by a continuous parameter. Since these equations are precisely the geodesic equations for the right-invariant (source-wise) L^2-type metric on the corresponding Lie groupoid, describe the differential geometry of this metric—specifically its sectional curvature, Ricci curvature, and conjugate points—analogously to Arnold’s differential-geometric description of the volume-preserving diffeomorphism group D_μ(M).

Let M be a manifold of arbitrary dimension. The inviscid Burgers equation ∂_t v + v·∇v = 0 can be viewed as a geodesic equation on the full diffeomorphism group D(M) endowed with a non-invariant L^2 metric, but once shock waves form the Lagrangian evolution no longer remains in D(M). Can one formulate an extension of Arnold’s geodesic/variational framework from D(M) to the semigroup Map(M) of self-maps of M—possibly in a Lipschitz class—so that it describes particle trajectories both before and after shock formation, recovers the pre-shock non-invariant L^2 geodesic description, and is compatible after collision with the Bogaevsky "circle law" for potential solutions with convex potentials, thereby capturing smooth solutions and their continuations beyond emergence of shock waves for Burgers-like and compressible fluid equations?

Can one find a variational description of a system of material particles moving in R^d, with d > 1, that stick upon collision, valid for both potential and non-potential fluid flows, and sufficiently flexible to describe the formation and subsequent development of shock waves for the system governed by the multi-dimensional Burgers equation?

Let M be an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold with volume form μ, and let D_μ(M) be the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of M. The standard kinetic-energy pairing on T_eD_μ(M) is the L^2 inner product on divergence-free vector fields, <v,w>_{L^2} = ∫_M g_x(v(x),w(x)) dμ, which in Arnold's hydrodynamic picture is extended to a right-invariant metric on D_μ(M). Describe a model whose configuration space is D_μ(M) and whose kinetic energy instead induces the left-invariant extension of this L^2 metric; moreover, determine whether any interesting physical systems genuinely realize this type of left-invariance.

For the local Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations ∂_t v + v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0, v(0)=v_0, on a fixed fluid domain M, with v tangent to ∂M when ∂M ≠ ∅, is the problem ill-posed in the Hadamard sense in the Besov spaces B^1_{∞,q}(M) for every intermediate index 1 < q < ∞? ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

Does the global two-point boundary value problem hold for 2D ideal hydrodynamics: if s > 2 and D_mu^s(M) denotes the H^s Sobolev completion of the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold M, equipped with the right-invariant L^2 kinetic-energy metric and its exponential map exp_e : T_e D_mu^s(M) -> D_mu^s(M), is it true that for every phi in D_mu^s(M) there exists (i) a divergence-free H^s vector field v in T_e D_mu^s(M) with exp_e(v) = phi, and (ii) a curve gamma : [0,1] -> D_mu^s(M) with gamma(0) = e and gamma(1) = phi that minimizes E(gamma) = (1/2) integral_0^1 ||gamma_dot(t)||_{L^2}^2 dt among all such curves?

Let M be a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold with volume form μ, let D^s_μ(M) denote the Sobolev H^s completion of the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms with s > 2, and equip D^s_μ(M) with the right-invariant L^2 kinetic-energy metric (1.3). For the associated energy/action functional E(γ) = (1/2)∫_0^1 ||γ̇(t)||^2_{L^2} dt on curves γ in D^s_μ(M) joining prescribed endpoints (as in the two-point variational problem), does E satisfy the Palais–Smale condition? ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

For s > 2, let D_mu^s(M) be the H^s Sobolev completion of the group of diffeomorphisms of M that preserve the Riemannian area form mu, endowed with Arnold's right-invariant kinetic-energy L^2 metric, whose value at the identity on divergence-free vector fields is the integral over M of their pointwise inner product against mu. If M is either (i) a compact surface, possibly with boundary, of genus at least 2, or (ii) a multi-connected bounded domain in R^2 with at least two holes, does there exist T > 0 and a nonconstant geodesic gamma: R -> D_mu^s(M) such that gamma(t + T) = gamma(t) for all t?

For an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold (M,μ), let D_μ(M) be the group of smooth μ-preserving diffeomorphisms equipped with Arnold’s right-invariant kinetic-energy L2 metric ⟨v,w⟩_{L2}=∫_M ⟨v,w⟩ dμ on divergence-free vector fields. How far is D_μ(M) from being an infinite-dimensional locally symmetric Riemannian space? In particular, make precise that the geodesic central symmetry about the identity is a smooth map but not an L2-isometry, distinguish this from the group inversion g↦g^{-1}, and explain how this non-symmetric (‘chiral’) geometry resolves Arnold’s paradox on T2: for the steady flow with stream function ψ=cos(ky), the sectional curvature of the group of exact area-preserving torus diffeomorphisms is nonpositive in every 2-plane containing ψ (and negative in most such planes), even though some parallel flows—such as those with convex velocity profiles on short tori—are Eulerian stable.

Extend the analyticity result of Theorem 6.1 to higher-dimensional incompressible Euler flows: if u(t, x) is a sufficiently regular/classical Euler solution on an n-dimensional manifold or domain M, with slip boundary condition when ∂M is nonempty, and x(t) is a particle trajectory solving dx/dt = u(t, x(t)), must x(t) be real-analytic in time for every n? If M has boundary, does the answer depend on whether ∂M is real-analytic? Relatedly, in the Yudovich class (divergence-free u with ||curl u||_{L^∞} < ∞, so trajectories are unique), can the currently known Gevrey time-regularity of trajectories be upgraded to real analyticity?

Let M be a compact analytic Riemannian 2-manifold with analytic boundary, and let YU(M) be the Yudovich space of divergence-free vector fields u on M such that curl u ∈ L∞(M). Let S_t be the Euler flow on YU(M), let O(u) = {S_tu : t ∈ R} be the orbit of u, and let \bar O(u) be the weak closure of O(u) in H^1(M). Define u ∈ YU(M) to be a generalized minimal flow if every w ∈ \bar O(u) satisfies ||curl w||L2(M) = ||curl u||L2(M), and denote by GM(M) the set of all such flows. Prove that GM(M) is a nonempty proper subset of YU(M). ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

Let M be a compact real-analytic Riemannian 2-manifold, possibly with boundary, and let YU(M) be the Yudovich space of divergence-free vector fields u on M such that curl u ∈ L∞(M). Let S_t denote the 2D Euler evolution on YU(M), let O(u0) be the orbit of u0 under S_t, and let O(u0)¯ be its weak H^1-closure. Assume that u0 ∈ YU(M) is a generalized minimal flow in the sense that ||curl w||L2(M) = ||curl u0||L2(M) for every w ∈ O(u0)¯. If u(t) = S_tu0, prove that for every t and every c ∈ R, each vorticity level line of ω(t, x) = curl u(t, x), i.e. each connected one-dimensional component of {x ∈ M : ω(t, x) = c}, is a real-analytic curve in M.

Let M be a compact analytic Riemannian 2-manifold, with or without boundary, and let YU(M) be the Yudovich space of divergence-free vector fields u on M such that curl u is in L∞(M). Let O(u) be the Euler orbit of u and Obar(u) its weak H^1-closure. If u in YU(M) is a generalized minimal flow in the sense of Definition 6.7, namely ||curl w||L2 = ||curl u||L2 for every w in Obar(u), then, in the blob/background picture described in §6.3 (where the domain is viewed as consisting of vorticity blobs B1,...,BN and a background region B0), prove that the vorticity is constant on the background region; equivalently, prove that curl u = c on B0 for some constant c. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

Let M be a fixed n-dimensional Riemannian manifold or domain (possibly with boundary) equipped with volume form μ, and consider the incompressible Euler equations ∂_t v + ∇_v v = -∇p, div_μ v = 0, with v tangent to ∂M when ∂M ≠ ∅. Define anisotropic function spaces that are more appropriate for ideal hydrodynamics, in the sense that they encode greater smoothness in directions tangent to the flow lines than in transverse directions, and prove existence and uniqueness theorems for Euler solutions in those spaces for every dimension n.

Let M be a compact analytic Riemannian 2-manifold, with or without analytic boundary, and let YU(M) be the Yudovich space of divergence-free vector fields u on M with curl u in L^infty(M). For the 2D Euler flow S_t on YU(M), call u a generalized minimal flow (GM-flow) if for every w in the weak H^1-closure of its orbit O(u) one has ||curl w||_{L^2(M)} = ||curl u||_{L^2(M)}. Determine the true regularity of GM-flows by identifying the anisotropic function spaces natural to them—spaces with enhanced smoothness along the distinguished flow/level-line direction and only finite transverse regularity—in which GM-flows should be studied.

Let M be a compact Riemannian 3-manifold, let D_mu^s(M) be the Sobolev H^s completion of the volume-preserving diffeomorphism group with s > 5/2, and let exp_e: T_e D_mu^s(M) -> D_mu^s(M) be the Riemannian exponential map of the right-invariant L2 metric. Quantify precisely how exp_e fails to be Fredholm in dimension 3 by analyzing the noncompact part K_0 of its derivative at initial velocity v_0, namely the r = 0 case of the decomposition d(exp_e) = A + K_r with A invertible and K_r w = (1-Delta)^(-r/2) P_e( i_w d(1-Delta)^(r/2) v_0^flat )^sharp; for example, determine or estimate the essential spectrum of K_0 and thereby make precise in what sense the 3D L2 case is a borderline failure of Fredholmness.

For a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold M, possibly with boundary, fix s > 2 and let D^s_μ(M) be the H^s Sobolev completion of the volume-preserving diffeomorphism group, endowed with Arnold's right-invariant kinetic-energy L^2 metric and exponential map exp_e. Given any geodesic γ(t)=exp_e(tv_0) issuing from the identity e, where v_0 is a divergence-free H^s vector field tangent to ∂M when ∂M is nonempty, determine the order (multiplicity) of the first conjugate point of exp_e along γ. Further, determine whether the existence of conjugate points in D^s_μ(M) is related to Arnold's stability criterion for stationary Euler flows on M, namely positive or negative definiteness of the second variation of the kinetic energy restricted to coadjoint orbits.

Let M be a compact two-dimensional manifold, possibly with boundary, and let D^s_μ(M) be the Sobolev H^s completion (s > 2) of the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of M, equipped with Arnold’s right-invariant L^2 kinetic-energy metric. Let exp_e : T_eD^s_μ(M) -> D^s_μ(M) be the corresponding L^2 exponential map, and for ε > 0 define B_ε = {v in T_eD^s_μ(M) : ||v||_{H^s} < ε} and U_ε = exp_e(B_ε). For η in D^s_μ(M), let C_ε(η) be the minimal N such that η = η_1 ◦ ... ◦ η_N with each η_i in U_ε, and define the absolute complexity by C(η) = limsup_{ε->0} ε C_ε(η). Show that for every L^2 geodesic γ(t) in D^s_μ(M), one has C(γ(t)) ≲ e^(t||γ̇(0)||_{H^s}). ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

Let M be a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let D^s_μ(M) be the Sobolev H^s completion of the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of M, with s > 2, equipped with Arnold’s right-invariant L^2 metric. Let exp_e : T_e D^s_μ(M) -> D^s_μ(M) be the corresponding Riemannian exponential map. For ε > 0, define B_ε = {v in T_e D^s_μ(M) : ||v||_{H^s} < ε}, U_ε = exp_e(B_ε), let C_ε(η) be the minimal N such that η = η_1 ∘ ... ∘ η_N with each η_i in U_ε, and define the absolute complexity of η by C(η) = lim sup as ε -> 0 of ε C_ε(η). Show that for a typical L^2 geodesic γ(t) starting from the identity e in D^s_μ(M)—where typical means that the complement of the corresponding set of initial velocities in T_e D^s_μ(M) has infinite codimension—we have linear complexity growth, i.e. C(γ(t)) ≃ t as t -> infinity (equivalently, up to multiplicative constants, C(γ(t)) grows linearly in t).

Let M be a compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, with volume form μ, and let D^s_μ(M) denote the H^s Sobolev completion of the group D_μ(M) of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms, for some s>2, so that T_e D^s_μ(M) is the H^s space of divergence-free velocity fields on M tangent to ∂M when ∂M≠∅. For a global solution u=u(t,x) of the incompressible Euler equations ∂_t u + u·∇u = -∇p, div u = 0 on M, is it possible to quantify the fluid's 'aging' by constructing a continuous Lyapunov function L:T_e D^s_μ(M)→R such that d/dt L(u(t,·)) ≥ 0 along every Euler trajectory, with equality only on a slim subset of T_e D^s_μ(M) (for example, a subset of infinite codimension), thereby allowing one to distinguish which of two velocity fields u(t1,·) and u(t2,·) corresponds to the earlier time? ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

Let M = T × (0, a), with T a one-dimensional torus, and let u(t, x) be a solution of the 2D incompressible Euler equations on M, with u tangent to ∂M. Assume that the initial velocity u0 is C^1-close on M to a plane-parallel flow u_ref(x1, x2) = (v(x2), 0), where v'(x2) > 0 and v''(x2) > 0 for every x2 in (0, a). Write ω(t, x) = curl u(t, x) for the scalar vorticity, assume that ∇ω0 ≠ 0 in M, and assume that one initial vorticity level line {ω0 = c} has a 'kink'. Show that, for every forward time t, the corresponding level line of ω(t, ·) still has a 'kink'; equivalently, the kink does not disappear as the fluid evolves in time. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

Let X be a complete metric space and S⊂X a compact set. For ε>0, define the Kolmogorov ε-entropy H_ε(S)=log_2 N_ε(S), where N_ε(S) is the minimal number of ε-balls in X needed to cover S. For a probability measure μ on X and parameter δ, define H_{ε,δ}(μ)=inf{H_ε(Y): Y⊂X is compact and μ(X\Y)≤δ}. Now assume X is a Hilbert space with chosen coordinates x_1,x_2,..., let X_n={x_i=0 for i>n}, let π_n:X→X_n be the orthogonal projection, partition X_n into ε-cubes C_j, and write K_j=π_n^{-1}(C_j). For compact S⊂X, let widetilde N(n,ε) be the number of cubes C_j meeting π_n(S), set widetilde N(ε)=sup_n widetilde N(n,ε), and define widetilde H_ε(S)=log_2 widetilde N(ε). For a probability measure μ on X, let widetilde H_{ε,δ}(μ) denote the Hilbert-space measure entropy introduced immediately before Problem 24, obtained from the cube partition entropies -∑_j μ(K_j)log_2 μ(K_j) by taking the supremum over n. Determine the basic properties of H_ε, H_{ε,δ}, widetilde H_ε, and widetilde H_{ε,δ}, and explain the precise relations among them, especially their principal asymptotics as ε→0 and their behavior for examples such as a d-dimensional cube with d-dimensional Lebesgue measure under rotations or other deformations inside a higher-dimensional Hilbert space.

For the incompressible Euler equations ∂_t u + u·∇u = -∇p, div u = 0 on a two-dimensional fluid domain M, let V^0 = {u in L^2(M, R^2) : div u = 0, u tangent to ∂M}, let μ_0 be a compactly supported probability measure on V^0 whose support lies in a well-posed class such as the Yudovich space Y = {u in V^0 : curl u in L^∞} or V^s = T_e D^s_μ with s > 2, and let μ_t be the pushforward of μ_0 by the Euler flow. Using the measure ε-entropy H_ε from Section 9.1, defined by finite-dimensional ε-cube projections H_{ε,n}(μ) = -Σ_j μ(K_j) log_2 μ(K_j) and H_ε(μ) = sup_n H_{ε,n}(μ), explain the entropy-decrease phenomenon described in the paper: namely, why one may expect that for a limiting measure μ_∞ of the transported ensemble, H_ε(μ_∞) = O(H_ε(μ_0)) as ε → 0, and for some μ_0 even H_ε(μ_∞) = o(H_ε(μ_0)), so that asymptotically liminf_{t→∞} H_ε(μ_t) is no larger than H_ε(μ_0); and explain why this does not contradict the Hamiltonian/Liouville structure of ideal fluid dynamics, since the velocity space V^0 records only half of the true phase space and the other half is the particle-position/flow-map variable in D_μ.

Let M be a two-dimensional domain or Riemannian manifold equipped with an area form μ, and consider the incompressible Euler equation for a divergence-free velocity field v tangent to ∂M when ∂M ≠ ∅: ∂_t v + ∇_v v = -grad p (equivalently, in the Euclidean-domain notation of (1.1), ∂_t v + v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0). View this equation in Arnold's Hamiltonian framework, where g = Vect_μ(M), g* ≅ Ω^1(M)/dΩ^0(M), and the Hamiltonian is the kinetic energy E(v) = (1/2)||v||^2_{L^2(M)}. Prove that this infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system is non-integrable by showing that the 2D Euler equation fails at least one of the several (not necessarily equivalent) definitions of integrability in infinite dimensions; the issue to settle is genuine dynamical integrability on a coadjoint orbit, not merely the existence of infinitely many enstrophy Casimirs or the generic Euler-Poincare Lax form. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

For the incompressible 2D Euler equation ∂_t v + v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0, explain the numerical phenomenon observed for smooth, sufficiently general initial vorticity on the two-dimensional torus and sphere that, under very small numerical viscosity, like-signed vortex structures merge into larger vortex blobs whose effective point-vortex dynamics is driven into an integrable regime—namely, 2 blobs on T^2, 3 blobs on S^2 for general angular momentum, and 4 blobs on S^2 when the initial angular momentum is zero—so that integrable point-vortex cases act as attractors for the large-time Euler dynamics. Then construct a dissipation model within the 2D Euler equation whose long-time evolution produces this same asymptotic integrable point-vortex dynamics.

Within the finite-dimensional Hamiltonian (Kirchhoff) point-vortex models that arise as approximations to the 2D Euler equation, study in detail the motion and bifurcation structure of systems with a small, unspecified number N of point vortices on each of the manifolds explicitly singled out in the paper: the half-plane, quarter-plane, hemisphere, quarter-sphere, disk, torus, cylinder, and half-cylinder.

On non-orientable surfaces such as the Möbius band, projective plane, and Klein bottle, determine the first non-integrable finite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems arising from a small number N of point vortices, and describe, for the group of area-preserving diffeomorphisms of such surfaces, the full set of Casimir invariants (that is, the metric-independent Lie-Poisson invariants specifying coadjoint orbits) together with finite-dimensional approximations analogous to those known in the orientable cases.

In the paper’s basic setup, let M ⊂ R^3 be a fixed fluid domain and consider the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations partial_t v + v·∇v = -∇p and div v = 0, with v tangent to ∂M if ∂M ≠ ∅. Prove that the induced Euler evolution S_t admits a wandering solution: namely, find a forward-global divergence-free initial datum v_0, an open neighborhood U of v_0 in a natural phase space/topology where the Euler flow is defined, and a time T > 0 such that S_t(U) ∩ U = ∅ for every t > T. This is exactly the 3D analogue sought in Problem 30 of the 2D wandering phenomenon mentioned just before it. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD2205.01143.pdf))

Let M be a closed Riemannian 3-manifold, and consider the incompressible Euler equation on M, ∂_t v + ∇_v v = -∇p with div v = 0, as a dynamical system on divergence-free vector fields endowed with the C^k topology. The paper notes that current KAM-based results give global non-mixing on any such M for non-integer k > 4, for any prescribed helicity and sufficiently large energy, and also a local non-mixing statement near a "typical" steady solution on S^3 for non-integer k > 10. Can one relax or remove these KAM-imposed restrictions on the smoothness index k of the C^k spaces and prove, in these same global and local 3D settings, the corresponding failure of topological transitivity and topological mixing for the Euler flow?

Let M be a compact 2n-dimensional manifold carrying an integrable system with first integrals F1,...,Fn in involution, functionally independent almost everywhere on M. If S ⊂ M is a singular submanifold on which the integrals become dependent (equivalently, dF1,...,dFn are linearly dependent along S), what restrictions does integrability impose on the dynamics on S? How wild can the dynamics on such a singular submanifold be, and can chaotic dynamics occur on a very small ('tiny') singular submanifold of an otherwise integrable system?

For steady incompressible Euler flows v on a three-dimensional domain M ⊂ R3, satisfying v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0, and v tangent to ∂M, explain the following paradox from the paper: Arnold's theory says that an analytic steady field that is not everywhere collinear with curl v is almost everywhere fibered by invariant tori and annuli, and that a similar fibration persists when v is everywhere collinear with its vorticity but the proportionality factor is a generic function, whereas Beltrami eigenfields satisfying curl v = λv can realize arbitrarily complicated topology; specifically, what should count as a typical steady field, and what notion of genericity is natural on the space of steady Euler fields? ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

Let M be a compact 3-dimensional manifold or domain equipped with a volume form mu and a Riemannian metric, and let u be an exact divergence-free vector field on M. Writing omega = iota_u mu, so that the ordinary helicity is H(u) = int_M omega wedge d^{-1}omega = int_M (u, curl^{-1}u) mu and the L^2-energy is E(u) = (1/2) int_M (u,u) mu, find a sequence of higher helicity invariants of such fields, analogous to the Milnor-Massey hierarchy for links, with the property that whenever all earlier invariants vanish on u, the first nonzero invariant yields a lower bound for E(u).

Find a direct link between the three-dimensional Gross–Pitaevskii/nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation by realizing the 1D equation as a reduction to singular filament-type solutions of the 3D equation, rather than obtaining it indirectly through the localized induction approximation and the binormal/Hasimoto route. Formulate the analogous reduction for the three-dimensional compressible Euler equations, namely a reduction to singular solutions supported on one-dimensional submanifolds.

For a fixed ambient fluid domain or Riemannian manifold, describe the differential geometry of the shape space of closed hypersurfaces enclosing a prescribed volume, equipped with the hydrodynamically induced nonlocal H^{-1/2} metric defined via Neumann-to-Dirichlet operators, whose geodesics describe potential fluid motions with vortex sheets or with free dynamic boundary.

Let M be an n-dimensional manifold, let PC∞(M, C) denote the projective space of smooth complex-valued wave functions on M, whose elements are cosets [ψ] of the unit L2-sphere, and let Dens(M) be the space of smooth probability densities. For nonvanishing wave functions, the Madelung transform is known to induce a symplectomorphism between PC∞(M, C\{0}) and T*Dens(M), and in fact a Kähler map when T*Dens(M) is equipped with its canonical symplectic structure and Sasaki-Fisher-Rao metric while PC∞(M, C\{0}) carries its natural symplectic structure and the Fubini-Study metric. Can one extend these symplectomorphism and Kähler-map results to wave functions ψ that are allowed to have zeros on M, and at the same time explain the quantization-condition controversy in the language of the momentum map for the semidirect product action of diffeomorphisms and smooth functions on wave functions viewed as half-densities?
