How far can psi fail to be an isomorphism? In particular, which additional hypotheses on Gamma and Delta, such as finite generation or finite presentation, are sufficient to force psi itself to be an isomorphism?

Find interesting characterizations of those complete Hausdorff topological groups G for which every nonidentity element g∈G is omitted by some open normal subgroup N◁G with soluble quotient G/N, and which arise as the true prosoluble completion PS(Γ) of a residually soluble discrete group Γ; in particular, how can one decide whether a given such G is isomorphic to PS(Γ) for some finitely generated Γ, and how can one decide whether it is isomorphic to PS(Γ) for some finitely presented Γ? ([mat.univie.ac.at](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~arjantseva/Abs/ahkJ.pdf))

Let G be the first Grigorchuk group, identified with its canonical dense image in its profinite completion PF(G) (equivalently, in its pro-2 completion P̂_2(G) = Ḡ ⊂ Aut(T), where T is the rooted dyadic tree). Does there exist an element g ∈ PF(G) \ G such that the proper finitely generated dense subgroup Δ := ⟨G, g⟩ has the congruence extension property, i.e. for every normal subgroup N ◁ Δ there exists an open normal subgroup M ◁ PF(G) with N = M ∩ Δ?

For an abstract group Γ that is not residually soluble, what can be said about the true prosoluble kernel Ker(φ_S:Γ→PS(Γ)), where PS(Γ) is the completion of Γ with respect to all normal subgroups N◁Γ for which Γ/N is soluble? Equivalently, by §5.D, determine D^∞(Γ)=⋂_{n≥0}D^n(Γ), where D^0(Γ)=Γ and D^{n+1}(Γ)=[D^n(Γ),D^n(Γ)]. As a benchmark, recover the Baumslag one-relator example Γ=⟨a,b | a=[a,a^b]⟩, for which Ker(φ_S)=D(Γ), D(Γ) is perfect, and Γ/D(Γ)≅ℤ; and investigate the same kernel for the examples explicitly listed in §6.F: other non-residually-soluble one-relator groups, wreath products Γ=S wr T as in §6.B with S soluble non-abelian and T soluble infinite, free products of nilpotent groups with amalgamation, parafree groups, and meta-residually soluble groups, in particular free-by-free groups that are not residually soluble. ([mat.univie.ac.at](https://www.mat.univie.ac.at/~arjantseva/Abs/ahkJ.pdf))

Does there exist a discrete group Gamma such that the canonical homomorphism phi_F: Gamma -> P_F(Gamma), where P_F(Gamma) is the profinite completion with respect to all normal subgroups of finite index, is injective, and the canonical homomorphism phi_S: Gamma -> P_S(Gamma), where P_S(Gamma) is the true prosoluble completion with respect to all normal subgroups N normal in Gamma for which Gamma/N is soluble, is injective, but the canonical homomorphism phi_FS: Gamma -> P_FS(Gamma), where P_FS(Gamma) is the inverse limit over all finite soluble quotients Gamma/N, is not injective?

Does there exist a finitely generated free group F, a residually soluble group Γ that is not free, and a homomorphism ψ: F → Γ such that, if D_0(G) = G and D_{j+1}(G) = [D_j(G), D_j(G)] denote the ordinary derived series of a group G, then for every j ≥ 1 the induced homomorphism F/D_j(F) → Γ/D_j(Γ) is an isomorphism?

Let z=(z1,…,zn) be commuting variables over ℂ, let Δ=∑_{i=1}^n ∂^2/∂zi^2, and let P(z)∈ℂ[z1,…,zn] be a homogeneous polynomial of degree 4 whose Hessian matrix Hes P(z)=(∂^2P/∂zi∂zj) is nilpotent. Must there exist an integer M such that Δ^m(P(z)^{m+1})=0 for every integer m≥M?

Let (M,F) be a compact foliated manifold, let E be a holonomy equivariant Hermitian vector bundle, and let σ̄ : Ψ̄^{0,-∞}(M,F,E) → S̄^0(G_{F_N}, L(π^*E) ⊗ |TG_N|^{1/2}) be the continuous extension of the transverse principal symbol map from Proposition 3.5, where Ψ̄^{0,-∞}(M,F,E) is the operator-norm closure of Ψ^{0,-∞}(M,F,E) in L(L^2(M,E)). Since Proposition 3.5 gives K(L^2(M,E)) ⊂ Iσ := Ker σ̄, under what additional hypotheses on (M,F) and E does one have Iσ = K(L^2(M,E))? In the sense of Remark 3.6, this is the precise question that makes σ̄ faithful modulo compact operators, so that its restriction to C_E^*(G) is the natural map π_E : C_E^*(G) → C_r^*(G), hence injective, and therefore forces the holonomy groupoid G to be amenable.

Let (M, F) be a compact foliated manifold of codimension q, let E → M be a vector bundle, and let A ∈ Ψ^m(M, E) be a positive transversally elliptic operator with positive transversal principal symbol. Theorem 3.12 proves the meromorphic continuation and residue-trace formula for the zeta function z ↦ tr(QA^{-z}) when Q ∈ Ψ^{l,-∞}(M, F, E). Does the same conclusion remain valid when Q is allowed to belong to the completed algebra ̅Ψ^{l,-∞}(M, F, E) and its symbol, viewed as an element of C^∞(G_{F_N}, L(π^*E) ⊗ |TG_N|^{1/2}), is not properly supported?

Let (M,F) be a closed foliated manifold of codimension q, endowed with a Riemannian metric g_M = g_F + g_H, where g_F is the restriction to TF and H = F^⊥. For 0 < h ≤ 1, let g_h = g_F + h^{-2}g_H, and let Δ_h denote the Laplace-Beltrami operator on functions for g_h (equivalently, in the scalar setting, Δ_h = Δ_F + h^2Δ_H). Let F_N be the linearized foliation on the conormal bundle N^*F, let Δ_{F_N} be the lift of the tangential Laplacian to F_N, let g_N be the fiberwise quadratic form on N^*F induced by g_H, and let tr_{F_N} be the canonical noncommutative trace associated with F_N. Is it true that the adiabatic spectrum of Δ_h satisfies the noncommutative Weyl formula
tr f(Δ_h) = (2π)^{-q} h^{-q} tr_{F_N} f(Δ_{F_N} + g_N) + o(h^{-q})
as h → 0, for every compactly supported smooth test function f on R?

Let (M,F) be a compact foliated manifold of dimension n = p + q, with both p and q even, equipped with a splitting TM = F \oplus H and a Riemannian metric g_M = g_F \oplus g_H; let g_h = g_F + h^(-2) g_H be the associated adiabatic family of metrics. If d_h = d_F + h d_H + h^2 theta is the corresponding decomposition of the de Rham differential and D_h = d_h + d_h^* is the associated adiabatic signature operator, let D_F = d_F + d_F^* be the leafwise signature operator on M, let D_{F_N} denote the leafwise signature operator for the linearized foliation F_N on the conormal bundle N^*F, and let sigma(D_H) be the transverse principal symbol of D_H, acting fiberwise on N^*F. Is it true that for every even function f in C_c^\infty(R), one has the asymptotic formula tr f(D_h) = (2 pi)^(-q) h^(-q) tr_{F_N} f(D_{F_N} + sigma(D_H)) + o(h^(-q)) as h -> 0^+?

Let (A,H,D) be the spectral triple associated with a compact Riemannian foliation (M,F), and let K belong to Ψ^{m,-∞}(M,F,E). Theorem 4.2 asserts that there exists K(t) in Ψ^{m,-∞}(M,F,E) such that, for any r and s, the family <D>^r(Φ_t(K)-K(t))<D>^{-s} is a smooth family of trace-class operators, where Φ_t(K)=e^{it<D>}Ke^{-it<D>}; moreover, if E is the trivial line bundle, the subprincipal symbol of D^2 vanishes, and k in S^m(G_{F_N}, |T G_N|^{1/2}) is the principal symbol of K, then the principal symbol of K(t) is k(t)=F_t^*(k). Assuming the same vanishing-subprincipal-symbol hypothesis on D^2, can one extend this second statement of Theorem 4.2 from the case of the trivial line bundle to the case of an arbitrary Hermitian vector bundle E?

Let (M,g) be a compact Riemannian manifold, let \bar{\Psi}^0(M) be the closure of the algebra \Psi^0(M) of order-zero pseudodifferential operators in the uniform operator topology of \mathcal{L}(L^2(M)), and define a one-parameter group of C*-automorphisms \Phi_t on \bar{\Psi}^0(M) by \Phi_t(T)=e^{it\sqrt{\Delta_g}}Te^{-it\sqrt{\Delta_g}}, where \Delta_g is the Laplace operator associated with g. Let F_t denote the geodesic flow on the cosphere bundle S^*M, together with its induced action on C(S^*M). Since Egorov's theorem identifies the principal-symbol dynamics of \Phi_t with F_t, can one define a quantum topological entropy of the noncommutative geodesic flow \Phi_t so that it is related to the classical topological entropy of the geodesic flow F_t?

Let (A, H, D) be the spectral triple associated, as in Theorem 4.2, with a compact Riemannian foliation, in the scalar case where E is the trivial holonomy-equivariant line bundle and the subprincipal symbol of D^2 vanishes, so that the noncommutative geodesic flow Φ_t on S^*A is related via the *-homomorphism P of Theorem 4.2 to the transverse geodesic flow F_t^* on the corresponding symbol algebra. Can one define a classical topological entropy h(F^*) for the transverse geodesic flow F_t^* and a quantum topological entropy h(Φ) for the noncommutative geodesic flow Φ_t in such a way that these two entropy notions are related?

Let (M,F) be a compact Riemannian foliated manifold, let FN be the linearized foliation on the conormal bundle N^*F, let G_FN be its holonomy groupoid, and let A = C^infty_prop(G_FN, |T G_N|^{1/2}) be the involutive algebra of properly supported smooth half-densities on G_FN, equipped with the natural noncommutative Poisson structure arising from the Block–Getzler construction for the transversally symplectic foliation FN. Can one define a notion of Hamiltonian flow for a noncommutative algebra with such a Poisson structure so that, for every function p homogeneous of degree 1 on a conic neighborhood of tilde N^*F in tilde T^*M whose restriction to tilde N^*F is constant along the leaves of FN, the one-parameter group F_t^* of automorphisms of A induced by the transverse Hamiltonian flow of p in the sense of Definition 4.1 is a noncommutative Hamiltonian flow?

Let (M, \mathcal F) be a compact manifold with a Riemannian foliation, let N^*\mathcal F be the conormal bundle, let \mathcal F_N be the induced linearized foliation on N^*\mathcal F, and let G_{\mathcal F_N} denote the holonomy groupoid of \mathcal F_N. Endow the convolution algebra C^\infty_{\mathrm{prop}}(G_{\mathcal F_N}, |T\mathcal G_N|^{1/2}) with the noncommutative Poisson structure coming from the transverse symplectic geometry of N^*\mathcal F/\mathcal F_N. Does there exist, for this noncommutative Poisson algebra, a strict deformation quantization in the sense of Rieffel by a continuous family of algebras of transverse pseudodifferential operators such that the fiber at \hbar=0 is C^\infty_{\mathrm{prop}}(G_{\mathcal F_N}, |T\mathcal G_N|^{1/2}) and the first-order commutator is governed by the above Poisson bracket?

Let (M, F) be a compact manifold endowed with a Riemannian foliation. For the Laplace operator associated with the adiabatic-limit setup considered in Section 3.4, how can one relate dynamical properties of the transverse geodesic flow of (M, F) to the asymptotic behavior, in the adiabatic limit, of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of that Laplacian?

Let (M,\mathcal F) be a compact foliated manifold of codimension q, let E\to M be a Hermitian vector bundle, and let P\in\Psi^{-q,-\infty}(M,\mathcal F,E) be a transverse pseudodifferential operator of critical transverse order -q, smoothing along the leaves, acting on L^2(M,E). Is it true that every such P belongs to the weak trace ideal \mathcal L^{1,\infty}(L^2(M,E)) and is Dixmier measurable, so that for every dilation-invariant generalized limit \omega one has Tr_\omega(P)=\tau(P), where \tau is the residue trace of the foliated pseudodifferential calculus?

Let Rf(alpha,p) = integral over l_{alpha,p} of f ds be the classical Radon transform on R^2, where l_{alpha,p} := {x in R^2 : alpha·x = p}, alpha is a unit vector in S^1, p is real, and ds denotes arclength on the whole line l_{alpha,p}. Suppose f is continuous on R^2, f restricted to l_{alpha,p} lies in L^1(l_{alpha,p}) for every alpha in S^1 and p in R, and there exist constants c > 0 and a fixed m >= 0 such that |f(x)| <= c(1 + |x|^m) for all x in R^2. If Rf(alpha,p) = 0 for every alpha in S^1 and every p in R, must f vanish identically on R^2?

Determine whether the following statement is true or false, without imposing any additional hypotheses such as L = M, smallness of |b - a|, or similar side conditions: let D be a bounded domain in R^n, n > 1, with smooth connected boundary S. Let L and M be elliptic, second-order, selfadjoint, strictly positive Dirichlet operators in D with real-valued coefficients, so that all functions involved are real-valued, and let a(x), b(x) be strictly positive functions smooth on the closure of D. If real-valued functions u and v satisfy Lu + a(x)v = 0 in D, -b(x)u + Mv = 0 in D, and u = v = 0 on S, must it follow that u = v = 0 in D? If not, construct a counterexample.

Let D ⊂ R^3 be a bounded domain, for example a box or a ball, and let 0 ≠ f ∈ L^2(D). Define F(z) = ∫_D f(x)e^{iz·x}dx for z ∈ C^3. For j = 1, 2, let L_j(z) be a polynomial of degree at least 1 and set V_j := {z ∈ C^3 : L_j(z) = 0}. Let H_j = L^2(V_j, dm_j), where dm_j are smooth, strictly positive, rapidly decaying measures on V_j such that every exponential e^{iz·x}, x ∈ R^3, belongs to H_j, and assume moreover that the decay is strong enough that for every h ∈ H_1 the function (Th)(u_2) := ∫_{V_1} h(u_1)F(u_1 + u_2) dm_1(u_1) belongs to H_2. Assume that V_1 and V_2 are transversal in the sense that there exist points p_j ∈ V_j whose tangent-space bases together form a basis of C^3. Must the operator T : H_1 → H_2 defined above always be non-finite-rank? ([math.ksu.edu](https://www.math.ksu.edu/~ramm/papers/547.pdf))

Let D⊂R^3 be a bounded domain (for example, a box or a ball), let f∈L^2(D) with f≢0, and define F(z):=∫_D f(x)e^{iz·x}dx for z∈C^3, so F is an entire function of exponential type. For j=1,2, let Lj(z) be a polynomial with deg Lj≥1, let Lj:={z∈C^3: Lj(z)=0} be the corresponding algebraic variety, and let Hj=L^2(Lj,dmj), where dmj is a smooth, rapidly decaying, strictly positive measure on Lj such that every exponential e^{iz·x}, x∈R^3, belongs to Hj, and such that the operator T:H1→H2 defined by (Th)(u2)=∫_{L1} h(u1)F(u1+u2)dm1(u1) indeed maps H1 into H2. Assume moreover that L1 and L2 are transversal, meaning that there exist points on L1 and L2 whose tangent-space bases together form a basis of C^3. Must T fail to be a finite-rank operator?

In base 10, for each integer n >= 1, let M_n be the integer obtained by concatenating the decimal expansions of n, n-1, ..., 2, 1, 2, ..., n-1, n; thus M_1 = 1, M_2 = 212, M_3 = 32123, and M_10 = 109876543212345678910. How many terms of this Mirror Sequence are prime numbers? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

For each integer n >= 1, let P_n be the base-10 integer obtained by concatenating, in order, the odd numbers 1,3,5,...,2n-1 and then the even numbers 2n,2n-2,...,2; thus P_1 = 12, P_2 = 1342, P_3 = 135642, P_4 = 13578642, and P_5 = 13579108642. Does there exist any n >= 1 and integers m > 1, r > 1 such that P_n = m^r?

Let S_0=(1,2,3,\dots). For each k\ge 1, obtain S_k from S_{k-1} by deleting every 2^k-th term of S_{k-1}, counting positions from 1 each time in the current surviving list. Let S be the increasing sequence of positive integers that survive every stage of this binary sieve (so S begins 1,3,5,9,11,13,17,21,25,27,29,33,\dots). Does S contain infinitely many primes, and, apart from the initial term 1, infinitely many composite numbers?

Let S_0 = {1,2,3,...}. For each integer k >= 1, form S_k from S_{k-1} by deleting every 3^k-th element of S_{k-1}, with positions counted anew from 1 inside the current remaining sequence; let S be the increasing sequence of positive integers that survive all stages (thus S begins 1,2,4,5,7,8,10,11,14,16,17,19,...). Does S contain infinitely many prime numbers, and infinitely many numbers that are not prime (equivalently here, infinitely many composite numbers)?

For each integer n ≥ 2, start with the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ... . At stage k = 1, 2, 3, ... , recount the current remaining sequence from 1 and delete every n^k-th term. Let S_n denote the remaining sequence after carrying out all stages of this n-ary power sieve. Does S_n contain infinitely many prime numbers, and infinitely many terms that are not prime? ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/6992817/florentin-smarandache-sequences-of-numbers-involved-in))

Starting from the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., consider the sequence called the k-ary Consecutive Sieve (second version), described in the paper by the rule "keep the first k numbers, skip the k+1 numbers" for k = 2, 3, 4, ... and beginning 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 14, 20, 25, 31, 34, 44, .... How many terms of this infinite sequence are prime numbers?

Let (u_i)_{i>=1} be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with u_i > 1. Starting from the natural numbers N = {1,2,3,...}, perform the following general-sequence sieve: at stage 1, keep one number among 1,2,...,u_1-1 and delete every u_1-th number; inductively, at stage k >= 2, from the current increasing sequence of survivors keep one number among the next u_k-1 remaining numbers and delete every u_k-th remaining number. The sequence (u_i) is called the sieve generator. Study the relationship between the sieve generator (u_i) and the increasing sequence of integers that remains after this sieve is carried out.

Let (u_i)_{i>=1} be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with u_i > 1, and let (v_i)_{i>=1} be a positive integer sequence with 1 <= v_i < u_i for all i. Starting from the natural numbers set N = {1,2,3,...}, define the more general sieve recursively as follows: at step 1, keep the v_1-th number among 1,2,3,...,u_1-1 and delete every u_1-th number; for each step i >= 2, keep the v_i-th number among the next u_i-1 numbers that remain after the previous steps and delete every u_i-th remaining number. With u_i and v_i regarded as sieve generators, study the relationship between the generator sequences (u_i), (v_i) and the remaining sequence produced by this more general sieve. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

In base 10, let n be a positive integer. Call n a pseudo-prime of third kind if some permutation of the positions of the digits in the decimal expansion of n, other than the identity permutation, yields a prime number when read as a decimal integer (so a leading zero may disappear). Are there infinitely many pseudo-primes of third kind that are themselves prime?

Are there infinitely many positive perfect squares n in ordinary decimal notation such that some nonidentity permutation of the positions of the decimal digits of n yields, after deleting any resulting leading zeros, a perfect square (possibly n itself when equal digits are swapped)?

Let n be a positive integer written in base 10. Call n a pseudo-cube of third kind if there exists a nonidentity permutation of its digit positions such that the resulting decimal numeral is a perfect cube, with leading zeros created by the permutation allowed and with repeated digits permitted to yield the same numeral. Are there infinitely many perfect cubes n that are pseudo-cubes of third kind? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

For each fixed integer m >= 2, in base 10, are there infinitely many positive integers n such that n is an m-th power and some nonidentity permutation of the positions of the decimal digits of n yields a decimal numeral that is also an m-th power, where any leading zeros in the permuted digit string are ignored when interpreting the resulting integer?
Prime Equation Conjecture: For a fixed positive integer k, are there only finitely many solutions in integers p, q, x, y with p > 1, q > 1, x > 1, and y > 1 to the equation x^p - y^q = k?

For a fixed positive integer k >= 2, does the Diophantine equation y = 2 x_1 x_2 ... x_k + 1 have infinitely many solutions in pairwise distinct prime numbers y, x_1, x_2, ..., x_k? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

Fix integers a and b with gcd(a,b)=1. For each of the following sequences indexed by n = 1, 2, 3, ..., determine the number of positive prime terms that occur: (i) a p_n + b, where p_n denotes the n-th prime; (ii) a^n + b, under the additional restriction a ∉ {-1, 0, 1}; and (iii) the two sequences n^n + 1 and n^n - 1.

For a fixed planar figure F in the Euclidean plane—or, in the paper’s stated generalization, for a fixed body B in Euclidean 3-space—and for a real number d>0, determine the maximum possible cardinality of a subset S⊂F (respectively S⊂B) such that |x-y|≥d for every pair of distinct points x,y∈S. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

Given a planar figure F in the Euclidean plane, or more generally a body B in Euclidean space, and a real number d > 0, determine the minimum cardinality of a set of points {A1, ..., Am} contained in F (respectively in B) such that for every point A in F (respectively in B) there exists an index i with |AAi| < d. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The supplied arXiv ID does not match this draft. Assuming you intended the classical Euclidean distance-realization problem rather than arXiv:math/0604019, the sharp stand-alone version is: For a fixed integer m >= 1, does every partition R^m = C_1 union ... union C_{m+1} contain an index i such that for every real d > 0 there exist x,y in C_i with ||x-y|| = d?

Let a_1,...,a_n be distinct digits from {1,2,...,9}, with 1 <= n <= 9. How many prime numbers can be written in base 10 using only the digits a_1,...,a_n, with repetitions allowed and no other digits permitted? In particular, is the set of such primes infinite?

For each positive integer n, let p_n denote the n-th prime and define P_n = 1 + p_1 p_2 ... p_n. Determine the cardinality of the set of indices n >= 1 for which P_n is prime; equivalently, how many terms of the Prime Product Sequence are themselves prime?

Factorial Product Sequence (paper item 182). For each positive integer n, let f_k = k! be the k-th factorial number and define F_n = 1 + product_{k=1}^n f_k = 1 + product_{k=1}^n k!. The sequence begins 2, 3, 13, 289, 34561, 24883201, 125411328001, 5056584744960001, ... . Determine how many terms F_n, as n ranges over all integers n >= 1, are prime.

In the sense of item 223 of the paper, call a number N lucky if there exist values for which a nontrivial incorrect operation or algebraic manipulation, resembling the corresponding correct operation and of the sort made in common student mistakes, nevertheless produces the same numerical output N as the correct operation does (for example, mistakes of the type sqrt(a) - sqrt(b) = sqrt(a - b), excluding trivial coincidences such as b = 0 or a = b in that example). Is the set of lucky numbers finite or infinite?

Let a generalized Smarandache palindrome (GSP) be an integer of the concatenated form a1a2...anan...a2a1 for some n >= 1, or a1a2...a_{n-1}a_na_{n-1}...a2a1 for some n >= 2, where a1, a2, ..., an are positive integers and the blocks may have different digit lengths. Are there infinitely many prime numbers that are GSPs?

In the scope of Section 1.1, can one determine whether a Dirac-type ether exists; whether Dirac's 1951 theory can remove the QED infinity difficulty; whether that theory reconciles the quantum-mechanical and electrodynamical descriptions of the electron; what dynamical mechanism underlies Koide's lepton-mass mixing matrix; whether neutrinos are massive; whether rishon/preon models of elementary particles predict better than conventional QCD; what physical mechanism explains quark confinement; and whether QCD is theoretically connected to quantum fluid dynamics? ([cds.cern.ch](https://cds.cern.ch/record/2847617/files/arXiv%3Amath_0609238.pdf))

Could one (a) formulate a quantum-liquid model of elementary particles that predicts elementary-particle masses, and (b) determine whether quarks or Harari rishons can exist in isolation either in Nature or in a strong electromagnetic-field environment, and whether quarks/rishons admit a theoretical explanation from the viewpoints of multivalued-logic Quantum Mechanics, Quaternion Quantum Mechanics—including a physical interpretation of a scalar in the quaternion field and a possible quaternion-type symmetry of neutrino mass—or the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a rotating Bose-Einstein condensate, including the resulting Magnus-effect contribution to the rotational dynamics of quarks?

Within the Harari rishon/preon framework summarized in Section 1.1, where quarks and leptons are composite states of T and V rishons, is there any physical mechanism by which a gravitational field affects quark and rishon charges; quark charges or masses can be altered; quark charge can be returned to the surrounding vacuum or converted into energy, and if so under what conditions; neutrino mass can transform into an isolated entity; and neutrinos can be found inside the human body? ([cds.cern.ch](https://cds.cern.ch/record/2847617/files/arXiv%3Amath_0609238.pdf))

Can one determine whether anti-hydrogen (antimatter hydrogen) has signatures in astrophysics, whether a large anti-hydrogen star—similar to a neutron star—in the cosmos would affect a normal star, whether anti-hydrogen is also formed in a normal star such as the Sun and what its signature would be, whether anti-hydrogen is compatible with the ring-model of the electron, whether a ring-model of the electron can be derived that is consistent with Dirac’s 1951 model and with anti-hydrogen experiment, what the actual trajectory of a deuterium nucleus is in the context of that ring-model, and whether there exists a theoretical basis for quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics that automatically includes anti-hydrogen?

Under the paper's definition of unmatter as any bindable system containing at least one matter building block and at least one antimatter building block, determine whether there are infinitely many unmatter combinations of quark/antiquark type and of lepton/antilepton type; in the quark sector, restrict to colourless states satisfying Q ≡ A (mod 3) and Q*A ≠ 0, where Q and A are the numbers of quarks and antiquarks. Assuming unmatter can also combine with matter and/or antimatter so that the resulting bound system may itself be matter, antimatter, or unmatter, can some such strong-interaction states occur within hadrons and leave signatures there, and can antimatter or unmatter be confined by a container whose walls are electromagnetic fields, with the attainable confinement duration determined?

Within the Brightsen nucleon cluster model for beta-stable isotopes, in which composite nuclei are built from the fundamental clusters {NPN, PNP, NP} (with halo clusters NN, PP, NNN also mentioned), can one determine, by theoretical derivation and experimentally testable predictions, whether the model's first seven claims are valid: (1) that the average prompt-neutron yields and light charged-particle emission in fission of U-235, U-233, Pu-239, and Pu-241 are explained by a universal four-step fission process; (2) that low-temperature transformation/low-energy reactions, including 104Pd(p, alpha)101Rh, and possibly low-energy fusion, arise from interactions between nucleon clusters; (3) that stable matter-antimatter nucleon-cluster unions ('unmatter entities') exist inside nuclei and imply that antimatter has antigravity and anti-mass, testable by comparing the gravitational acceleration of antihydrogen and hydrogen; (4) that electromagnetic radiation tuned to the exact magnetic moment of a specific NPN, PNP, or NP sub-cluster can eject that cluster from a dangerous radioactive nucleus and thereby induce transmutation to less radioactive daughter nuclei via fission and/or beta or alpha decay; (5) that one Helium-4 sub-cluster isodyne consists of two weakly stable deuteron [NP] clusters with distinct energy levels, spin, and magnetic moments; (6) that forces within NPN, PNP, and NP clusters are stronger than forces between such clusters because of different spin-doublet and spin-triplet combinations; and (7) that the next magic numbers are N = 172, Z = 106, A = 278 (Seaborgium-278), requiring shell structure to be explained in terms of nucleon clusters rather than independent nucleons in an average field?

Given a prescribed circle of radius n, determine the maximum number of pairwise non-overlapping circles of radius 1 that can be contained in it under the condition that each packed circle is tangent to at most two other packed circles. In the same sense, determine the corresponding extremal problem for circles of radius Φ(n), where Φ is a given function of n, contained in a circle of radius n; for circles of radius 1 contained in a given triangle (in the spirit of Malfatti's problem); and analogously for spheres, cones, cylinders, regular pyramids, and, more generally, for prescribed plane figures inside a prescribed planar figure, and in space as well.

For each integer base B >= 2, let [m]_B denote the standard base-B expansion of the positive integer m, written without leading zeros, and define C_B(n) to be the positive integer whose base-B expansion is the concatenation [1]_B[2]_B...[n]_B. Thus, in base 10, C_10(1)=1, C_10(2)=12, C_10(3)=123, C_10(4)=1234, and so on. Determine how many terms of the Consecutive Sequence {C_10(n)}_{n>=1} are prime; more generally, for each fixed base B >= 2, determine how many terms of {C_B(n)}_{n>=1} are prime.

For the two open problems posed in §2.3-§2.4 of the paper, determine whether: (i) for each fixed positive integer k>2, the Diophantine equation y=2x1x2...xk+1 has infinitely many solutions with x1,...,xk,y all prime numbers (with no distinctness condition imposed); and (ii) writing N* for the set of positive integers, there exists a largest integer l>3 such that every countable partition N*=⨆_{i=1}^∞ Ci into pairwise disjoint nonempty classes contains at least one class Ci that includes an arithmetic progression a,a+d,...,a+(l-1)d with d>0; if so, find the maximum such l.

For each fixed pair of integers k,s with k>3 and 1<s<k, let p_1,...,p_{k-s} and q_1,...,q_s be positive prime integers, with no prime occurring in both collections {p_1,...,p_{k-s}} and {q_1,...,q_s}. If k is odd, does every odd integer n admit a representation n=p_1+\cdots+p_{k-s}-(q_1+\cdots+q_s)? If so, does this remain true under the stronger requirement that all k primes p_1,...,p_{k-s},q_1,...,q_s be pairwise distinct, and how many such representations does each odd integer have? Likewise, if k is even, does every even integer n admit such a representation, again with the same two follow-up questions on pairwise distinctness of all k primes and on the number of representations?

Let a rank-n magic square mean an n x n array of numbers whose row sums, column sums, and two main diagonal sums are all equal. Determine whether there is any upper bound on the possible ranks n for such additive magic squares; whether there exists a general algorithm that constructs a magic square of arbitrary prescribed rank n; whether analogous rank-n squares can be defined by requiring equality of the corresponding row, column, and diagonal values when addition is replaced by multiplication, and separately when it is replaced by division; whether rank-n magic squares may be formed with fractional entries rather than integers; and whether, in the speculative sense intended by the paper, there is any plausible connection between magic-square structure and hadronic (quark) charges, including whether any particular rank n is especially natural for such a connection.

Let Z(n) denote the pseudo-Smarandache function: for each integer n>1, Z(n) is the least positive integer m such that n divides 1+2+...+m. For k>=0, define the k-fold iterate by Z_0(n)=n and Z_k(n)=Z(Z_{k-1}(n)) for k>=1. Call an integer palindromic if its decimal expansion reads the same forwards and backwards. Determine whether there exists a largest nonnegative integer m such that, for some integer n>1, every iterate Z_k(n) is palindromic for k=0,1,...,m; if such a largest m exists, determine it, and if not, prove Ashbacher's conjecture that no largest such m exists.

Let a Smarandache geometry mean a geometry with at least one Smarandachely denied axiom, i.e. an axiom that behaves in at least two different ways within the same space. In the specific geometry of §2.9 obtained by replacing Euclid’s fifth postulate so that, for suitable choices of a line and an exterior point, the parallel axiom can occur in each of the five ways listed there—exactly one parallel, finitely many k>2 parallels, no parallel, infinitely many but not all parallels, and all lines through the point parallel—determine whether the circle equation x^2 + y^2 = r^2 remains valid; if it does, determine how many nontrivial solutions it has. For this same multispacial geometry, determine whether there is a rule analogous to the Archimedean triangle theorem and prove the corresponding theorem. Separately, for Smarandache geometries in general, determine whether there exists a single general model from which particular Smarandache geometries can be recovered by varying parameters.

For integers x, y, z, how many other nontrivial integer solutions does the Diophantine equation x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 1 have besides (9,10,-12) and (-6,-8,9)? More generally, for integers A, B, C, D with gcd(A,B,C)=1, how many integer solutions (x,y,z) does A x^3 + B y^3 + C z^3 = D have; and, in the explicit n-variable diagonal-cubic extension stated in the paper, for integers A_1,...,A_n,b with gcd(A_1,...,A_n)=1, how many integer solutions (x_1,...,x_n) does A_1 x_1^3 + A_2 x_2^3 + ... + A_n x_n^3 = b have? The paper leaves the word nontrivial undefined.

In the paper's sense of a multi-space as a union of many different spaces, and taking Smarandache geometries to be particular multispaces formed by unions of geometrical spaces, can one formulate a general theory that explains how heterogeneous spaces are connected (for example nanoscale, world-scale, and cosmic-scale spaces, or inorganic and organic nanoscale spaces), determine how Smarandache geometries—that is, geometries with at least one "Smarandachely denied" axiom, meaning an axiom that behaves in at least two different ways within the same space—should be used in physics in light of the use of Weyl and Kähler geometries in quantization, and assess whether nanochips could function as additional human memories by storing an external body of information, being implanted into the brain, and being searchable by the user? citeturn5view0turn7view1turn6view0

Consider the following five qualitative open problems in celestial mechanics and Earth dynamics: (1) is it possible to accelerate a photon, or any other particle already traveling at about 0.99 c, so that its speed exceeds c; (2) is it possible to construct a flexible bridge between two planets that would permit terrestrial traffic, while allowing a smooth escape from the gravitational field of one planet, a smooth entry into the gravitational field of the other, and accommodating the continuous motion of the planets; (3) if a planet were cut into two separated parts, would equal halves re-attract and reform a single planet or instead separate further, and what changes if one part is significantly larger than the other; (4) taking a fixed point on Earth from which the Moon is visible only when it is above the local horizon, and analogously a fixed point on the Moon from which Earth is visible, why is Earth seen above from the Moon while the Moon is also seen above from Earth; and (5) for a tunnel joining opposite sides of the Earth, first through the center and then in an off-center configuration, determine whether a dropped object oscillates through the center and eventually stops or floats there, how much force is needed to push a free-falling elevator from the center toward the far surface and whether inertia carries it beyond the center, whether passengers experience Coriolis effects or feel gravity during free fall, how ocean water behaves if one tunnel mouth lies at the bottom of an ocean, and whether in the off-center case the tunnel midpoint plays a role analogous to the Earth's center.

In Section 3.2.1-3.2.4, the paper asks the following compound astrophysical/relativistic question: What is the dynamical origin of quasars and pulsars, and are they ejected from the centres of galaxies; why has the graviton not been observed experimentally, supposing it is the particle carrying the gravitational field; why did general relativity not predict the precession of planets other than Mercury, and can those precession effects be predicted and compared with observation; and, provided general relativity is correct, is it possible to create a real stargate (sometimes called an Einstein-Rosen bridge) enabling travel from one place in this galaxy to another galaxy, and if so, under what conditions could it be kept open while continuing to connect the same places so that return travel is possible without violating the causality principle?

Resolve the consecutive astrophysical open problems posed in Sections 3.2.5-3.2.9 of the paper: assuming the observed large-scale galactic 'knots' are real, can the sponge-like structure of the universe be described in the form of topological knot theory, what astrophysical consequences would that have relative to more conventional general-relativity predictions, and would dark matter still be required in such a framework; do solar neutrinos have mass, and do they come from the surface of the Sun or from its interior dynamics; for a double-star system of equal masses, can the pair rotate around a common circular orbit, can the passage of another equal-mass object produce a triple-star system, how can the system's velocities be inferred from observational data and can the same data admit different interpretations, and can one find an 'n-star system, with n < 3' in the paper's literal wording; where do comets come from and how were they produced in the past, are they composed of antimatter or water, or are they to be explained instead by a plasma-discharge mechanism; and where do gamma-ray bursts come from, what role do they play in star-formation processes, and are they created when antimatter comets collide with stars?

Assuming the standard Hubble relation z = Hr/c and, as in §3.2.10, that the dominant part of the observed redshift is Doppler so that z = v/c, do Tifft’s reported discrete redshift/velocity increments (36.6 km/s and 72.2 km/s) imply, for galaxies in the same cluster, a quantized distance law δr = (c/H)δz and hence r_n = r_0 + nδr for integers n = 1, 2, 3, ...; and, if so, can this quantized-distance picture be extended to other astrophysical phenomena by interpreting it as evidence for astrophysical topologically quantized vortices satisfying ∮ p·dr = Nh, in the Gross-Pitaevskii / quantum-phion-condensate picture and by analogy with cosmic strings, with the nearby cited observations (CMB-spectrum fits, galaxy rotation curves, Fundamental Plane clusters, and quasar redshift data) used to assess support for or against that interpretation? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

Does the Pioneer anomaly—a Sun-directed anomalous acceleration of order ~8.74 x 10^-10 m/sec^2 reported after the Pioneer spacecraft entered the orbit of Jupiter—imply a modified gravitation theory, for example through the Brownstein–Moffat correction a_p = -δG(r)M⊙/r^2 with δG(r) = G0 α(r)[1 - e^{-r/λ(r)}(1 + r/λ(r))], and, within that scope, how can one account for its non-detection before Jupiter, determine whether it exhibits other detectable higher-order gravitational effects, decide whether Jupiter's gravitational field affects the Pioneer orbit, and assess whether the data indicate a significant difference between the gravitational fields of the inner planets and the Jovian planets corresponding to a 'two-fluid' model of superfluidity?

Within the Earth-specific Newtonian viewpoint introduced in §4.1, can one derive a governing Newtonian dynamical equation for Earth’s geophysical processes, cast it as a Cauchy initial-value problem with a numerical solution, determine the role of the Coriolis force in that equation, and then—if a mathematical model exists—decide whether global warming is linked to earthquakes, whether fluctuations in solar radiation are linked to earthquakes and to Earth climatic changes, and how well such a model predicts new climatic changes such as large volcanic activity or hurricanes? ([cds.cern.ch](https://cds.cern.ch/record/2847617/files/arXiv%3Amath_0609238.pdf))

Can one formulate a Newtonian dynamical model for geophysical processes inside the Earth that explains the Chandler polar wobble of the Earth's rotation axis by deciding whether the wobble is more plausibly due to internal geodynamics, specifically rotational inertia and quadrupole moments, or to external forcing such as the Sun's motion or fluctuations in solar radiation; determining the role of Coriolis forces in that model; establishing whether the wobble can be predicted at least a few months ahead and whether it has any plausible linkage with some earthquakes due to Earth instability; and, under the additional speculative assumptions that Earth may be viewed as an electric capacitor and planetary systems as rotating superconductors describable by a Gross-Pitaevskii/Euler/quaternionic rigid-body model coupled to electromagnetic torque, deciding whether an artificial electromagnetic field could stabilize the Chandler wobble?

Can the paper's governing Newtonian dynamical equation for geophysical processes on Earth—understood in the surrounding discussion as the Newtonian geophysical dynamics whose local formulation raises Cauchy-form and Coriolis-force questions, and whose nearby background includes the proposal that planetary systems, including Earth, may be modeled as rotating superconductors through the Gross-Pitaevskii/Ginzburg-Landau and quaternionic rigid-body framework—be translated into a general-relativistic expression; if so, what genuinely new experimentally testable predictions follow from that relativistic reformulation; and, in the sense of the condensed-matter analogue of general relativity cited by the authors (Volovik et al.), does such a reformulation support treating geophysical processes like Earth's as condensed-matter superconductivity, and what experimentally verifiable implications would a superconductivity model of Earth have? ([cds.cern.ch](https://cds.cern.ch/record/2847617/files/arXiv%3Amath_0609238.pdf))

In Beth’s classical circularly polarized-light / birefringent-plate experiment, where the doubled-beam setup is claimed to exert a torque on the plate despite vanishing Poynting (energy-flux) transfer, can classical Maxwell electrodynamics be supplemented by a nonzero electromagnetic spin tensor so that the torque is explained as spin flux and thereby provide a classical electromagnetic description of quantum spin; and, within that same spin-based framework, is there a plausible linkage between spin, the Aharonov effect, and hidden-variable interpretations of quantum mechanics?

Analyze the five specific relativity scenarios posed in Section 7.1 of the paper: (1) determine the geometric character of a 'relativistic rotating plane' in the 'Unruh experiment'—Minkowskian, Euclidean, or Riemannian; (2) decide whether the equivalence principle applies to a disc rotating at high speed whose out-of-plane forces resemble an accelerating field; (3) determine whether a person inside an elevator that is simultaneously in free-fall and rotating around its vertical centre feels a gravitational force, or a force larger than what the equivalence principle requires; (4) in the scenario where an aeroplane at altitude 1 km drops an empty elevator-room and, one second later, drops four grenades along the elevator's path, determine whether any grenade reaches the elevator before ground impact and, if so, which grenade; and (5) determine whether 'space temperature' affects spacetime curvature or the spacetime metric.

Let p(λ) be a normalized hidden-variable density, ∫p(λ)dλ = 1, and let C''(·) denote the observed average correlation/chance for two spin components whose relative angles are indicated. Starting from the Bell inequality written in the paper as C''(φ) - C''(δ) - C''(δ - φ) ≤ 1, can one replace the classical binary outcome assumption P(A) + P(B) = 1 by the Dezert-Smarandache mass relation m(A) + m(B) + m(A∪B) + m(A∩B) = 1, so as to allow multivalued photon-pair positions/outcomes A∪B and A∩B, and thereby justify and experimentally test the modified inequality C''(φ) - C''(δ) - C''(δ - φ) + C''(δ∪φ) + C''(δ∩φ) ≤ 1 as a more precise refinement of the standard local hidden-variable description of quantum reality? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

Is there, in the context of quantum physics, a valid theoretical relation describing mind–matter interaction that is supported by experimental observation, can be used to explain other known quantum phenomena, has a plausible linkage to cymatics observations, and yields new testable predictions concerning the hidden structure of water; in particular, do the cited reports of water-crystal changes under exposure to human language, music, or printed messages, together with related cymatics observations, represent a real physical effect rather than merely an untested hypothesis?

In the specific framework proposed in Section 7.4, does the superconducting Gross-Pitaevskii/Ginzburg-Landau-Schrödinger model for an order parameter Psi(x,t), after the standing-wave substitution Psi(x,t)=exp(-iEt/hbar)u(x) and the paper’s truncation of the Maclaurin expansion to the approximate form (23), admit the biquaternionic reduction asserted in Conjecture 1—namely, that for a given particular solution of the alternative Schrodinger equation (26), the approximate Gross-Pitaevskii solution reduces to the first-order biquaternion equation (32), of the same Maxwell-type as equation (30)—and, if so, does this specific quaternionic electrodynamics of superconductors have experimental support, account for the Meissner effect and Josephson junctions, relate coherently to BCS theory, and predict concrete superconducting phenomena not already predicted by BCS?

Does there exist a solar model with a neutron flux from the core in which some neutrons are captured by nuclei while the rest beta-decay to ionized hydrogen, and in which successive reactions p+n -> d, d+n -> t, t -> ^3He via beta decay, ^3He+n -> ^4He, and analogous neutron-capture/beta-decay steps up the periodic table to iron and beyond produce the isotopes observed in the solar photosphere, such that the total energy released by these reactions accounts for all of the Sun's thermal energy and luminosity and the total neutrino yield agrees with observation, thereby removing the need to take the standard 4p -> ^4He + 2e+ + 2nu_e proton-fusion reaction as the Sun's primary power source? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

Within the paper's closed-system energy-conservation framework, can one formulate and minimize a least-squares variational functional Π that compares a quantity Q computed from candidate laws with the corresponding quantity Q' computed directly from the law of Energy Conservation, so as to derive simultaneously, in the specific example of a charged point mass of mass m and charge q2 rolling from A to B down a long incline in the electric field of an electrified globe of charge q1 and radius R, a modified Coulomb law of inverse non-square / variable-dimension fractal form f = k q1 q2 / r^D (with either constant D or D = D(r)) together with the paper's one-parameter constant-dimension fractal deformation of Newton's second law; and, in that same framework, does the resulting modification allow short-range Coulomb repulsion as r -> 0, support a Hausdorff-fractal version of Newton's second law, and motivate a flat-metric gravitational theory capable of reproducing the standard tests of general relativity and any observational evidence for fractal dynamics?

In the sense of §7.7 of the paper, should one treat the gravitational coefficient as the usual constant G0 = 6.67×10^-11 N·m^2/kg^2 only in the static state, and in all other cases replace Newton’s law by an inverse-square law F = -GMm/r^2 with a state-dependent coefficient G determined from the paper’s improved gravitation formula by G = G0(1 + 3G0Mp/(c^2r^2)), where M and m are the two masses, r is their separation, c is the speed of light, and p is the half normal chord of the orbit of m about M (p = a(1-e^2) for an ellipse, p = a(e^2-1) for a hyperbola, p = y^2/(2x) for a parabola), and does this proposed rule reproduce the paper’s three benchmark cases with the stated bounds: Mercury’s perihelion advance, (1 + 5.038109×10^-8)G0 ≤ G ≤ (1 + 1.162308×10^-7)G0; gravitational deflection of a photon orbit around the sun, G0 ≤ G ≤ 2.5G0; and a small ball moving down a long incline on Earth’s surface, either via the constant-dimension-fractal relation G = G0r^0.00011 giving 1.001725G0 ≤ G ≤ 1.001735G0 or via the variable-dimension-fractal relation G = G0r^δ with δ = 1.206×10^-12x, x = 0 at the beginning static state, giving G0 ≤ G ≤ 1.000012G0? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

Assuming the "fractal explanation" described in the immediately preceding section, can a scale-invariance principle provide a coherent explanation that reconciles the observed differences in properties and behaviours between microscopic and macroscopic phenomena, specifically between (i) a few grains of sand and the vast terrain of the Sahara, (ii) an individual particle and transport phenomena, (iii) a micromolecule and a macromolecule such as DNA, and (iv) a patternless or simple small patch of an object and the complicated, though repeated, pattern of fractals?

In the sense of §7.9 of the paper, and starting from the claim that some geophysicists take the oldest coral reef to be about 4200 years old and therefore argue that the Earth cannot be much older, what is the link between the age of a coral reef and the age of the Earth, is there experimental evidence from coral reef data that the Earth-day was less than 24 hours in the past, and, if such evidence exists, how should it be validated against other related data so as to determine the aggregate conclusion about the Earth’s age and any implications for Earth’s climatic changes?

Using the heuristic setup of Section 7.10—Landauer's relation for one bit, E_erase ≈ kT ln(2), together with the cited superconductivity-model relation (1/2) hbar omega ≈ k T_c—does there exist a valid theoretical relation between Planckian quantization and the quantization of information; if so, does that relation provide a sound theoretical basis for quantum computation, does it also connect quantization of information with Maxwell's equations and superconductivity phenomena, and is there any experimental observation supporting these proposed linkages? ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/UnfoldingLabyrinth.pdf))

Assuming that the reported Bohr-Sommerfeld-type quantization of celestial motion is a genuine empirical effect—namely, that for a body orbiting a central mass M the closed-orbit condition ∮_Γ p·dx = 2πnh (with Γ a closed classical orbit, p the momentum, and n = 1,2,3,...) together with Newtonian force balance GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r leads to a quantized semimajor-axis law r_n = a_n = n^2GM/v_0^2 (where G is Newton’s constant and v_0 a specific velocity)—what is the physical origin of this macroquantization in astrophysics and celestial motion? More specifically, which explanation is most consistent with the observed planetary and exoplanet orbital data: (i) the Bohr-Sommerfeld/Nottale scale-relativity framework itself, (ii) a macroquantum-condensate or superfluid-vortex model of the vacuum or cosmos, (iii) cosmic turbulence with logarithmic-type interaction, or (iv) a deeper theory linking these mechanisms; and what observations would verify or refute these alternatives?

For every set of real numbers X (equivalently, every separable zero-dimensional metric space), let O be the family of nontrivial open covers of X, Ω the family of open ω-covers of X, and Γ the family of open γ-covers of X, where an open cover U is an ω-cover if X is not a member of U and every finite F⊆X is contained in some U∈U, and U is a γ-cover if U is infinite and each x∈X belongs to all but finitely many members of U. Is it true that X satisfies Ufin(O, Ω) if and only if X satisfies Sfin(Γ, Ω)? Here Ufin(A,B) means that for every sequence (U_n) of members of A with no finite subcover, there exist finite F_n⊆U_n such that {∪F_n : n∈N} is a member of B; and Sfin(A,B) means that for every sequence (U_n) of members of A, there exist finite F_n⊆U_n such that ∪_{n∈N} F_n is a member of B. In this sets-of-reals setting, the covers may be assumed countable.

In the setting of sets of real numbers, let X be a set of reals, let O be the family of all nontrivial open covers of X, let Ω be the family of open ω-covers of X, and let Γ be the family of open γ-covers of X. For cover classes A and B, define Sfin(A,B) to mean that for every sequence (Un)n∈N of members of A there exist finite sets Fn ⊆ Un such that ⋃n∈N Fn is a member of B; define Ufin(A,B) to mean that for every sequence (Un)n∈N of members of A having no finite subcover, there exist finite sets Fn ⊆ Un such that {⋃Fn : n ∈ N} is a member of B. Assuming that Ufin(O,Ω) is not equal to Sfin(Γ,Ω), must every set of reals X satisfying Ufin(O,Γ) also satisfy Sfin(Γ,Ω)?

Can there exist a Borel, non-σ-compact subgroup H of a Polish group P and a subspace X ⊆ H, endowed with the inherited topology, such that H is generated as a group by X and X has the Hurewicz property Ufin(O, Γ); that is, for every sequence (Un)n∈N of open covers of X with no finite subcover, there are finite families Fn ⊆ Un such that {∪Fn : n ∈ N} is a γ-cover of X (equivalently, each x ∈ X belongs to ∪Fn for all but finitely many n)?

Let X⊆ℝ be a set of reals with the Hurewicz property Ufin(O,Γ); that is, for every sequence (𝒰_n)n∈ω of open covers of X there exist finite subfamilies 𝒱_n⊆𝒰_n such that {⋃𝒱_n:n∈ω} is a γ-cover of X. Suppose X⊆B⊆ℝ and B is Borel. Must there exist a σ-compact set F with X⊂F⊂B? In particular, is this always true when B is an F_{σδ} subset of ℝ?

In ZFC, does there exist a set of reals X⊆R with |X|=b such that for every sequence ⟨Un:n∈N⟩ of countable open γ-covers of X, one can choose Un∈Un for each n so that {Un:n∈N} is again a γ-cover of X? Here a γ-cover of X means an infinite family of open subsets of X such that every x∈X belongs to all but finitely many members of the family, and b is the bounding number.

Working in ZFC, does there exist a set of reals X ⊆ ℝ with |X| = 𝔡, where 𝔡 is the dominating number (the least cardinality of a family D ⊆ ω^ω such that for every f ∈ ω^ω there is g ∈ D with f(n) ≤ g(n) for all but finitely many n), such that X satisfies Sfin(Ω,Ω); that is, for every sequence ⟨𝒰_n : n ∈ ℕ⟩ of open ω-covers of X, there exist finite subfamilies 𝔽_n ⊆ 𝒰_n such that ⋃_{n∈ℕ} 𝔽_n is again an open ω-cover of X, where an open ω-cover means a nontrivial open cover 𝒰 of X with the property that every finite F ⊆ X is contained in some U ∈ 𝒰? ([nzdr.ru](https://www.nzdr.ru/data/media/biblio/kolxoz/M/MD/MDgt/Pearl%20E.%20%28ed.%29%20Open%20Problems%20in%20Topology%20II%20%28Elsevier%2C%202007%29%28ISBN%200444522085%29%28723s%29_MDgt_.pdf))

Working in ZFC, is there a direct construction—meaning one that does not proceed by a dichotomic argument splitting on an independent set-theoretic hypothesis and its negation—of a set of reals M ⊆ ℝ, with the usual subspace topology, such that M satisfies Sfin(Ω, Ω) but fails Ufin(O, Γ)? Here O denotes the family of all nontrivial open covers of M, Ω the family of open ω-covers of M (every finite F ⊆ M is contained in some member), and Γ the family of open γ-covers of M (infinite open covers whose members contain each x ∈ M all but finitely often); equivalently spelled out, Sfin(Ω, Ω) means that for every sequence (U_n : n ∈ ℕ) of ω-covers of M there exist finite F_n ⊆ U_n such that ⋃_{n∈ℕ} F_n is an ω-cover of M, while Ufin(O, Γ) means that for every sequence (U_n : n ∈ ℕ) of open covers of M with no finite subcover there exist finite F_n ⊆ U_n such that {⋃F_n : n ∈ ℕ} is a γ-cover of M. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

Is it consistent with ZFC that every set of reals X satisfying Sfin(B, B) is countable, where B is the family of countable nontrivial covers of X by Borel subsets of X, and Sfin(B, B) means that for every sequence ⟨Un:n∈N⟩ of members of B there exist finite families Fn⊆Un such that ⋃n Fn is again a member of B?

Assume the Continuum Hypothesis. For a set of reals X ⊆ R, let B, BΩ, and BΓ denote the families of countable Borel covers, countable Borel ω-covers, and countable Borel γ-covers of X, respectively; covers are nontrivial, an ω-cover is one in which every finite F ⊆ X is contained in some member, a γ-cover is an infinite cover whose members contain each x ∈ X all but finitely often, S1(A,B) means that for every sequence (Un)n∈N of members of A one can choose Un ∈ Un so that {Un : n ∈ N} ∈ B, and Sfin(A,B) means that for every such sequence one can choose finite Fn ⊆ Un so that ⋃n Fn ∈ B. Does CH imply that, for each of the five exact satisfaction-patterns corresponding respectively to settings (d), (e), (g), (j), and (l) in Figure 4, there exists a set of reals X whose satisfied properties among the seven Borel-case nodes S1(BΓ,BΓ), S1(BΓ,BΩ), Sfin(B,B), Sfin(BΩ,BΩ), S1(BΩ,BΓ), S1(BΩ,BΩ), and S1(B,B) are exactly one of the following sets: {S1(BΓ,BΩ), Sfin(B,B)}; {S1(BΓ,BΩ), Sfin(B,B), S1(B,B)}; {S1(BΓ,BΩ), Sfin(B,B), Sfin(BΩ,BΩ), S1(B,B)}; {S1(BΓ,BΓ), S1(BΓ,BΩ), Sfin(B,B), S1(B,B)}; {S1(BΓ,BΓ), S1(BΓ,BΩ), Sfin(B,B), Sfin(BΩ,BΩ), S1(B,B)}? ([carmamaths.org](https://carmamaths.org/jon/Preprints/Books/Open%20Probs%20in%20Top/open2.pdf))

Assume Martin's Axiom. Does there exist an uncountable set of reals X ⊆ R such that for every sequence (𝒰_n)_{n∈N} of countable Borel ω-covers of X, one can choose U_n ∈ 𝒰_n for each n so that {U_n : n ∈ N} is a Borel γ-cover of X? Here each 𝒰_n is a nontrivial cover of X by Borel subsets of X, an ω-cover means that every finite F ⊆ X is contained in some member of 𝒰_n, and a γ-cover means an infinite cover in which each x ∈ X belongs to all but finitely many members. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

Let X be a set of real numbers. For a sequence (A_n)_{n∈N} of subsets of X, define lim inf A_n = ⋃_{m∈N} ⋂_{n≥m} A_n, and for a family F of subsets of X let L(F) be the smallest family containing F and closed under this lim inf operation. Say that X has the δ-property if for every open ω-cover U of X, one has X ∈ L(U), where an open ω-cover is a family U of open subsets of X such that X ∉ U and every finite F ⊆ X is contained in some member of U. Is the δ-property equivalent to the Gerlits–Nagy γ-property, i.e. must every such X satisfy that every open ω-cover of X contains a γ-cover of X (equivalently, satisfy S1(Ω,Γ)), where a γ-cover is an infinite open cover in which each point of X belongs to all but finitely many members?

Let X=⋃_{n∈ℕ} X_n, where X_1⊆X_2⊆⋯ are sets of real numbers with the subspace topology from ℝ. Assume that each X_n satisfies \binom{\Omega}{\Gamma} (equivalently, S1(Ω,Γ)); that is, every open ω-cover of X_n contains a γ-subcover, where an open ω-cover is a nontrivial open cover such that every finite subset of X_n is contained in some member, and a γ-cover is an infinite open cover each point of X_n belongs to all but finitely many members. Must X also satisfy \binom{\Omega}{\Gamma}?

For a set of reals X, let BΩ(X) denote the family of all countable Borel ω-covers of X, where covers are nontrivial and an ω-cover means that every finite subset of X is contained in some member of the cover. If X satisfies S1(BΩ, BΩ) (respectively, Sfin(BΩ, BΩ))—that is, from each sequence of members of BΩ(X) one can choose one member (respectively, finitely many members) from each cover so that the chosen family is again a countable Borel ω-cover of X—must every finite power X^n, n ≥ 1, with the product topology, satisfy the same property? ([nzdr.ru](https://www.nzdr.ru/data/media/biblio/kolxoz/M/MD/MDgt/Pearl%20E.%20%28ed.%29%20Open%20Problems%20in%20Topology%20II%20%28Elsevier%2C%202007%29%28ISBN%200444522085%29%28723s%29_MDgt_.pdf))

For a set of reals X, let BΩ(X) denote the family of countable Borel ω-covers of X, meaning countable families U of Borel subsets of X such that X ∉ U and every finite F ⊆ X is contained in some U ∈ U; and let BΓ(X) denote the family of countably infinite Borel γ-covers of X, meaning countable Borel covers U of X such that each x ∈ X belongs to all but finitely many members of U. Writing S1(BΩ,BΓ) for the property that for every sequence (Un)n∈ℕ with each Un ∈ BΩ(X), one can choose Un ∈ Un so that {Un : n ∈ ℕ} ∈ BΓ(X), is it true that whenever X ⊆ ℝ satisfies S1(BΩ,BΓ), then for every positive integer n the finite power X^n, with the product topology, also satisfies S1(BΩ,BΓ)? ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4751a09b2173c9726c9936b8b6ae7acd3ae230b3&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

Let X1,...,Xn be sets of real numbers. Assume that each Xi satisfies both Ufin(O, Γ) and S1(O, O), where O is the family of nontrivial open covers of Xi, Γ is the family of open γ-covers of Xi (that is, infinite open covers such that each point of Xi belongs to all but finitely many members), Ufin(O, Γ) means that for every sequence of open covers of Xi with no finite subcover one can choose finite subfamilies whose unions form a γ-cover, and S1(O, O) means that for every sequence of open covers of Xi one can choose one element from each cover and still cover Xi. Must the finite product X1×...×Xn, with the product topology, also satisfy Ufin(O, Γ) ∩ S1(O, O)?

Is it consistent with ZFC that the class of sets of reals satisfying Sfin(Ω,Ω) is closed under finite unions? Equivalently: is there a model of ZFC in which, whenever X,Y ⊆ R each satisfy Sfin(Ω,Ω), then X ∪ Y also satisfies Sfin(Ω,Ω), where a set Z satisfies Sfin(Ω,Ω) if for every sequence (U_n)_{n∈N} of nontrivial open ω-covers of Z, there exist finite subfamilies F_n ⊆ U_n such that ⋃_{n∈N} F_n is again an open ω-cover of Z, and an ω-cover is an open cover such that every finite subset of Z is contained in some member of the cover?

For a set of real numbers X (equivalently, a zero-dimensional separable metrizable space), let Ω be the family of nontrivial open ω-covers of X, Γ the family of nontrivial open γ-covers of X, and T the family of nontrivial open τ-covers of X, where an open cover U of X is an ω-cover if every finite F⊆X is contained in some U∈U, is a γ-cover if U is infinite and each x∈X belongs to all but finitely many members of U, and is a τ-cover if U is large (each x∈X belongs to infinitely many members of U) and for every x,y∈X either {U∈U : x∈U and y∉U} is finite or {U∈U : y∈U and x∉U} is finite. Is the subcover property Ω choose Γ equal to Ω choose T; that is, does every open ω-cover of X contain a γ-subcover if and only if every open ω-cover of X contains a τ-subcover?

For a set of real numbers X, let O be the family of open covers of X, Ω the family of open ω-covers of X (every finite F⊆X is contained in some member of the cover), Γ the family of open γ-covers of X (the cover is infinite and each x∈X belongs to all but finitely many members), and T the family of open τ-covers of X, where covers are understood to be nontrivial (X is not itself a member of the cover), a large cover is one in which each x∈X belongs to infinitely many members, and a τ-cover is a large cover 𝒰 such that for every x,y∈X either {U∈𝒰:x∈U and y∉U} is finite or {U∈𝒰:y∈U and x∉U} is finite. Must every set of reals X satisfying S1(Ω, T)—that is, for every sequence (𝒰_n)n∈ℕ of members of Ω there exist U_n∈𝒰_n such that {U_n:n∈ℕ} is a τ-cover of X—also satisfy Ufin(O, Γ)—that is, for every sequence (𝒱_n)n∈ℕ of open covers of X with no finite subcover there exist finite families 𝔽_n⊆𝒱_n such that {⋃𝔽_n:n∈ℕ} is a γ-cover of X?

For a set of real numbers X, where a cover means an open cover of X with X not itself a member, let Ω be the family of open ω-covers of X, Γ the family of open γ-covers of X, and T the family of open τ-covers of X (that is, large open covers 𝒰 such that for every x, y in X, either {U in 𝒰 : x in U and y not in U} is finite or {U in 𝒰 : y in U and x not in U} is finite). If Split(A, B) denotes the property that every cover 𝒰 in A can be partitioned into two disjoint subcovers 𝒱 and 𝒲, each containing a subfamily that is a member of B, must Split(Ω, T) imply Split(T, Γ)? ([nzdr.ru](https://www.nzdr.ru/data/media/biblio/kolxoz/M/MD/MDgt/Pearl%20E.%20%28ed.%29%20Open%20Problems%20in%20Topology%20II%20%28Elsevier%2C%202007%29%28ISBN%200444522085%29%28723s%29_MDgt_.pdf))

Let X⊆ℝ∖ℚ, let Cp(X) be the space of all continuous real-valued functions on X with the topology of pointwise convergence, and let 0 denote the constant zero function. For collections A,B, write S1(A,B) to mean that for every sequence (Un)n∈ℕ of members of A, there exist Un∈Un for each n such that {Un:n∈ℕ} is a member of B. Let Γ0 be the family of countably infinite subsets A⊆Cp(X) with 0=lim A (equivalently, 0∉A and every neighborhood of 0 contains all but finitely many points of A), and let Γ be the family of open γ-covers of X, where a γ-cover is an infinite nontrivial open cover U of X such that each x∈X belongs to all but finitely many members of U. Since S1(Γ,Γ) for X is known to imply S1(Γ0,Γ0) for Cp(X), does the converse hold? Equivalently, is S1(Γ0,Γ0) for Cp(X) equivalent to S1(Γ,Γ) for X? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))

For a topological group K with identity e_K, let Onbd(K) be the family of nontrivial open covers of K of the form {k·U : k ∈ K}, where U is a neighborhood of e_K, and let O(K) be the family of all nontrivial open covers of K. Is there, in ZFC, a pair of topological groups G and H such that for each K in {G,H} and every sequence (Cn) of members of Onbd(K), there exist finite subfamilies Fn ⊆ Cn with ⋃n Fn ∈ O(K), while the product group G × H, with the product topology, fails this same property Sfin(Onbd(G × H), O(G × H))? ([nzdr.ru](https://www.nzdr.ru/data/media/biblio/kolxoz/M/MD/MDgt/Pearl%20E.%20%28ed.%29%20Open%20Problems%20in%20Topology%20II%20%28Elsevier%2C%202007%29%28ISBN%200444522085%29%28723s%29_MDgt_.pdf))

Is it consistent with ZFC that the pseudo-intersection number p is strictly smaller than the tower number t; that is, that the least cardinality of a centered family F ⊆ [ω]^ω with no infinite pseudo-intersection is smaller than the least cardinality of a tower T ⊆ [ω]^ω (a family linearly ordered by ⊆*, where A ⊆* B means A \ B is finite) with no infinite pseudo-intersection?

Let X⊆R be a set of reals satisfying Ufin(O,Ω): whenever (U_n)_{n∈N} is a sequence of nontrivial open covers of X, none containing a finite subcover, there exist finite subfamilies F_n⊆U_n such that {∪F_n:n∈N} is an ω-cover of X (that is, every finite subset of X is contained in some ∪F_n). Is it true that for every continuous image Y of X in Baire space N^N (with the product topology), the subspace G_Y={g∈N^N: there exist a positive integer k and f_1,...,f_k∈Y with g<=*max{f_1,...,f_k}} also satisfies Ufin(O,Ω), where g<=*h means g(n)≤h(n) for all but finitely many n and max{f_1,...,f_k}(n)=max_{1≤i≤k} f_i(n)?

For each positive integer n, let H_n be the semiregular hexagon on the triangular lattice with side lengths 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1, 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1 in cyclic order (equivalently, the 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1 semiregular hexagon), and let C_n denote its central location, i.e. the pair of innermost unit triangles. Show that exactly one-third of the lozenge tilings of H_n contain the lozenge covering C_n.

For each positive integer n, let H_n be the hexagon in the triangular lattice with internal angles 120° and side lengths n, n+1, n, n+1, n, n+1 in cyclic order. Remove the central unit equilateral triangle from H_n. Determine exactly the number of lozenge tilings of the resulting region, where a lozenge is a unit rhombus formed by two adjacent unit triangles. ([library.slmath.org](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book38/files/propp.pdf))

For each integer n>=1, determine exactly the number of lozenge tilings of the semiregular hexagon on the triangular lattice with side lengths 2n, 2n+3, 2n, 2n+3, 2n, 2n+3 in cyclic order (all interior angles 120 degrees), after deleting the middle unit triangle from each of the three sides of length 2n+3.

For each integer n >= 1, let H_n be the regular hexagon of side length n on the triangular lattice (equivalently, the n,n,n,n,n,n semiregular hexagon), and let a lozenge be the union of two adjacent unit equilateral triangles. Among the six central unit triangles of H_n, remove one upward-pointing triangle and one downward-pointing triangle. Up to symmetry there are exactly two cases: the removed central triangles are opposite, or they are adjacent. Determine, for each n, the exact number of lozenge tilings of the resulting region in each case. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))

For positive integers a,b,c, let H(a,b,c) be the semiregular hexagon with side lengths a,b,c,a,b,c, and let K_{a,b,c} be the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the finite honeycomb graph dual to H(a,b,c) (equivalently here, the ordinary bipartite adjacency matrix). Let C_{a,b,c} be the integer b-by-b Carlitz matrix obtained from K_{a,b,c} by integral row and column reductions, with (i,j)-entry C_{ij} = (a+c choose a+i-j). Determine the finite abelian group coker_Z(C_{a,b,c}) = Z^b / im(C_{a,b,c}) — equivalently coker_Z(K_{a,b,c}), and hence the common cokernel of the three Carlitz matrices arising from permuting a,b,c — and, if possible, give a direct interpretation of this cokernel in terms of lozenge tilings (equivalently matchings) of H(a,b,c).

For a bipartite planar graph G with a fixed black/white bipartition, let K be any Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of G, meaning the signed bipartite adjacency matrix whose rows correspond to white vertices, whose columns correspond to black vertices, and whose nonzero entries are +/-1 on adjacent white-black pairs. Writing K* for the adjoint of K, the paper notes that although the choice of K is not canonical, the spectrum of KK* is independent of that choice. What combinatorial significance does this spectrum have?

For each integer n >= 2, let A_n be the Aztec diamond of order n, i.e. the union of 2n rows of unit squares with row lengths 2, 4, ..., 2n, 2n, ..., 4, 2. Delete the unique pair of unit squares of A_n (up to the symmetries of the square) whose centers are a chess knight's move apart, meaning they differ by (±1, ±2) or (±2, ±1), and which are as close to the center of A_n as possible subject to that constraint. Determine an explicit formula, as a function of n, for the number of tilings of the resulting region by 1x2 and 2x1 dominos.

For each integer n >= 1, let R_n be the standard 2n-by-(2n+1) Aztec rectangle. Delete its unique central unit square. Determine an explicit exact formula for the number of tilings of the resulting region by 1-by-2 and 2-by-1 dominoes. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))

For each admissible integer n, find an exact formula for the number of tilings by 1-by-2 and 2-by-1 dominos of the standard (2n − 1)-by-2n Aztec rectangle with one unit square adjoining its central square removed.

For each positive integer n, let K_n be the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the bipartite graph dual to the Aztec diamond of order n, with rows indexed by white vertices and columns by black vertices under a fixed checkerboard coloring, and with the sign convention that each nonzero entry corresponding to a vertical domino whose white square is on top is replaced by -1 (all other nonzero entries remaining +1). Prove that the sum of all entries of K_n^{-1} is ((n-1)(n+3))/2 - 2^(n-1) + 2. As stated in the paper, this identity has been verified for n = 1, ..., 8.

Let W_{x,y} denote the Aztec window obtained by deleting from the center of the Aztec diamond of order y the concentric Aztec diamond of order x, where x and y are integers with 0 <= x < y. Determine a general formula for the number T(W_{x,y}) of tilings of W_{x,y} by 1x2 and 2x1 dominos. In particular, for each fixed even integer w, determine explicitly the polynomial in x giving T(W_{x,x+w}), and incorporate the parity obstruction noted in the paper that when w is odd and x is large enough, W_{x,x+w} has no domino tilings.

Let Z(G)=\sum_M \prod_{e\in M} w(e), where M ranges over the perfect matchings of a finite edge-weighted graph G. Characterize the local replacements of a weighted subgraph of G by another weighted subgraph, with the rest of the graph unchanged, for which the resulting graph G' satisfies Z(G')=c\,Z(G) for a correction factor c determined explicitly from the local replacement data alone, including the special case c=1.

Let Q_n be the n-cube, i.e. the n-dimensional cube graph on 2^n vertices. Using the paper's convention that "matching" means "perfect matching," determine a formula, as a function of n, for the number of perfect matchings of Q_n.

Let a_n denote the number of matchings of the n-dimensional cube graph Q_n (that is, the number of subsets of edges of Q_n in which no two edges share a vertex). Lovasz's reflection-orbit argument gives the congruence a_n ≡ n (mod 2). Can one extend this argument to determine, for each fixed integer m >= 1, the residue class of a_n modulo 2^m for all n >= 1?

For every n ∈ ℕ and every complex matrix A ∈ C^{n×n}, write A[α,β]=det A(α,β) for minors of submatrices indexed by α,β ⊆ {1,…,n} with |α|=|β|, and call A[α,β] almost principal if its dispersal |α|−|α∩β| equals 1. If A is a strict GKK matrix, meaning that A is a P-matrix (all principal minors A[α,α] are positive) and A[α,β]A[β,α] > 0 for every almost principal minor, must A be positive stable (that is, must every eigenvalue of A have positive real part)? More specifically, if A is also a τ-matrix in the sense that l(B):=min(σ(B)∩R) with min ∅ := ∞, A satisfies l(A(α,α)) ≤ l(A(β,β)) < ∞ whenever ∅ ≠ β ⊆ α, and l(A) ≥ 0, must A be positive stable? ([people.math.wisc.edu](https://people.math.wisc.edu/hans/paper_archive/other_papers/hs144.pdf))

For each n in N, determine the least integer d=d(n) such that the following implication holds: if A in C^{n x n} is a P-matrix (that is, every principal minor A[gamma]:=det A(gamma,gamma) is positive) and, for every pair of index sets alpha,beta subseteq {1,...,n} with |alpha|=|beta| and dispersal |alpha|-|alpha∩beta| <= d, the minors satisfy A[alpha,beta]A[beta,alpha] >= 0, then A is positive stable (equivalently, every eigenvalue of A has positive real part). Is this least sufficient threshold d(n) independent of n?

For each of the following classes C of complex square matrices, define C_{≤N} := {A in C : ord(A) ≤ N}: (1) the family {A_{m,k,t} : m,k are positive integers and t in (0,1)} in the notation of Holtz [11] as cited in this paper; (2) the class of GKK τ-matrices; (3) the class of GKK matrices; and (4) the class of τ-matrices. Here, for index sets α,β of equal size, A[α,β] denotes the corresponding minor and A[α] := A[α,α] a principal minor; a P-matrix is one with A[α] > 0 for all principal minors; a GKK matrix is a weakly sign-symmetric P-matrix, meaning A[α,β]A[β,α] ≥ 0 for every almost-principal minor; if l(B) := min(σ(B) ∩ R) with min(∅) := ∞, then A has eigenvalue monotonicity when l(A(α,α)) ≤ l(A(β,β)) < ∞ whenever ∅ ≠ β ⊆ α; and a τ-matrix is a P-matrix with eigenvalue monotonicity and l(A) ≥ 0. A matrix is positive stable if every eigenvalue has positive real part. Determine, for each class C, the maximal N such that every matrix in C_{≤N} is positive stable.

For each positive integer N and each of the following classes C of complex square matrices: (i) the family A_{n,k,t} introduced in Holtz [11], with n,k in N and 0 < t < 1; (ii) GKK tau-matrices; (iii) GKK matrices; and (iv) tau-matrices, let C_{<=N} denote the subclass of matrices in C whose order is at most N. Here a P-matrix is one with all principal minors positive; a GKK matrix is a weakly sign-symmetric P-matrix, meaning A[alpha,beta]A[beta,alpha] >= 0 for every almost principal minor A[alpha,beta]; and a tau-matrix is a P-matrix A such that l(A(alpha,alpha)) <= l(A(beta,beta)) < infinity whenever emptyset != beta subseteq alpha, and l(A) >= 0, where l(A) := min(sigma(A) intersect R) and min(emptyset) := infinity. Determine the largest positive integer N such that every matrix A in C_{<=N}, of order m, satisfies abs(arg(lambda - l(A))) <= pi/2 - pi/m for every eigenvalue lambda in sigma(A).

For a fixed positive integer N, let C_N denote the subclass of matrices of order at most N in one of the following classes C: (i) the family {A_{m,k,t} : m,k in N, t in (0,1)} defined in Holtz [11]; (ii) GKK tau-matrices; (iii) GKK matrices; or (iv) tau-matrices. Here matrices are complex and square; a GKK matrix means a weakly sign-symmetric P-matrix, and a tau-matrix means a P-matrix satisfying eigenvalue monotonicity l(A(alpha,alpha)) <= l(A(beta,beta)) < infinity whenever emptyset != beta subseteq alpha, together with l(A) >= 0, where l(A) := min(sigma(A) ∩ R) and min emptyset := infinity. Must every stable matrix A in C_N (that is, every A with sigma(A) contained in the open right half-plane) satisfy the spectral-angle inequality |arg(lambda - l(A))| <= pi/2 - pi/N for every eigenvalue lambda in sigma(A)?

Let ⟨n⟩ denote the set of all increasing sequences alpha with entries in {1,2,...,n}. For a matrix A in C^{n x n}, write A(alpha, alpha) for the corresponding principal submatrix and A[alpha] := det A(alpha, alpha), with the convention A[emptyset] := 1. Given n in N and a family of complex numbers (p_alpha) indexed by all nonempty alpha in ⟨n⟩, does there exist a complex n x n matrix A such that A[alpha] = p_alpha for every nonempty alpha in ⟨n⟩?

Let n be a positive integer and let A in C^{n x n}. For each subset alpha subseteq {1, ..., n}, write A[alpha] := det A(alpha, alpha), with A[emptyset] := 1. Call A a GKK tau-matrix if: (i) A is a P-matrix, i.e. A[alpha] > 0 for all alpha; (ii) A is weakly sign-symmetric, i.e. A[alpha, beta] A[beta, alpha] >= 0 whenever #alpha = #beta = #(alpha union beta) - 1; and (iii) with l(B) := min(sigma(B) intersect R) and min(emptyset) := infinity, one has eigenvalue monotonicity l(A(alpha, alpha)) <= l(A(beta, beta)) < infinity for every nonempty beta subseteq alpha subseteq {1, ..., n}, and also l(A) >= 0. For j = 0, ..., n, define c_j := (sum over all alpha with #alpha = j of A[alpha]) / binom(n, j). Must every GKK tau-matrix satisfy Newton's inequalities c_j^2 >= c_{j-1} c_{j+1} for each j = 1, ..., n - 1?

For every n ≥ 1 and every n×n M-matrix A (in the standard matrix-theoretic sense), define c_j(A) := (1 / binom(n,j)) sum_{α⊆{1,...,n}, |α|=j} det A(α,α) for j=0,...,n, with c_0(A)=1 via A[∅]:=1. Must A satisfy the Newton inequalities c_j(A)^2 ≥ c_{j-1}(A)c_{j+1}(A) for every j=1,...,n−1? ([people.math.wisc.edu](https://people.math.wisc.edu/hans/paper_archive/other_papers/hs144.pdf))

Let n be a positive integer and let A ∈ C^{n x n}. For each j = 0,...,n, define c_j(A) := (1 / binom(n,j)) sum_{α ⊆ {1,...,n}, |α| = j} A[α], where A[α] = det A(α,α) is the principal minor indexed by α and A[∅] := 1.
